locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Stonehenge Avenue
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A processional way of two parallel banks with outside ditches, from the north-east entrance of Stonehenge along the solstice axis for about 530 m, then curving east across Stonehenge Bottom and King Barrow Ridge and down to the River Avon at West Amesbury, about 2.7 km in all. Built in Stage 3.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Course: from the OSM tracing of the ditch-bounded polygons (good to about 5-10 m). The first 35 m (from the earthwork entrance to the start of the mapped polygons) and the last 190 m to the West Amesbury henge are straight EXTRAPOLATIONS. Width: corridor about 12 m between banks, ditches about 20 m apart (EH 2010; OSM polygons 23 m); bank size is modelled. Date: antler picks 2345-2200 BCE, Darvill 2430-2200 BCE; modelled 2315 BCE; built here 2400-2300. No earlier first stretch is attested in the sources read (Parker Pearson argues natural periglacial stripes under it were followed; this does not date a built Avenue). Banks were already low in 1625 (lowered from year 1 CE by convention); ploughing levelled much of it after Stukeley's time.

phases.label: Avenue: fresh chalk
phases.dateNote: Darvill et al. 2012 Stage 3 (2480-2280); EH: antlers 2345-2200 BCE; modelled 2315 BCE, built within 2400-2300 BCE here.

phases.label: Avenue: weathering
phases.dateNote: Weathering (chalk showing through patchy turf) is a modelled convention.

phases.label: Avenue: grassed
phases.dateNote: Grassed by this date (modelled).

phases.label: Avenue: ploughed-down earthwork
phases.dateNote: Later ploughing and silting are undated; lowering at year 1 CE is a convention. In 1625 the earthwork was a low, partly ploughed-down bank; it was ploughed further after 1625.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Durrington Walls henge
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: The largest henge in Britain: a circular enclosure about 500 m across with a huge outer bank about 3 m high and a deep ditch, built c. 2480-2450 BCE over the line of an earlier ring of timber posts, beside the Neolithic village on the slope to the Avon.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Position (centre +/-60 m) and outline are an ELLIPSE (466 x 490 m, Gazetteer of Great Britain), NOT a surveyed outline. Ditch about 5.5 m deep, 18 m wide at the top, 7 m at the base (Wikipedia; Current Archaeology gives other figures); modelled ditch 14 m wide, bank 25 m wide and 3 m high (up to 30 m wide in Wikipedia). Entrances: sources CONFLICT (N, S and E, with N and S blocked 2-3 centuries later, per Current Archaeology; Wikipedia lists NW and SE). The first reading is drawn, with entrances 14 m wide (unsourced). In 1625 the earthwork is shown ploughed down (bank 1.8 m): that change is undated and a convention.

phases.label: Henge dug: fresh chalk, three entrances
phases.dateNote: Completed c. 2480-2450 BCE along the old post-pit line (Current Archaeology / Bristol). Modelled 2460 BCE.

phases.label: Henge weathering
phases.dateNote: Weathering is a modelled convention.

phases.label: Henge grassed, N and S entrances blocked (east entrance only)
phases.dateNote: N and S entrances blocked two or three centuries later (c. 2250 BCE, modelled).

phases.label: Ploughed-down earthwork
phases.dateNote: Ploughing is undated; the lowered bank at year 1 CE is a convention.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Durrington Walls timber ring (beneath the later bank)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A great ring of up to about 300 timber posts, roughly 5 m apart, 440-450 m across, enclosing the valley and village before the henge bank was raised along the same line.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Post pits are found by radar and excavation; the post height (about 5 m, Current Archaeology; Wikipedia says 7 m and 1.5 m diameter) and whether the ring was a palisade or free-standing posts are inferred. It lasted at most about 50 years, then the posts were pulled and the sockets packed with chalk (the 2015 'standing stones' claim was refuted in 2016). Drawn as a circle of radius 222 m; the real line may be oval.

phases.label: Timber ring of about 300 posts
phases.dateNote: Built c. 2490-2480 BCE, lasting up to about 50 years; posts pulled before the henge bank and ditch (c. 2480-2450 BCE). Years modelled.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Durrington Walls Southern Circle (timber)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A circular setting of concentric rings of timber posts inside the henge, oriented to midwinter sunrise (south-east), beside the settlement.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Position only +/-60-100 m (the Wikipedia text cannot be reconciled with the enclosure ellipse). Rings: the sources say four rings, later six; NO ring radii, post counts, sizes or heights are in anything read. The sizes drawn (six rings, outer ring 40 m across, posts 0.7 m thick and 5 m high) are borrowed by analogy from Woodhenge and are CONJECTURAL. Whether it was roofed is unknown. The end date is unknown; posts are shown rotting after 2400 BCE (a placeholder). It was not replaced by stone in anything read.

phases.label: Southern Circle of timber posts (illustrative)
phases.dateNote: Wikipedia: c. 2600 BCE with four rings, two more c. 200 years later; Current Archaeology: expanded with c. 200 posts c. 2480-2450 BCE. The accounts conflict; built here 2520-2500 BCE to match the settlement. Decay 2400-2300 BCE is a placeholder.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Durrington Walls Northern Circle (timber)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A smaller timber circle found by Wainwright in 1966 just north of the Southern Circle.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Nothing is known of its rings, posts, date or end: the two rings of 9 and 12 m radius, 5 m posts and a position 90 m north of the Southern Circle are placeholders. Decay after 2400 BCE is a placeholder.

phases.label: Northern Circle of timber posts (illustrative)
phases.dateNote: Undated; shown with the Southern Circle (placeholder).

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Woodhenge (six oval rings of timber posts)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: Six concentric oval rings of timber posts (168 post-holes; outer ring 43 x 40 m), inside a ditch and bank 110 m across overall, with a single north-east entrance, near Durrington Walls.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: The 168 post-holes and the outer ring size are excavated. The split of posts between rings, the ring spacing, the post sizes and especially the HEIGHTS (up to 7.5 m, inferred) are modelled; whether the posts stood free, were roofed or lintelled is unknown (lintels are deliberately not drawn). The long-axis bearing of the ovals is not stated in anything read: 50 degrees (towards the NE entrance) is a visual choice. When the posts decayed or were removed is unknown: shown rotting 2350-2150 BCE as a placeholder, although the ditch is dated 2470-2000 BCE and use is reported c. 1800 BCE. Modern concrete markers are not shown.

phases.label: Woodhenge: six oval rings of timber posts
phases.dateNote: Ditch dated 2470-2000 BCE (Wikipedia); posts modelled erected 2470 BCE. Decay is a placeholder.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Woodhenge ditch and bank
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: The ditch (up to 12 m wide, 2.4 m deep) and bank (10 m wide, 1 m high) enclosing Woodhenge, 110 m across overall, with a north-east entrance.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Overall diameter, widths and heights are from Wikipedia; whether the bank lay outside the ditch is assumed (outer, as for a henge); the ditch radius (38 m) is derived from 110 m overall. Entrance width (20 degrees) is a visual choice. Ploughing and levelling are mentioned but undated; the low grassed bank in 1625 is a modelling choice.

phases.label: Woodhenge ditch and bank: fresh chalk
phases.dateNote: Ditch dated 2470-2000 BCE (Wikipedia); built 2480-2470 BCE here.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Coneybury henge
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: An oval ditched enclosure about 45 x 55 m south-east of Stonehenge, excavated in the 1980s; the ditch was about 4 m wide and 3 m deep. Levelled by ploughing.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: NO absolute date was found: the 2700 BCE start is a placeholder (pottery from the early Neolithic to the Middle Bronze Age). Whether it had a bank, inside or outside, is not documented (none drawn). Orientation of the oval is unknown (drawn long axis east-west). The levelling is thought to be medieval ridge-and-furrow ploughing: shown decaying 1200-1500 CE as a placeholder. The Coneybury Anomaly pit (early Neolithic, 12 m NW) is not drawn.

phases.label: Coneybury henge: fresh chalk
phases.dateNote: Placeholder date; no absolute date retrieved.

phases.label: Coneybury henge: weathering
phases.dateNote: Weathering is a modelled convention.

phases.label: Coneybury henge: grassed, silting ditch

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: West Amesbury henge and 'Bluestonehenge'
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: On the Avon bank at the end of the Avenue: a circle of about 25 stones (probably bluestones, from the shape of the sockets), later removed, then a small henge (ditch about 25 m across, outer bank).
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Only stone sockets survive; their stones are inferred to be bluestones, ring about 10 m across, up to about 27 sockets (25 drawn). Erection date UNCERTAIN (Wikipedia 3400-2500 BCE from two arrowheads; 3000 BCE is a guess); the stones were removed 2469-2286 BCE (antler dates), perhaps to Stonehenge (unproven); the ditch and outer bank c. 2400 BCE. 'Ditch about 25 m wide' is taken as the ring's diameter. Position is approximate (OSM: 'approximate location from photos').

phases.label: Circle of about 25 stones (bluestones inferred)
phases.dateNote: Erection date a guess (3000 BCE; Wikipedia range 3400-2500 BCE). Removal dated 2469-2286 BCE; 2400 BCE modelled.

phases.dateNote: Ditch and outer bank c. 2400 BCE (Wikipedia).

phases.label: Small henge: weathering

phases.label: Small henge: grassed, faint bank
phases.dateNote: Still a faint bank by 1625 (modelling choice).

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Cuckoo Stone
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A squat sarsen set up in a pit between Woodhenge and Durrington Walls, with cremations around it c. 2000 BCE. It lies fallen today.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: No dimensions are in the sources read: 1.8 x 1.2 m and 1.3 m high are INVENTED to suit 'squat'. It was erected before 2000 BCE (2800 BCE is a placeholder); a post first stood in the socket. When it fell is unknown, so it is drawn standing throughout; it may have fallen at any time before 1625.

phases.label: Cuckoo Stone standing
phases.dateNote: Erected before 2000 BCE (Wikipedia); 2800 BCE is a placeholder.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Normanton Down barrows
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A cemetery of round barrows on the ridge south of Stonehenge, burials roughly 2600-1600 BCE; about 35 survived in 1957. 33 round barrows are drawn.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Burials span roughly 2600-1600 BCE; Wilsford G7 is probably 2000-1800 BCE. Bush Barrow has its own landmark. Barrow positions are from OpenStreetMap outlines; every FORM is generic (bowl) and the sizes are only the mapped outlines' equivalent circles (clamped to 8-40 m, heights assumed): OSM gives no bell, disc or saucer forms, and Wikipedia says Normanton Down has bells, many discs, a saucer and a pond without saying which. Which barrow was raised when within 2200-1500 BCE is not known: the three build phases assign each barrow to a period by a fixed pseudo-random rule, so the SEQUENCE shown is illustrative. Tier is set by the group's centre.

phases.label: Normanton Down barrows: first barrows (fresh chalk)
phases.dateNote: Burials roughly 2600-1600 BCE (Wikipedia); first barrows modelled from 2200 BCE (placeholder), later barrows to 1550.

phases.label: Normanton Down barrows: more barrows added
phases.dateNote: Barrows added in this period are drawn in fresh chalk; the older ones are grassed.

phases.label: Normanton Down barrows: later barrows added
phases.dateNote: As above.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Old and New King Barrows (King Barrow Ridge)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: Early Bronze Age round barrows along King Barrow Ridge, where the Avenue climbs the ridge (Old and New King Barrows together). 18 round barrows are drawn.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Early Bronze Age only (EH); no dates or counts retrieved beyond the mapped outlines. Old and New King Barrows are merged into one landmark here. Barrow positions are from OpenStreetMap outlines; every FORM is generic (bowl) and the sizes are only the mapped outlines' equivalent circles (clamped to 8-40 m, heights assumed): OSM gives no bell, disc or saucer forms, and Wikipedia says Normanton Down has bells, many discs, a saucer and a pond without saying which. Which barrow was raised when within 2200-1500 BCE is not known: the three build phases assign each barrow to a period by a fixed pseudo-random rule, so the SEQUENCE shown is illustrative. Tier is set by the group's centre.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: The richest Early Bronze Age burial near Stonehenge (gold lozenge, daggers), c. 1950 BCE, 3.3 m high and 49 m across overall, excavated by Cunnington in 1808 (after the period shown).
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Date c. 1950 BCE (Wessex culture). Position identified by coordinates within 5 m of a mapped outline. Form shown as a bowl barrow 40 m across with a 2.5 m ditch: the sources give overall diameter (49 m, or 40 m wide) and height only, not the form.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Vespasian's Camp hillfort
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: An Iron Age hillfort of about 14 ha on a spur above the Avon, 730 m north-south, with a bank up to 40 m wide and 6 m above the ditch floor, a ditch 10 m wide and an outer counterscarp bank (defences 68 m wide in all).
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: The CONSTRUCTION DATE IS A PLACEHOLDER: nothing retrieved says more than 'Iron Age' (700-600 BCE shown). The ring is the OSM outline of the rampart, re-sampled to 24 points; no entrance gap is drawn (none known). Bank 25 m wide and 4 m high above ground are modelled from the dimensions quoted (6 m above the ditch floor); the counterscarp is not drawn. The name is Camden's (16th century), not Roman. A medieval road over the hilltop and the 18th-century landscaping are not drawn.

phases.label: Hillfort rampart: fresh chalk
phases.dateNote: Placeholder date: Iron Age, 700-600 BCE.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Amesbury Abbey (nunnery, then Fontevraud priory)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: A Benedictine nunnery said to be founded c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth; dissolved by Henry II in 1177 and refounded as a Fontevraud priory; dissolved at the Dissolution (1539 or 1540) and demolished, the estate going to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Dates: foundation c. 979, 1177 refoundation (Wikipedia); the Dissolution is given as 1540 (Amesbury article) while the brief says 1539: 1540 is used. The BUILDINGS are unknown: no plan, no precinct boundary (the geography notes give only a placeholder rectangle), and no source for the conventual church's form or position. The church here is a generic stand-in, placed beside the parish church (about 45 m west of it): the parish church St Mary and St Melor may itself be the surviving priory church (Wikipedia). The 979 church and the 1177 priory church are drawn identically because nothing says the fabric changed. The date of demolition after the Dissolution is unknown; shown decaying until 1580 as a placeholder.

phases.label: Benedictine nunnery church (form unknown)
phases.dateNote: Founded c. 979 (Wikipedia); the building date of the church is a placeholder.

phases.label: Fontevraud priory church (form unknown)
phases.dateNote: Refounded 1177 as a Fontevraud priory; dissolved c. 1539-1540 (sources differ). Demolition and removal of materials undated; gone by 1580 is a placeholder.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Parish church of St Mary and St Melor, Amesbury
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: The Grade I parish church of Amesbury, which may be the surviving priory church. It survived the demolition of the priory.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: The sources read give no date for the building and no plan: shown from 1177 as a placeholder and drawn as a generic aisled church with a west tower (the real form and any 1625 alterations are not modelled). Whether it is the priory church or an earlier parish church is unresolved.

phases.label: Parish church (generic form)
phases.dateNote: Placeholder: the date of the fabric is not in the sources read.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Amesbury Abbey house (Seymour, 16th century)
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: After the Dissolution the Crown granted the estate to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford, whose family held it until 1675. A Seymour house stood here in the 16th century.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: NO description, plan or date of any 16th-century house is in the sources read. The 1661 and 1834-40 mansions are later than the timeline. The position is the OSM point for the present Amesbury Abbey house, the form is a generic hall, and the 1560 date is a placeholder.

phases.label: Seymour house (generic hall, form unknown)
phases.dateNote: Granted to Seymour in the 1540s; house date a placeholder.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: River Avon
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: The Hampshire (Wiltshire) Avon flowing south from Bulford past Durrington and Amesbury, round Vespasian's Camp and West Amesbury, about 10 km of the river within the modelled area. The Avenue ends on its bank at West Amesbury.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: The course is the MODERN centreline (OSM) with side channels and water meadows omitted; the prehistoric and medieval channel will have meandered differently, and the course was changed by water-meadow works. Width 10 m is an estimate, not tagged in OSM. Alder-hazel carr and sedge fringed the floodplain in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, and channel sedimentation rose with clearance c. 800-500 BCE (not modelled).

phases.label: River Avon (modern course)
phases.dateNote: Always present; the course shown is modern.

locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.name: Roman building near the Cuckoo Stone
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.summary: Excavation south-west of the Cuckoo Stone found a small rectangular Roman building with coins, thought a probable shrine.
locations/stonehenge/landmarks.json.uncertainty: Only existence and rough position (south-west of the stone) are attested. Size (12 x 7 m), form, roof and the dates (100-410 CE) are PLACEHOLDERS; it is drawn as a generic hall. Other Roman-period activity (coins and pottery at the stones, a settlement near the Avon, arable colluviation) is not drawn.

phases.label: Small Roman building (generic form)
phases.dateNote: Roman Britain 43-410 CE; building dates not known.

national/places-wales.json.name: Bryn Celli Ddu
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Neolithic passage tomb on Anglesey under a mound about 26 m across, with a passage aligned on the midsummer sunrise. Cadw describes an earlier bank-and-ditch enclosure with a stone circle on the same spot.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The dates are approximate (around 3000 BC is the usual estimate) and come from general knowledge, not from the Cadw page, which gives no years. Whether a henge really preceded the tomb is disputed; the end of use is not dated.

national/places-wales.json.name: Barclodiad y Gawres
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Neolithic passage tomb on the west coast of Anglesey. Several stones carry zig-zags and spirals like those in Irish tombs; Cadw notes Bryn Celli Ddu is the only other tomb in the UK with such art.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: No radiocarbon date is cited here; about 3000 BC is the conventional estimate by analogy with the Irish tombs. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Pentre Ifan
national/places-wales.json.summary: The best-preserved Neolithic portal dolmen in Wales: a capstone of about 16 tonnes on three uprights, once at the end of a cairn some 30 m long. Excavated by W. F. Grimes in 1936-7.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Not closely dated. Coflein says the Nevern valley dolmens were built about 6,000 years ago; Cadw says the capstone has stood for over 5,000 years. The start date here is a middle estimate and the end of use is a guess.

national/places-wales.json.name: Tre'r Ceiri
national/places-wales.json.summary: A stone-walled hillfort at about 480 m on Yr Eifl in Llŷn, crowded with some 150 round and sub-rectangular huts. Excavation shows it was probably built in the later Iron Age and stayed in use until at least the 4th century AD.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein gives only 'later Iron Age' for the foundation and 'at least the 4th century' for the end; the years 200 BC and AD 400 are placeholders for those phrases. A Bronze Age cairn on the summit is older than the fort.

national/places-wales.json.name: Great Orme copper mines

phases.label: Mines disused
phases.note: Mining resumed here in the late 17th century, after this timeline ends.

national/places-wales.json.summary: Bronze Age copper mines in the limestone of the Great Orme, with kilometres of tunnels dug with bone and stone tools. Nineteen radiocarbon dates span about 1700-900 BC; a 2019 study argues for a boom about 1600-1400 BC that supplied metal across Britain and as far as the Baltic.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The boom model rests on metal chemistry and is one research group’s reading. Radiocarbon dates give ranges, not years. The marker is placed at the mine site from general knowledge of its position (Pleiades and Wikidata give only the headland).

national/places-wales.json.name: Parys Mountain

phases.label: No mining known
phases.note: Large-scale mining began in 1768, after this timeline ends.

national/places-wales.json.summary: A copper-bearing hill in north Anglesey. Hammerstones and charcoal found in old workings point to Early Bronze Age mining; Roman working is inferred from stamped copper ingots found on Anglesey and Pleiades lists it as a Roman mine.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Weakly evidenced. The Bronze Age dates are radiocarbon ranges recalled from the literature, not fetched; Roman mining is an inference with no dated workings, and its start and end years are placeholders. Later opencast mining destroyed much of the evidence.

national/places-wales.json.name: Llyn Cerrig Bach
national/places-wales.json.summary: A small lake in west Anglesey where more than 150 iron and bronze objects, including chariot fittings, swords, spearheads and slave chains, were found in peat in 1942-3 during airfield building. They are read as offerings made over several centuries.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The objects were recovered from dredged peat, not excavated, so the span of deposition (about 300 BC to AD 100 on the style of the objects) is approximate, and any link with the Roman attack on Anglesey in AD 60 is conjecture. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Castell Henllys
national/places-wales.json.summary: A small inland promontory fort in north Pembrokeshire, about 88 by 74 m, excavated over many seasons. The main gateway was begun in the 5th century BC; occupation inside ended about the turn of the era, when a settlement was set up in the annexe.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein mentions a possible late or post-Roman reoccupation, which is not shown. The end date of the annexe settlement is a guess.

national/places-wales.json.name: Caerleon

phases.label: Legionary fortress of Legio II Augusta

national/places-wales.json.summary: One of three permanent legionary fortresses in Roman Britain, base of the Second Augustan Legion from about AD 75, with baths, barracks and an amphitheatre still visible. A Norman castle and small borough followed in the late 11th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Pleiades gives c. AD 75-300 for the legion’s base; how much of the legion remained after the late 3rd century, and what happened here between about 400 and the Norman castle (recorded in Domesday Book; 1086 is that date, recalled from general knowledge), is poorly known.

national/places-wales.json.name: Segontium
national/places-wales.json.summary: The main Roman fort of north-west Wales, founded under Agricola about AD 77 for a 1,000-strong auxiliary regiment and linked by road to Chester and Caerleon. Coins show it was held until about 394, longer than any other fort in Wales.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Cadw gives about AD 394 for the end, from coins; Pleiades gives c. 338. The later date is used here.

national/places-wales.json.name: Carmarthen
national/places-wales.json.summary: The westernmost town of Roman Britain, Moridunum, capital of the Demetae, with an amphitheatre. A royal castle was founded on the Tywi in the early 12th century and the borough became the centre of English royal government in south-west Wales.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Pleiades confirms only that Moridunum was the civitas capital of the Demetae. The fort date (c. AD 75), the change to a town (early 2nd century), the castle date (1109) and the claim that Carmarthen was the largest Welsh town in the later Middle Ages come from general knowledge. Continuity between about 400 and 1100 is not demonstrated.

national/places-wales.json.name: Caerwent

phases.label: Venta Silurum, town of the Silures

national/places-wales.json.summary: The Roman market town and administrative centre of the Silures, founded about AD 75-80. Its town walls, among the best preserved in northern Europe, still surround the village.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The town was small by the standards of Roman Britain (about 18 hectares). The pace of decline after the late 4th century is not well dated; an early medieval church community is recorded here but not shown as a separate phase.

national/places-wales.json.name: Dolaucothi gold mines

phases.label: Workings disused
phases.note: Documented mining resumed about 1853, after this timeline ends.

national/places-wales.json.summary: The only known Roman gold mine in Britain, at Pumsaint in Carmarthenshire: opencasts, adits and long aqueducts spread over at least a kilometre, beside a Roman fort.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein says only that several features are thought to be Roman or earlier. Mining probably began soon after the conquest of the area in the 70s AD, but neither the start nor the end is dated and pre-Roman working is possible. The years are placeholders.

national/places-wales.json.name: Nidum
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Roman auxiliary fort on the west bank of the river Neath. Excavation shows a first fort of about AD 75-80, a smaller one of 80-90 held until about 125, reoccupation from about 140 to 170 and a late military phase about 275-320.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: All dates are the excavators’ brackets as summarised by Coflein.

national/places-wales.json.name: Abergavenny
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Roman fort guarding the Usk valley road, known as Gobannium. A Norman lord built a castle and priory here in the late 11th century and a walled market town grew beside them.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Pleiades confirms only a fort and civil settlement. The fort’s dates (founded in the late 50s AD, given up in the 2nd century) and the castle date (c. 1087) are from general knowledge and are approximate.

national/places-wales.json.name: Usk
national/places-wales.json.summary: Site of an early legionary fortress, Burrium, built in the mid-50s AD during the war against the Silures and given up when the legion moved; Caerleon replaced it about AD 75. A Norman castle and planted borough followed in the 12th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Pleiades confirms only a Roman fort. The fortress dates (c. AD 55-67), the later small fort and the castle date are from general knowledge; the later two are rough.

national/places-wales.json.name: Canovium

phases.label: Auxiliary fort at the Conwy crossing

national/places-wales.json.summary: A Roman auxiliary fort at Caerhun, guarding the crossing of the Conwy on the road from Chester to Caernarfon. It was occupied, with breaks, from Agricola’s campaign of AD 77/8 into the 4th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The breaks in occupation are not shown, and the end date is a placeholder for ‘the 4th century’.

national/places-wales.json.name: Tomen y Mur
national/places-wales.json.summary: An upland Roman fort in Meirionnydd with a rare set of surrounding earthworks: a small amphitheatre, parade ground, bath-house and practice camps. A castle mound was later raised inside it.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein dates the fort to the late 1st century, ‘occupied into the 2nd century if not later’, and the mound to the 12th or 13th century, possibly after Norman armies camped here in the late 11th or early 12th. The years used are placeholders within those ranges.

national/places-wales.json.name: Y Gaer, Brecon
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Roman fort west of Brecon, founded about AD 75 where two main roads met and garrisoned by a Spanish cavalry regiment, the Vettones.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The foundation date is Cadw’s. The end date is a guess; later Roman use was intermittent. The position is from general knowledge of the site.

national/places-wales.json.name: St Davids
national/places-wales.json.summary: The monastery founded by St David in the 6th century became the leading church of Wales and, under Norman bishops from 1115, a cathedral. The present church was begun in 1181; a 12th-century pope ruled two pilgrimages here equal to one to Rome, and Bishop Henry de Gower built the great palace in 1328-47.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Nothing of the early monastery has been found and its foundation date is traditional. Only the papal privilege and the palace dates come from the Cadw page; 1115 (first Norman bishop) and 1181 (present cathedral begun) are from general knowledge. The shrine was dismantled at the Reformation, which is not shown as a phase.

national/places-wales.json.name: Llantwit Major

phases.label: Monastery and school of St Illtud

national/places-wales.json.summary: Llanilltud Fawr, the monastery of St Illtud in the Vale of Glamorgan, was remembered as the great school of early Christian Wales; the 7th-century Life of St Samson is the earliest witness. Carved stones of the 9th-11th centuries commemorate kings of Glywysing.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The foundation date follows the Dictionary of Welsh Biography’s floruit for Illtud (c. 475-525) and is approximate. No early monastic buildings have been found. The Norman takeover date is rounded.

national/places-wales.json.name: Bangor

phases.label: Monastery and bishop’s seat of St Deiniol

national/places-wales.json.summary: A monastery founded by St Deiniol in the 6th century, the seat of the bishops of Gwynedd. The cathedral was rebuilt in stone in the 12th century and damaged in the wars of 1211, 1282 and 1402.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives Deiniol’s death as 584 and notes it may really be 572; the foundation year is a guess within his lifetime. The 12th-century rebuilding and the war damage are from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Llandaff
national/places-wales.json.summary: A church on the Taff associated with Saints Teilo, Dyfrig and Euddogwy. Bishop Urban began the present cathedral in 1120 and the Book of Llandaff was compiled to back its claims.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The early history rests on 12th-century documents written to support the bishopric; the start date is a placeholder. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Deganwy

phases.label: Stronghold of the kings of Gwynedd

national/places-wales.json.summary: Twin hills above the Conwy estuary: by tradition the seat of Maelgwn, king of Gwynedd, in the 6th century. It was burnt by lightning in 812 and destroyed by the English in 822. Robert of Rhuddlan held it in the late 11th century; Henry III built a great castle in 1245-50, which Llywelyn ap Gruffudd destroyed in 1263.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The link with Maelgwn is tradition supported by 5th-6th-century imported pottery; the start date is a placeholder. Coflein notes the borough was still active in 1305, which is not shown.

national/places-wales.json.name: Dinefwr

phases.label: Chief castle of the princes of Deheubarth
English royal castle and small borough

national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle above the Tywi near Llandeilo, thought to have been founded in the later 12th century by the Lord Rhys and remembered as the principal court of Deheubarth. The standing remains are 13th and early 14th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The Welsh law-books name Dinefwr as the chief court of the south, but no remains older than the 12th century are known, so no earlier phase is shown. The dates 1165 and 1277 (taken by Edward I) are from general knowledge; Coflein says it was still maintained in the early 15th century and may have been replaced by Newton House later that century.

national/places-wales.json.name: Mathrafal

phases.label: Enclosure and mound, by tradition the court of Powys

national/places-wales.json.summary: An earthwork enclosure and mound on the river Banwy, named in later tradition as the chief court of the kings of Powys.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Excavation in 1989 did not find an early medieval royal site: the mound belongs with an oval enclosure filled in by about 1310-1430, the square enclosure was built after about 1200, and the ‘royal court’ tradition is traced only to the mid 13th century. It is shown here only for its 13th-century phase.

national/places-wales.json.name: Aberffraw

phases.label: Chief court of the kings and princes of Gwynedd

national/places-wales.json.summary: By tradition the chief seat of the kings of Gwynedd, on the west coast of Anglesey; the princes styled themselves ‘prince of Aberffraw’ in the 13th century. The settlement declined after a great storm in 1331 altered the coast.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein reports the royal seat as tradition. The position of the llys within the village is not securely established and the start date is a placeholder; documentary references begin in the 7th-9th centuries.

national/places-wales.json.name: Dinas Emrys

phases.label: Stone tower of the princes of Gwynedd

national/places-wales.json.summary: A rocky stronghold above Nant Gwynant, the legendary site of Vortigern’s fortress and Merlin’s dragons. Excavations in 1910 and 1954-6 found Iron Age, Roman and early medieval occupation; a stone tower was added at the end of the 12th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The phases of occupation are not closely dated and the years are placeholders. The Vortigern story is 9th-century legend.

national/places-wales.json.name: Llangorse crannog
national/places-wales.json.summary: The only crannog (artificial island) known in Wales, built in Llangorse Lake for the king of Brycheiniog from timbers felled between AD 889 and 893. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that a Mercian army sent by Æthelflæd destroyed ‘Brecenanmere’ in 916 and took the king’s wife captive.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The identification of ‘Brecenanmere’ with the crannog is probable, not certain.

national/places-wales.json.name: Dinas Powys hillfort
national/places-wales.json.summary: A small defended hilltop near Cardiff, excavated by Leslie Alcock in the 1950s. Imported Mediterranean and Gaulish pottery, glass and fine metalworking show a wealthy household of the 5th to 7th centuries.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The dating of the ramparts has been revised more than once and the end date is approximate. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Pillar of Eliseg

phases.label: Inscribed memorial cross of the kings of Powys

national/places-wales.json.summary: The shaft of a 9th-century cross near Llangollen, set up by Cyngen, king of Powys (died 854/5), in honour of his great-grandfather Eliseg. Its long Latin inscription, now illegible, traced the dynasty’s descent.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Cadw’s page dates the pillar only to the 9th century; the attribution to Cyngen depends on a transcript of the inscription made in 1696, and the year shown is a placeholder within his reign.

national/places-wales.json.name: Chepstow

phases.label: Castle and borough at the Wye crossing

national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle on a cliff above the Wye, begun in 1067 by William fitz Osbern, earl of Hereford, and one of the first Norman strongholds in Wales. Its great tower is among the oldest stone castle buildings in Britain; a walled port town grew beside it.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Some scholars date the great tower to William I’s visit of 1081 or later, not to fitz Osbern.

national/places-wales.json.name: Pembroke
national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle on a tidal promontory, established by the Normans about 1093-4 and never taken by the Welsh. The round great tower was built at the start of the 13th century; Henry Tudor, later Henry VII, was born here in 1457.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein gives ‘about 1094’ for the foundation. The link of the great tower with William Marshal and the birth of Henry VII are from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Cardiff
national/places-wales.json.summary: A series of Roman forts stood beside the Taff from the late 50s AD to the late 4th century. About 1081 William I set a castle inside the walls of the last fort, and the borough beside it became the head of the lordship of Glamorgan and one of the larger towns in Wales.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The date of the stone fort (late 3rd century) and the size of the medieval town are from general knowledge; the Roman name is uncertain (Pleiades offers ‘Tamion?’). Nothing is known of the site between the 4th and 11th centuries.

national/places-wales.json.name: Caerphilly Castle
national/places-wales.json.summary: The largest castle in Wales, begun in 1268 by Gilbert de Clare, lord of Glamorgan, against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. Its concentric walls and wide artificial lakes were new to Britain.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The date by which the castle was ruinous is approximate (it was derelict when John Leland saw it in the 1530s).

national/places-wales.json.name: Dolwyddelan Castle

phases.label: Castle of the princes of Gwynedd

national/places-wales.json.summary: A stone keep guarding a route through Snowdonia, built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, ruler of Gwynedd from 1201 to 1240. It fell to Edward I in 1283, who refitted it.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The building date is not recorded; 1210 is a placeholder within Llywelyn’s reign. The castle was lived in again from the late 15th century, which is not shown.

national/places-wales.json.name: Castell y Bere

phases.label: Castle of the princes of Gwynedd, then English

national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle on a rock in the Dysynni valley, begun in 1221 by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth to guard the southern border of Gwynedd. It was taken by Edward I’s forces in 1283 and given up after the Welsh rising of 1294.

national/places-wales.json.name: Dolbadarn Castle

phases.label: Castle of the princes of Gwynedd

national/places-wales.json.summary: A round stone tower at the foot of the Llanberis pass, most likely built by Llywelyn ap Iorwerth in the late 12th or early 13th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Cadw gives only ‘late 12th or early 13th century’; 1210 is a placeholder. The end date reflects the removal of its timber to Caernarfon in 1284, a detail from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Criccieth Castle

phases.label: Castle of the princes of Gwynedd

national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle on a headland in Cardigan Bay. Llywelyn ap Iorwerth built the twin-towered gatehouse, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd added the outer ward, Edward I refitted it, and Owain Glyndŵr burnt it in 1404.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The first building date is not recorded; about 1230 is the usual estimate, from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Flint
national/places-wales.json.summary: The first of Edward I’s castles in Wales, begun in 1277 and largely finished by 1284, with a planned borough beside it. Richard II met Henry Bolingbroke here in 1399.

national/places-wales.json.name: Rhuddlan

phases.label: English burh, then Welsh royal seat

national/places-wales.json.summary: The lowest crossing of the Clwyd. Edward the Elder founded a burh here in 921; it was Gruffudd ap Llywelyn’s seat until 1063; Robert of Rhuddlan raised a motte in 1073. Edward I began the present concentric castle in 1277 and issued the Statute of Rhuddlan here in 1284.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Only the 1277 date comes from Cadw and the Statute from the Bodleian guide. The burh of ‘Cledemutha’ (921), Gruffudd’s court and the motte of 1073 are from general knowledge; the identification of Cledemutha with Rhuddlan is generally, not universally, accepted.

national/places-wales.json.name: Conwy

phases.label: Edward I’s castle and walled town

national/places-wales.json.summary: Edward I and Master James of St George built the castle and a 1.3 km circuit of town walls here between 1283 and 1287. The site had been the Cistercian abbey of Aberconwy, burial place of Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, which the king moved up the valley to Maenan.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The abbey phase (founded 1186, on this site from the 1190s) is from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Caernarfon

phases.label: Court of the princes of Gwynedd
Edward I’s castle and walled borough; seat of government for North Wales

national/places-wales.json.summary: Edward I began the castle and walled borough in 1283, with a quay, all at once; work lasted 47 years and was still unfinished about 1330. It was the centre of royal government in North Wales. The castle was in decay by the 16th century.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The Norman motte of about 1090 and the Welsh court that followed are from general knowledge and their dates are approximate.

national/places-wales.json.name: Harlech Castle
national/places-wales.json.summary: A concentric castle on a crag above Cardigan Bay, begun in May 1283 and largely complete by 1289. Owain Glyndŵr took it in 1404 and kept his court and family here until it was retaken in 1409; it fell again to the Yorkists in 1468 after a long siege.

national/places-wales.json.name: Beaumaris

phases.label: Edward I’s unfinished castle; borough and port

national/places-wales.json.summary: The last of Edward I’s Welsh castles, begun in 1295 after the rising of Madog ap Llywelyn. Money ran short and work petered out by the 1320s, leaving the towers below their planned height. The borough became the main port of Anglesey.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Glyndŵr’s supporters held it from 1403 for about two years, which is not shown as a phase.

national/places-wales.json.name: Kidwelly
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Norman ringwork of the early 12th century, rebuilt in stone as a concentric castle in the late 13th and 14th centuries. The Lord Rhys captured it in 1159.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Cadw gives only ‘early 12th century’; 1106 (the grant to Bishop Roger of Salisbury) is from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Montgomery
national/places-wales.json.summary: Henry III began the stone castle about 1223 against Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, replacing the nearby timber castle of Hen Domen. It withstood attacks in 1228, 1231 and 1245. The treaty that recognised Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales was sealed at the nearby ford in 1267.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The marker is at the stone castle; Hen Domen lies about 1.5 km north-west. Its foundation about 1071 by Roger of Montgomery is from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Dolforwyn Castle
national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle built by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1273 on a ridge above the Severn, in defiance of the king and facing royal Montgomery. Roger Mortimer took it in 1277 after a two-week siege.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Cadw says only that it was abandoned in the 14th century; the end year is a placeholder.

national/places-wales.json.name: Raglan Castle

phases.label: Fortress-palace of the Herberts and Somersets

national/places-wales.json.summary: A late medieval fortress-palace in Gwent. Sir William ap Thomas built the moated Great Tower about 1435 and his son William Herbert, earl of Pembroke, enlarged it.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: An earlier manor stood here; it is not shown.

national/places-wales.json.name: Denbigh

phases.label: De Lacy castle and walled borough

national/places-wales.json.summary: A Welsh princely residence of Dafydd ap Gruffudd, whose attack on Hawarden in 1282 set off Edward I’s final war. Henry de Lacy then built a large castle and walled town on the site; the half-built castle was captured in the rising of 1294.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The start date of the Welsh court is a placeholder. The position is from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Sycharth
national/places-wales.json.summary: A motte and bailey in the Cynllaith valley, the chief home of Owain Glyndŵr. A poem of about 1390 praises its fine timber hall on a green mound; it was burnt in 1403 and has no later history.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Coflein says the castle may be as early as the 12th century but direct evidence is lacking; the start date here marks only the 14th-century hall.

national/places-wales.json.name: Castell Dinas Brân

phases.label: Castle of the princes of Powys Fadog

national/places-wales.json.summary: A hilltop castle above Llangollen, built inside an Iron Age hillfort by the rulers of northern Powys in the 1260s and burnt by its own garrison before Edward I’s army in 1277.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The building date is an estimate. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Tintern Abbey
national/places-wales.json.summary: The first Cistercian abbey in Wales, founded in 1131 on the Wye. The great church was begun in 1269. The abbey surrendered in 1536 in the first round of the dissolution.

national/places-wales.json.name: Strata Florida Abbey
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Cistercian abbey in the Ceredigion uplands, founded in 1164 by a Norman lord and soon taken under the patronage of the Lord Rhys. The monks entered their new church in 1201. Welsh princes were buried here and it supported the Welsh cause; it closed by 1539.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The first community may have begun on a different site nearby before moving here in the 1180s; the marker is at the later abbey.

national/places-wales.json.name: Valle Crucis Abbey
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Cistercian abbey near Llangollen, founded in 1201 by Madog ap Gruffudd, prince of northern Powys, and named after the nearby Pillar of Eliseg. It was dissolved in 1537.

national/places-wales.json.name: Neath Abbey
national/places-wales.json.summary: Founded in 1130 by the Norman knight Richard de Granville; by the late 13th century one of the wealthiest abbeys in Wales.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The dissolution year (1539) and the abbey’s first affiliation to Savigny are from general knowledge; Cadw’s page gives neither.

national/places-wales.json.name: Margam Abbey
national/places-wales.json.summary: A Cistercian abbey founded about 1147 and dissolved in 1536, thought to stand on an earlier monastic site: early Christian carved stones were found around it. The western part of the nave survives as the parish church.

national/places-wales.json.name: Basingwerk Abbey
national/places-wales.json.summary: An abbey near Holywell on the Dee estuary, founded in 1131 and much rebuilt in the 13th century. Wat’s Dyke reaches the estuary close by.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The dissolution year is from general knowledge. The first community may have been at a different site nearby.

national/places-wales.json.name: Swansea

phases.label: Norman castle and borough of Gower

national/places-wales.json.summary: The castle at the mouth of the Tawe was founded in or soon after 1106 as the head of the Norman lordship of Gower; a borough and port grew beside it. The first castle was earth and timber, rebuilt in stone probably between 1221 and 1284.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Size is a rough judgement; medieval Swansea had perhaps 1,000-2,000 people. A Norse origin for the name is often suggested but no Viking-age settlement has been found.

national/places-wales.json.name: Haverfordwest
national/places-wales.json.summary: A castle founded about 1110 by Tancred, a Fleming, at the tidal limit of the Western Cleddau. The town below it became one of the largest and richest in medieval Wales.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The town’s later size is from general knowledge; it was made a county in itself in the late 15th or 16th century.

national/places-wales.json.name: Brecon

phases.label: Norman castle, priory and walled town

national/places-wales.json.summary: Bernard de Neufmarché defeated the king of Brycheiniog near here in 1093 and built a castle and a Benedictine priory (now the cathedral) at the meeting of the Usk and Honddu. A walled town followed.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The marker is at the priory church. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Wrexham

phases.label: Market settlement in the lordship of Bromfield

national/places-wales.json.summary: A market town on the Welsh side of the border, first recorded in the 12th century. It was never a chartered walled borough but by the 16th century was among the most populous towns in Wales.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The first mention (a castle at ‘Wristlesham’, 1161) and the growth of the town are from general knowledge; the phase dates are approximate.

national/places-wales.json.name: Aberystwyth
national/places-wales.json.summary: Edward I’s brother Edmund began the castle and borough in 1277, at first called Llanbadarn. Owain Glyndŵr held it from 1404 to 1408.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: An earlier castle of the same name stood about 2 km to the south. The Dictionary of Welsh Biography confirms Glyndŵr’s capture of Aberystwyth in 1404; the other dates are from general knowledge.

national/places-wales.json.name: Monmouth
national/places-wales.json.summary: William fitz Osbern built a castle where the Monnow meets the Wye soon after 1066; a priory and walled town followed. Henry V was born in the castle in 1386 or 1387. A Roman fort, Blestium, had stood here.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The Roman fort is not shown as a phase. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Machynlleth

phases.label: Market town
phases.note: Owain Glyndŵr is said to have held a parliament here in 1404.

national/places-wales.json.summary: A small market town in the Dyfi valley, with a market charter of 1291. By tradition Owain Glyndŵr was crowned Prince of Wales and held a parliament here in 1404.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The 1404 parliament rests on later tradition and a few contemporary references; the ‘Parliament House’ shown in the town is a later building. Dates here rest on general knowledge of the standard literature, not on a source fetched for this entry.

national/places-wales.json.name: Battle of Mynydd Carn
national/places-wales.json.summary: In 1081 Gruffudd ap Cynan, returning from exile in Ireland, and Rhys ap Tewdwr defeated and killed Trahaearn ap Caradog, Caradog ap Gruffudd and Meilyr ap Rhiwallon. The victory secured Gwynedd for Gruffudd’s line and Deheubarth for Rhys’s.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The battlefield has not been found. Sources place it a day’s march from St Davids at a hill with a cairn; the marker uses the grid reference in the Coflein record, which is one suggestion among several in Pembrokeshire.

national/places-wales.json.name: Battle of Crug Mawr
national/places-wales.json.summary: In 1136 Owain and Cadwaladr of Gwynedd with Gruffudd ap Rhys routed a Norman and Flemish army near Cardigan; many of the defeated drowned in the Teifi. It was the largest Welsh victory of the rising that followed Henry I’s death.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Gerald of Wales places the battle at the hill of Crug Mawr (probably Banc-y-Warren, used for the marker); a Welsh chronicle suggests it was fought nearer Cardigan castle and the river.

national/places-wales.json.name: Battle of Orewin Bridge
national/places-wales.json.summary: On 11 December 1282 the king’s forces with Roger Mortimer and Gruffudd ap Gwenwynwyn came on the Welsh army without warning near Builth. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, and his leading men were killed; native rule in Wales ended within months.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Only Walter of Guisborough gives a location (a bridge and ford on the Irfon), and his account resembles his own description of Stirling Bridge. The marker uses Coflein’s grid reference; where and how Llywelyn died is disputed.

national/places-wales.json.name: Battle of Bryn Glas
national/places-wales.json.summary: On 22 June 1402 Owain Glyndŵr’s men defeated the levies of Herefordshire at Pilleth in Maelienydd and captured Edmund Mortimer, who then joined Glyndŵr’s cause.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: Chronicles name the hill of Bryn Glas west of Pilleth church, but fieldwork there has found no trace of the fighting and other sources point to neighbouring hills.

national/places-wales.json.name: Battle of Bryn Derwin
national/places-wales.json.summary: In 1255 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd defeated his brothers Owain and Dafydd and became sole ruler of Gwynedd west of the Conwy, the first step toward his principality.
national/places-wales.json.uncertainty: The battlefield is not located; the marker is at the pass of Bwlch Derwin on the border of Arfon and Eifionydd, the usual identification, placed from general knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Stonehenge

phases.label: Circular ditch, bank and cremation cemetery

national/places.json.summary: The ditch and bank were dug about 3000 BCE and the great stones set up about 2500 BCE. The bluestones were rearranged two or three centuries later and the last known digging, the Y and Z holes, dates to 1800-1500 BCE.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Phase boundaries are rounded radiocarbon estimates. How long it stayed in active use after 1500 BCE is not known.

national/places.json.name: Durrington Walls

phases.label: Large seasonal settlement of the Stonehenge builders

national/places.json.summary: A very large late Neolithic settlement beside the Avon, later enclosed by Britain's largest henge. It is linked to the building of the sarsen phase at Stonehenge, 3 km away.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates are rounded from memory of the Stonehenge Riverside Project results (settlement about 2500 BCE, in use for only a few decades). Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Avebury

phases.label: Henge and stone circles under construction
Abandoned monument; a village grows inside it in the Middle Ages

national/places.json.summary: The largest stone circle in Britain, inside a huge henge ditch, built and altered from about 2850 to about 2200 BCE. Its monuments were abandoned around 1800 BCE.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Internal sequence of the circles and avenues is not closely dated.

national/places.json.name: Silbury Hill

phases.label: Completed mound; a Roman roadside settlement later lay at its foot

national/places.json.summary: The largest artificial prehistoric mound in Europe, probably raised over a short period between about 2470 and 2350 BCE. Its purpose is unknown.
national/places.json.uncertainty: No burial has been found; the function is a matter of conjecture.

national/places.json.name: West Kennet Long Barrow
national/places.json.summary: One of the largest Neolithic chambered tombs in Britain, built around 3650 BCE, used for at least a thousand years and blocked with great sarsens around 2000 BCE.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Construction date is a modelled radiocarbon estimate; the date of final blocking is approximate. Dates are English Heritage's round figures.

national/places.json.name: Windmill Hill

phases.label: Causewayed enclosure, a seasonal gathering place

national/places.json.summary: The largest known Neolithic causewayed enclosure, three rings of interrupted ditch on a low hill near Avebury.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Start date is a modelled estimate; the length of use is uncertain. Dates are English Heritage's figures: built around 3675 BCE, in use until around 2500 BCE, largely abandoned by the end of the third millennium.

national/places.json.name: Hambledon Hill
national/places.json.summary: A chalk spur in Dorset used twice: as a large early Neolithic enclosure complex and, three thousand years later, as a multivallate hillfort.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Both date ranges are approximate; the end of Iron Age occupation is not well fixed. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Cissbury
national/places.json.summary: Among the earliest flint mines in Britain, with over 200 shafts on the South Downs, later enclosed by one of the largest hillforts in Sussex.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The mines began around or soon after 4000 BCE; all four dates are rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Langdale axe quarries

phases.label: Stone axe quarries on Pike of Stickle

national/places.json.summary: High fell-side quarries whose green volcanic stone was made into polished axes found all over Britain.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date range is approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Castlerigg
national/places.json.summary: A ring of 38 stones among the Lake District fells, probably raised in the late Neolithic.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Never securely dated by excavation. English Heritage puts it at about 4,500 years ago; Aubrey Burl's case for about 3200 BCE, which would make it one of the earliest circles in Britain, is described there as not strongly supported.

national/places.json.name: Thornborough Henges
national/places.json.summary: Three large henges in a line across the Ure-Swale plain, the largest ritual complex between the Thames and Orkney.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Not closely dated. English Heritage says the three henges were built about 4,500 to 5,000 years ago, over an older cursus, and stayed a focus for burials into the early Bronze Age (a nearby timber row is put at 1800-1600 BCE). The end date here is a judgement.

national/places.json.name: Arbor Low

phases.label: Henge with a circle of limestone slabs

national/places.json.summary: A henge and recumbent stone circle on the White Peak limestone plateau.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Not closely dated. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Grime's Graves

phases.label: Mines disused; brief Bronze Age pit digging, then middens and a settlement from about 1400 BCE
Hollows in heathland; a hundred meeting place from about 939

national/places.json.summary: A field of more than 400 late Neolithic flint mine shafts in the Norfolk Breckland, worked from about 2600 to about 2100 BCE.

national/places.json.name: Holme timber circle (Seahenge)

phases.label: Timber circle around an upturned oak

national/places.json.summary: A ring of 55 split oak posts around an inverted tree stump, built on a saltmarsh. Tree rings show the timbers were felled in 2049 BCE.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The felling date is precise; how long the circle was used is unknown, so the end date is nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Flag Fen

phases.label: Timber causeway and platform being built
Causeway used for offerings of metalwork

national/places.json.summary: A kilometre-long post alignment and timber platform across the fen edge near Peterborough, built in stages between about 1365 and 967 BCE and used for ritual deposits long afterwards.
national/places.json.uncertainty: End of use is approximate (deposits continued for more than 1,200 years in all). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Must Farm

phases.label: Pile-dwelling settlement, burned within about a year

national/places.json.summary: A small late Bronze Age settlement of round houses on stilts over a fen channel, destroyed by fire very soon after it was built and preserved in the silt.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Built about 850 BCE; the year is approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Grimspound

phases.label: Walled Bronze Age settlement of 24 round houses
Abandoned as the upland climate worsened

national/places.json.summary: The best-known of the Bronze Age enclosed settlements on Dartmoor, part of a moor then divided by long field boundaries (reaves).
national/places.json.uncertainty: Never dated by modern excavation; the range is the conventional one. English Heritage gives 'probably late Bronze Age (about 1500-800 BC)' and notes the settlement pattern was changing by about 1000 BCE; there is still no radiocarbon date.

national/places.json.name: Uffington White Horse and Castle
national/places.json.summary: A 110 m stylised horse cut into the chalk of the Berkshire Downs, with an early Iron Age hillfort on the ridge above.
national/places.json.uncertainty: English Heritage reports the horse as dated to the later Bronze Age or Iron Age, between 1740 and 210 BCE; the start date used here sits inside that bracket and is not a measurement. The hillfort's 700 BCE start is from memory.

national/places.json.name: Maiden Castle

phases.label: Enlarged multivallate hillfort, over 100 round houses
Occupation shrinks to the eastern end
Romano-British temple inside the old ramparts

national/places.json.summary: The largest hillfort in Britain. In the middle Iron Age (about 400-120 BCE) it was the main settlement of southern Dorset; by the Roman invasion it was almost empty.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The story of a Roman assault in 44 CE is now questioned. The end of the temple is not dated; 430 is nominal.

national/places.json.name: Danebury
national/places.json.summary: The most thoroughly excavated hillfort in Britain, with streets of round houses and thousands of grain storage pits; perhaps 200-350 people lived inside.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Population is an excavator's estimate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Cadbury Castle

phases.label: Cleared by the Roman army; little occupation
Refortified hilltop with a great hall
Emergency burh and mint of Aethelred II

national/places.json.summary: A Somerset hillfort reoccupied on a large scale in the late 5th and 6th centuries, one of the strongest pieces of evidence for post-Roman British lordship in the south-west.
national/places.json.uncertainty: All dates are rounded from excavation reports recalled from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Glastonbury Lake Village

phases.label: Iron Age village on an artificial island

national/places.json.summary: A waterlogged Iron Age village in the Somerset Levels, exceptionally well preserved.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date range approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Hengistbury Head

phases.label: Promontory settlement behind the Double Dykes
Trade falls away after Caesar's Gallic wars

national/places.json.summary: The main known port of late Iron Age Britain before Caesar: Italian wine, glass and figs came in, and metals went out to Armorica.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The peak is inferred from wine amphorae, most of which predate 50 BCE. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Stanwick

phases.label: Vast earthwork enclosure of the Brigantes
Abandoned after the Roman conquest of the north

national/places.json.summary: Some 300 hectares of earthworks in North Yorkshire, probably the seat of the Brigantian rulers who were clients of Rome until about 69 CE.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The link to Queen Cartimandua is an inference; dates are approximate. English Heritage dates the ramparts to the 1st century CE, with occupation from the middle of the century and decline after 70; the start year 40 is approximate.

national/places.json.name: London

phases.label: Londinium founded beside a Thames bridge
Londinium, rebuilt after Boudica; chief town of the province
Lundenwic, a trading town on the Strand; bishopric from 604
Lundenburh: settlement returns inside the walls
Norman and medieval London, far the largest town in England
Jacobean London, roughly 200,000 people or more

national/places.json.summary: Founded about 47-50 CE, burned in 60/61, the largest town of Roman Britain, then almost deserted for two centuries. From the late 9th century it grew back inside its Roman walls and by 1377 had about three times as many taxpayers as any other English town.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Sizes are relative ranks, not populations. Descend into the London site for dated, sourced detail. Roman dates checked against the London Museum timeline (founded 47-50, burned 60-61, wall 200-220, end 400-410) and English Heritage (founded about 50, wall about 200). Post-Roman dates and all sizes still rest on Wikipedia and judgement.

national/places.json.name: Colchester

phases.label: Colonia Claudia Victricensis, first capital of the province
Roman walls with little urban life
Burh restored under Edward the Elder
Castle on the temple podium; cloth town

national/places.json.summary: The chief centre of late Iron Age Britain, then a legionary fortress and the first Roman colonia, burned by Boudica in 60/61. It was tenth among English towns in the 1377 poll tax.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Coin use ends in the early 5th century; what followed is obscure. Fortress (c. 44), colony (c. 49-50), the Boudican fire (60-1), walls built after the fire, 917 and the castle of the 1070s are from VCH Essex vol. 9. The 20 BCE start, the 275 step and the phase sizes are judgement.

national/places.json.name: St Albans

phases.label: Verlamion, a centre of the Catuvellauni
Rebuilt Verulamium, walled in the 3rd century
Roman town deserted; shrine of St Alban on the hill
Abbey of St Alban and market town

national/places.json.summary: The third great town of Roman Britain by tradition, burned by Boudica in 61. The medieval abbey and town grew on the hill outside the Roman walls, around the supposed grave of Britain's first martyr.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Roman occupation ended between about 400 and 450. The abbey's foundation by Offa about 793 is a later tradition. English Heritage confirms the Boudican destruction about 60 and a town wall built 265-270. Other dates, including Offa's foundation of the abbey (a later tradition), are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: York

phases.label: Eboracum, legionary fortress of the Ninth, then the Sixth Legion
Fortress and colonia, capital of Britannia Inferior
Eoforwic: Northumbrian bishopric (archbishopric 735) and trading settlement
Northern capital under English earls, then Norman castles and minster
Late medieval and Tudor York, seat of the Council of the North

national/places.json.summary: Founded as a legionary fortress in 71. Two emperors died here and Constantine was proclaimed here in 306. It was the Viking capital of the north from 866/7 to 954 and the second town of England in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The 5th and 6th centuries are almost blank. York had slipped to about fifteenth by wealth in the 1520s. 71, 627, 735, 866 and 954 are confirmed by VCH City of York, which attributes the colonia to Severus. Later rankings follow tax tables reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Lincoln

phases.label: Legionary fortress of the Ninth Legion
Reduced; a church stands in the old forum
Danish borough, one of the Five Boroughs
Norman castle and cathedral; a leading wool town

national/places.json.summary: A fortress of about 60 CE turned into a colonia for veterans, probably in 86. It revived under Danish rule and stood among the four or five largest English towns from Domesday to the 13th century.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The colonia date is the favoured estimate, not a recorded one. Whether Lincoln was a 4th-century provincial capital is debated. The move of the see to Lincoln in 1072 is confirmed by English Heritage. Roman and Danish dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Gloucester

phases.label: Minster of St Peter; later a Mercian burh
Refounded burh of Aethelflaed; royal crown-wearing place

national/places.json.summary: A colonia founded under Nerva at the lowest crossing of the Severn. It was eighth by Russell's Domesday estimate and seventeenth in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's capture of Gloucester in 577 is a late and doubtful record. The 679 and c. 900 dates are from memory. The minster of about 679-81, Aethelflaed's refoundation (fortified by 902-14, St Oswald's by 909) and the see of 1541 are from VCH Gloucester. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Chester

phases.label: Deva, legionary fortress: Second Legion Adiutrix from about 74, Twentieth Legion from about 90
Burh restored by Aethelflaed; port for Ireland
County palatine capital and base for the conquest of north Wales
Cathedral city; the Dee is silting

national/places.json.summary: Begun in the mid 70s as the largest legionary fortress in Britain and held until the late 4th or early 5th century. Refortified in 907, it became the seat of a Norman marcher earldom.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The date of the legion's departure is not known. 74, about 90 and 907 are from VCH Cheshire; 1071 for the earldom is from memory.

national/places.json.name: Wroxeter
national/places.json.summary: Founded as a military base about 47 and refounded as a city in the 90s. At 78 hectares it was one of the largest cities of Roman Britain. It was never built over.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The centre was abandoned by the mid 5th century; claims of grand timber rebuilding into the 6th or 7th century are now doubted.

national/places.json.name: Silchester

phases.label: Calleva Atrebatum, civitas capital, walled about 200
Abandoned; walls stand around open fields

national/places.json.summary: An Iron Age centre founded about 20-10 BCE which became a Roman town and, unusually, was never reoccupied.
national/places.json.uncertainty: English Heritage puts the abandonment 'sometime between AD 550 and 650'; 600 is the midpoint.

national/places.json.name: Richborough

phases.label: Rutupiae, port town with a 25 m monumental arch

national/places.json.summary: Widely believed to be the landing place of 43 CE and long the formal gateway to Britain. The town was cleared after 250 for a fort, rebuilt in stone in 275-290.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The arch is dated only to between 85 and 150. Coins show activity into the early 5th century.

national/places.json.name: Canterbury

phases.label: Seat of the Kentish kings and of Augustine's mission; archbishopric
Cathedral city and, after 1170, the chief pilgrim shrine in England
Cathedral city; shrine and abbey destroyed

national/places.json.summary: Roman capital of Kent, then from 597 the centre of the English church. It was fourteenth in the 1377 poll tax and tenth by wealth in the 1520s.
national/places.json.uncertainty: How much life continued inside the walls between about 420 and 597 is disputed. St Augustine's Abbey was dissolved in 1538 (from memory). 597-8 (English Heritage, St Augustine's), Becket's murder in 1170 and the end of the priory in 1540 (VCH Kent) are confirmed. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Winchester

phases.label: Old Minster; West Saxon see from the 660s
Replanned burh and royal city of Wessex and England
Royal and episcopal city, losing ground to London

national/places.json.summary: Roman Venta, refounded by Alfred with a new street grid and the largest burh in the Burghal Hidage. It was second only to London at Domesday but thirtieth in the 1377 poll tax.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Domesday omits Winchester, so its 11th-century size is an estimate (about 6,000). The 880 date for the replanning is approximate. VCH Hampshire gives the Old Minster's foundation as 643 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) or 639 (Winchester Annals); 648 here follows another Chronicle reading. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Cirencester

phases.label: Corinium Dobunnorum, second largest town of Roman Britain by area

national/places.json.summary: Civitas capital of the Dobunni and, on the usual reconstruction, capital of the 4th-century province of Britannia Prima.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Its role as a provincial capital is an inference from one inscription. English Heritage dates the amphitheatre to the early 2nd century and notes the Chronicle's capture of 577. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Bath

phases.label: Aquae Sulis: temple of Sulis Minerva and baths
Cathedral priory and small cloth town

national/places.json.summary: A sanctuary and bathing complex around the hot spring, not an ordinary town. The Roman Baths' own timeline has the buildings collapsing by about 500 and a Saxon church founded in 675.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The temple is usually dated to the 60s-70s; the museum timeline only says the Romans came to Bath about 50. VCH Somerset dates the nunnery charter to 676, a year later than the museum timeline, and puts the bishop's move to Bath in 1088.

national/places.json.name: Exeter

phases.label: Cloth port, about sixth richest town in England

national/places.json.summary: The western end of the Fosse Way, held successively as fortress, Roman town, burh and cathedral city. It ranked 24th in 1377 and 6th in the 1520s.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Fortress and town dates are rounded from memory. Rankings are from tax records, which measure taxpayers or wealth. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Leicester

phases.label: Danish borough, one of the Five Boroughs

national/places.json.summary: Civitas capital of the Corieltauvi and later one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. It ranked eighteenth in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Roman dates are approximate. English Heritage: occupied soon after 43, street grid and civitas capital by the 2nd century, baths about 160, peak in the late 3rd century; the year 50 is approximate. Danish and later dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Chichester
national/places.json.summary: Roman capital of the client kingdom of Togidubnus and its successor civitas, refortified as a burh and made a bishop's seat in 1075.
national/places.json.uncertainty: VCH Sussex has Chichester a burh of some importance by 894-5 and confirms the move of the see from Selsey. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Fishbourne Roman Palace

phases.label: Palace of four wings around a formal garden

national/places.json.summary: The largest Roman residence known north of the Alps, commonly linked to the client king Togidubnus.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The owner is not attested. Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Dorchester

phases.label: Durnovaria, civitas capital of the Durotriges

national/places.json.summary: Founded about 70 CE, after nearby Maiden Castle had emptied.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Post-Roman history is poorly known; the 900 date is nominal.

national/places.json.name: Caistor St Edmund

phases.label: Venta Icenorum, civitas capital of the Iceni
Abandoned; Norwich later grows 5 km to the north

national/places.json.summary: A small Roman town laid out in Iceni territory after the Boudican revolt and never built over.
national/places.json.uncertainty: End date uncertain; some activity continued into the Anglo-Saxon period. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Aldborough

phases.label: Roman trading settlement on the road north
Isurium Brigantum, planned town and civitas capital of the Brigantes

national/places.json.summary: The northernmost civitas capital of Roman Britain: a trading settlement from about 70, laid out as a planned town about 120 and walled in stone in the late 2nd century.
