national/places.json.uncertainty: Foundation date approximate. Foundation and planning dates are English Heritage's; the end of town life is not dated.

national/places.json.name: Carlisle

phases.label: Luguvalium: fort, then town and civitas capital of the Carvetii
Walled town in British Rheged, then Northumbria
Castle and town planted by William II; bishopric from 1133

national/places.json.summary: The Roman town at the west end of the frontier. It was taken into the English kingdom only in 1092.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The first fort is tree-ring dated to 72/3 (from memory). The centuries between 876 and 1092 are obscure. English Heritage gives the first fort as AD 72 and William II's castle as 1092. The 876 desertion and the 1133 bishopric are from memory.

national/places.json.name: Brough-on-Humber

phases.label: Petuaria: fort, then small town at the Humber ferry

national/places.json.summary: Usually taken to be the civitas centre of the Parisi, on the strength of one theatre inscription.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Status and dates are uncertain. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Water Newton

phases.label: Durobrivae, pottery-making town on Ermine Street

national/places.json.summary: A walled small town at the centre of the Nene Valley pottery industry; the earliest Christian silver plate from the Roman empire was found here.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Catterick

phases.label: Cataractonium, fort and roadside town on Dere Street

national/places.json.summary: A Roman fort and town at the Swale crossing; Bede names it as a place where Paulinus baptised.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Corbridge

phases.label: Succession of forts at the Tyne crossing
Coria, garrison town and supply base behind the Wall

national/places.json.summary: The most northerly town of the Roman empire, where Dere Street crossed the Tyne.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates rounded. Fort and town dates are English Heritage's (first fort on this site about 86, legionary base and town from the 160s).

national/places.json.name: Vindolanda

phases.label: Sequence of timber, then stone forts on the Stanegate

national/places.json.summary: A fort built before Hadrian's Wall and rebuilt nine times. Its ink writing tablets, of about 100 CE, are the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The Vindolanda Trust says only that the first fort predates the Wall and that the site was finally abandoned in the 9th century; 85 is the usual estimate.

national/places.json.name: Housesteads

phases.label: Vercovicium, infantry fort on Hadrian's Wall

national/places.json.summary: Built within a decade of 122 for an 800-strong infantry regiment, and held to the end of the 4th century.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The garrison may have stayed into the early 5th century; the end date is nominal.

national/places.json.name: Chesters

phases.label: Cilurnum, cavalry fort where the Wall crosses the North Tyne

national/places.json.summary: Built about 124 for a 500-strong cavalry regiment and occupied until the Roman army left Britain.

national/places.json.name: Birdoswald

phases.label: Banna, Wall fort above the Irthing gorge
Timber halls built over the granaries

national/places.json.summary: A Wall fort where large timber halls show a community staying on under local leaders after Roman pay stopped.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The post-Roman halls are dated only loosely. English Heritage: the site was cleared for the Wall in 122 and the fort finished before 138. The post-Roman hall dates are from memory.

national/places.json.name: South Shields

phases.label: Arbeia, fort at the mouth of the Tyne
Supply base with over twenty granaries

national/places.json.summary: The sea port of Hadrian's Wall, turned into a granary depot for the Severan campaigns in Scotland.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Dover

phases.label: Dubris, base of the Classis Britannica, with twin lighthouses
Burh, port and minster of St Mary in Castro
Royal castle and head port of the Cinque Ports

national/places.json.summary: The shortest crossing to Gaul. The Roman lighthouse of about 130 still stands inside the castle, whose great tower Henry II built in 1179-89; the castle held out against a French siege in 1216-17.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The fleet-base and shore-fort dates are from memory; Domesday suggests about 2,000 people.

national/places.json.name: Portchester

phases.label: Royal castle and embarkation point for France

national/places.json.summary: The best preserved Roman fort north of the Alps, reused as a burh and a medieval castle.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The Latin name is an identification, not a certainty. English Heritage: built probably between 285 and 290 (coins date it after about 268), occupied through the 5th century, given to the king in 904, castle built in one corner after the Conquest. The year 1100 for the castle is approximate.

national/places.json.name: Pevensey

phases.label: William's landing place; Norman castle inside the Roman walls
Decaying castle on a silted haven

national/places.json.summary: Built about 290 (tree-ring date). William of Normandy landed here on 28 September 1066 and a medieval castle grew within the Roman circuit.
national/places.json.uncertainty: English Heritage gives 471 for the Saxon storming recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; the Chronicle's own year is 491 and neither is reliable.

national/places.json.name: Burgh Castle

phases.label: Gariannonum, Saxon Shore fort on the Great Estuary

national/places.json.summary: A shore fort overlooking the wide estuary that then covered the lower Yare and Waveney.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date approximate. English Heritage: built in the late 3rd century; Bede's monastery of St Fursa (about 630) may have been here.

national/places.json.name: Reculver

phases.label: Regulbium, fort at the north mouth of the Wantsum
Parish church; the sea is eating the fort

national/places.json.summary: An early Saxon Shore fort guarding the channel that then made Thanet an island; a Kentish minster was founded in it in 669.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Dates are English Heritage's: fort of the early 3rd century, monastery founded 669, no longer monastic by the 10th century.

national/places.json.name: Rochester

phases.label: Durobrivae, walled town at the Medway bridge
Gundulf's cathedral priory (monks from 1080); stone keep added later

national/places.json.summary: Where Watling Street crossed the Medway. England's second-oldest see was founded here in 604.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 604 and 1080 are from VCH Kent. Roman dates are from memory, as is the keep (about 1127).

national/places.json.name: Manchester

phases.label: Mamucium, fort on the Chester-York road
Burh repaired by Edward the Elder; a village
Market town with a collegiate church (1421)

national/places.json.summary: A Roman fort, then for centuries a minor place. It is included to show how small the later industrial cities still were in 1625.
national/places.json.uncertainty: All dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Lancaster

phases.label: Fort above the Lune, rebuilt as a coastal fortress about 340

national/places.json.summary: A Roman fort site that became the castle and shire town of a county palatine.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Charterhouse-on-Mendip

phases.label: Mendip lead mining under local custom

national/places.json.summary: Lead was being mined on Mendip under army control within six years of the invasion: stamped ingots are dated to 49 CE.
national/places.json.uncertainty: End of Roman working and the restart of medieval mining are approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Wirksworth

phases.label: Lead working at a reduced scale
Lead mines of Repton abbey, then of the Crown

national/places.json.summary: Centre of the Peak District lead field, worked in the Roman period and recorded again from the 8th century and in Domesday.
national/places.json.uncertainty: That Wirksworth is Roman Lutudarum is probable but unproven; all dates are nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Tintagel

phases.label: High-status British stronghold importing Mediterranean wine and oil
Castle of Richard, Earl of Cornwall

national/places.json.summary: A defended headland with more imported 5th-7th century Mediterranean pottery than any other site in Britain, probably a seat of the rulers of Dumnonia.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Its exact status is inferred from the finds. Dates rounded. English Heritage: occupied from the 5th to the mid 7th century, then little activity for over 500 years; Richard of Cornwall acquired the site in 1233. The 1331 decline is from memory.

national/places.json.name: West Stow

phases.label: Early Anglo-Saxon village of timber halls and sunken huts

national/places.json.summary: A fully excavated early English village, standing here for the thousands of small farming settlements of the 5th to 7th centuries.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Sutton Hoo

phases.label: Royal burial ground of the East Angles
Barrow cemetery, later an execution site

national/places.json.summary: A mound cemetery above the Deben. The great ship burial of about 625 is most often thought to be that of King Raedwald.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The identity of the dead man is unknown; the date rests on the coins. Start and end of the cemetery are approximate.

national/places.json.name: Rendlesham

phases.label: Royal vill of the East Anglian kings

national/places.json.summary: Named by Bede as a royal residence; excavation since 2008 has found a large, rich settlement 6 km from Sutton Hoo.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Ipswich

phases.label: Gipeswic, trading town of the East Angles
Cloth port, among the ten richest English towns

national/places.json.summary: One of the four great trading towns (wics) of 7th-9th century England and continuously a town ever since. It was 27th in 1377, 8th in the 1520s and 7th in the 1662 hearth tax.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Foundation in the early 7th century is from excavation, recalled from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Southampton

phases.label: Clausentum, small Roman port at Bitterne
Hamwic, planned trading town of Wessex
Medieval Southampton on a new site; port for Winchester and Normandy

national/places.json.summary: Hamwic, on the west bank of the Itchen, held perhaps 2,000-3,000 people at its height about 700-850. The walled medieval port grew a little to the south-west.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Hamwic's population is an estimate; the dates of the shift between sites are approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Sandwich

phases.label: Port at the mouth of the Wantsum
Cinque Port and naval assembly point
Haven silted; home to Flemish weavers from 1561

national/places.json.summary: The successor to Richborough as the main port of east Kent, until its haven silted in the 15th and 16th centuries.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Yeavering

phases.label: Ad Gefrin, royal vill of Bernicia with great halls and a timber grandstand

national/places.json.summary: A Northumbrian royal centre below the hillfort of Yeavering Bell. In 627 Paulinus spent 36 days here baptising in the River Glen.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Bede says only that it was abandoned under later kings; both dates are approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Bamburgh

phases.label: Rock fortress of the Bernician kings
Seat of the English lords of northern Northumbria

national/places.json.summary: The citadel of Bernicia, traditionally taken by Ida in 547, and the base of the English earls who survived north of the Tyne after the Vikings took York.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 547 is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's date and not reliable. 1095 is from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Lindisfarne

phases.label: Monastery and bishopric founded by Aidan
Deserted by the community of St Cuthbert
Ruin; a Tudor fort is built nearby

national/places.json.summary: Founded in 635 from Iona. Cuthbert died here in 687 and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made about 710-725. Raided on 8 June 793, left for good in 875, and refounded as a cell of Durham by 1122 until its closure in 1537.

national/places.json.name: Jarrow and Wearmouth
national/places.json.summary: Benedict Biscop's 'one monastery in two places', the home of Bede (died 735) and for a time the most learned house in northern Europe.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The marker is at Jarrow; Wearmouth is 10 km to the south-east. English Heritage does not date a Viking attack.

national/places.json.name: Whitby

phases.label: Streaneshalch, double monastery founded by Hild
Fishing port below the ruined abbey

national/places.json.summary: Founded about 657 and the scene of the synod of 664 that settled the dating of Easter. Abandoned in the 9th century, refounded about 1078 and suppressed in 1539.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The date of abandonment is not known; 867 is nominal.

national/places.json.name: Hexham
national/places.json.summary: Wilfrid's church, built with stone from Roman Corbridge; its 7th-century crypt survives.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Ripon

phases.label: Minster rebuilt after King Eadred burned it

national/places.json.summary: A Northumbrian monastery whose 7th-century crypt survives under the later minster.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Durham

phases.label: Shrine of St Cuthbert on the river peninsula
Norman cathedral, castle and seat of the prince-bishops
Cathedral city of a county palatine

national/places.json.summary: Cuthbert's relics came to rest here in 995 after the community's long wandering from Lindisfarne by way of Chester-le-Street.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 995 and the foundation stone of 11 August 1093 are confirmed by VCH Durham, which dates the priory's dissolution to 1540; the phase here ends at 1539.

national/places.json.name: Beverley

phases.label: Minster at the grave of John of Beverley
Cloth town, twelfth in the 1377 poll tax

national/places.json.summary: A minster town which grew into one of the larger towns of medieval England before its cloth trade moved to the West Riding.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Phase dates are approximate. VCH East Riding: John of York buried here in 721; the college and sanctuary are traditionally Athelstan's (930s). Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Tamworth

phases.label: Chief royal residence of the Mercian kings

national/places.json.summary: Mercia had no fixed capital, but its kings issued more charters at Tamworth than anywhere else. A 9th-century watermill has been excavated here.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The start date is nominal; 874 and 913 are Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Repton

phases.label: Double monastery and burial place of Mercian kings
Winter camp of the Viking Great Army

national/places.json.summary: A Mercian royal mausoleum. The Great Army wintered here in 873-4, and a D-shaped earthwork and a mass grave of at least 264 people have been excavated.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Monastery foundation date is approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Torksey

phases.label: Winter camp of the Viking Great Army

national/places.json.summary: The Great Army's camp of 872-3 covered some 55 hectares, larger than most towns of the day.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The size comes from metal-detected finds; dates other than 872-3 are approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Lichfield

phases.label: See of the Mercians, founded by Chad

national/places.json.summary: The church centre of Mercia and, for sixteen years under Offa, the seat of a third English archbishop.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. 669 is confirmed by VCH Staffordshire; the archbishopric of 787-803 rests on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Worcester

phases.label: Burh built for the bishop by Aethelred and Aethelflaed
Cathedral city and Severn bridge town

national/places.json.summary: Chosen as the bishop's seat for the kingdom of the Hwicce in 679-680. It was 26th in 1377 and 12th in the 1662 hearth tax.
national/places.json.uncertainty: VCH Worcestershire puts the burh at an unknown date between 872 and 899. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Hereford

phases.label: See of the Magonsaete at a Wye ford
Marcher earl's castle and cathedral city

national/places.json.summary: The English frontier town against south Wales, burned by a Welsh and Irish force in 1055. Tenth by Russell's Domesday estimate, 21st in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Early dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Shrewsbury

phases.label: Mercian burh in a loop of the Severn
Marcher earl's castle and abbey; wool and Welsh cloth town

national/places.json.summary: The chief town of the middle March, 19th in the 1377 poll tax and 14th in 1662.
national/places.json.uncertainty: First recorded in 901 (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Glastonbury

phases.label: Great Benedictine abbey reformed by Dunstan
Small town beside the ruined abbey

national/places.json.summary: The richest abbey in England at Domesday and again at the Dissolution. Its last abbot was hanged on the Tor in 1539.
national/places.json.uncertainty: A British monastery before about 700 is possible but unproven. Early dates from memory. VCH Somerset accepts King Ine (688-726) as builder of the minster and Dunstan's reform; exact years are approximate. Dissolution date from Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Malmesbury

phases.label: Cloth town; abbey nave kept as the parish church

national/places.json.summary: A hilltop abbey and burh; King Aethelstan was buried here in 939.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Foundation date approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Sherborne

phases.label: Abbey; the see moves to Old Sarum

national/places.json.summary: Bishop's seat for Wessex west of Selwood from 705 until the Council of London of 1075 moved it to Old Sarum.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 705, the Benedictine refoundation of 998, the removal of the see in 1075 and the surrender of 18 March 1539 are from VCH Dorset.

national/places.json.name: Wells

phases.label: Church of canons; the bishop's seat moves to Bath in 1088-90

national/places.json.summary: A cathedral city that never grew large: the church, not trade, was its reason for being.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 909 and the move to Bath in 1088-90 are from VCH Somerset. The 705 minster is tradition; 1180 for the Gothic rebuilding and the joint title of Bath and Wells (1245) are from memory.

national/places.json.name: Athelney

phases.label: Alfred's refuge in the Somerset marshes

national/places.json.summary: The island fort from which Alfred rallied Wessex in the spring of 878 before Edington.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Abbey date approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Wallingford

phases.label: Burh at the Thames ford, equal largest in the Burghal Hidage

national/places.json.summary: Rated at 2,400 hides, the same as Winchester. William crossed the Thames here in 1066. Its Saxon ramparts survive.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The Burghal Hidage is dated to after 914 or, on another view, the 870s-880s; 880 is nominal. VCH Berkshire confirms the Burghal Hidage listing and a castle in being by 1071. The 880 start and the sizes are judgement; ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Wareham

phases.label: Burh between two rivers; seized by the Danes in 876
Small port; Poole takes its trade

national/places.json.summary: A West Saxon burh of 1,600 hides whose earth ramparts still enclose the town on three sides.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Shaftesbury

phases.label: Hilltop burh; Alfred founds a nunnery about 888
Richest nunnery in England and its town

national/places.json.summary: A burh of 700 hides and the home of the wealthiest house of nuns in medieval England, dissolved in 1539.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Lewes

phases.label: Castle of the Warennes and Cluniac priory

national/places.json.summary: A burh of 1,300 hides and the chief town of Norman Sussex; about 2,000 people at Domesday.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Hastings

phases.label: Port wrecked by storms and French raids

national/places.json.summary: A burh of 500 hides which gave its name to the battle fought 10 km inland.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The storm-damage date is approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Oxford

phases.label: Minster of St Frideswide at a Thames crossing
One of the larger English towns

national/places.json.summary: A late Saxon border burh of 1,400 hides which Darby put at about 5,000 people in 1066. Schools gathered here in the 12th century; it was sixteenth in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 727 is a legendary date. The university's growth from 1167 is the traditional account, from memory. VCH Oxfordshire: first recorded in 911; St Frideswide's house is a tradition placed about the start of the 8th century (727 is her traditional death); by 1066 exceeded only by London, York, Norwich, Lincoln and Winchester. 1167 for the schools is the conventional date, not checked.

national/places.json.name: Cambridge

phases.label: Duroliponte, small Roman town on Castle Hill
Desolate; Bede calls it a ruined little city
Danish army base, then English shire town

national/places.json.summary: A river-crossing town where scholars fleeing Oxford settled in 1209; they had a chancellor by 1226. It was 22nd in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Roman and Danish dates approximate. 875, the castle of 1068 and the clerks first mentioned in 1209 are in VCH Cambridgeshire.

national/places.json.name: Norwich

phases.label: Anglo-Scandinavian trading settlement on the Wensum
Castle, cathedral and the largest provincial city in England
Worsted-weaving city, hard hit by plague

national/places.json.summary: Not a Roman town: it grew from the 10th century and Darby gives it about 6,500 people in 1066. Sixth in 1377, it was second only to London in the 1520s and in 1662.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The move of the bishopric from Thetford in 1094 is from memory. Sizes are relative ranks. VCH Norfolk: see moved from Thetford by Herbert de Losinga, cathedral foundation stone laid 1096. Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia; the pre-1066 phases are judgement.

national/places.json.name: Thetford

phases.label: Winter base of the Great Army, then a large Anglo-Scandinavian town
Seat of the East Anglian bishop
Declining town with a Cluniac priory (founded 1103-4)

national/places.json.summary: Sixth largest town in Domesday England and briefly a cathedral city, then eclipsed by Norwich.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The priory dates (founded 1103-4, surrendered February 1540) are from English Heritage and VCH Norfolk; VCH also records the bishop's move from Thetford to Norwich under Herbert de Losinga. The 1072 start of the see and the town's ranking still rest on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Bury St Edmunds
national/places.json.summary: One of the richest abbeys in England, built over the body of the East Anglian king killed by the Danes in 869. Fifteenth in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. 903 (or a little later), 1020 and the surrender of 4 November 1539 are from VCH Suffolk. Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Ely

phases.label: Double monastery of Aethelthryth on an island in the Fens

national/places.json.summary: A fen-island monastery that became one of the great cathedrals; 23rd in the 1377 poll tax.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 673, 870, 970, 1109 and the surrender of 18 November 1539 are confirmed by VCH Cambridgeshire. The 1377 rank follows a table reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Peterborough

phases.label: Abbey church kept as a cathedral (see founded 1541)

national/places.json.summary: A fen-edge abbey whose monks kept the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle going until 1154.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 655-6, 870, the refoundation of about 966 (finished 972) and the surrender of 1539 are from VCH Northamptonshire. 1541 for the new see is from memory.

national/places.json.name: Derby

phases.label: Danish borough, one of the Five Boroughs

national/places.json.summary: A Danish army base taken by Aethelflaed in 917.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The capture date is from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Nottingham

phases.label: Great Army's winter base, then a Danish borough
English borough with a Trent bridge
Royal castle and twin English and French boroughs

national/places.json.summary: One of the Five Boroughs; 29th in the 1377 poll tax.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 868 and 1068 from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Stamford

phases.label: Danish borough, one of the Five Boroughs
Pottery and cloth town with a great fair

national/places.json.summary: A Danelaw borough which Darby put at about 3,000 people in 1086.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Northampton

phases.label: Danish army base, then English shire town
Royal castle and one of the chief towns of the Midlands

national/places.json.summary: A favoured meeting place of 12th-century kings and councils; 28th in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Phase dates approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Warwick

phases.label: Castle of the earls of Warwick and county town

national/places.json.summary: Listed at 2,400 hides in the later Burghal Hidage manuscripts.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 914 and 1068 from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Old Sarum

phases.label: Deserted; still returns two members of parliament

national/places.json.summary: A hillfort of about 400 BCE reused for a mint in 1003, a Norman castle and a cathedral (see moved here 1075). The clergy left for the new city of Salisbury in the 1220s.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The date of final desertion is approximate.

national/places.json.name: Salisbury

phases.label: New cathedral city laid out in the meadows
Cathedral city with a shrinking cloth trade

national/places.json.summary: Founded in 1220 to replace Old Sarum. It was eighth in the 1377 poll tax and seventh by wealth in the 1520s.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Phase boundaries are approximate. VCH Wiltshire: churchyard consecrated 1219, cathedral consecrated 1258.

national/places.json.name: Bristol

phases.label: Burh and port at the bridge over the Avon
Castle and port trading with Ireland and Gascony
Third town of England; a county from 1373

national/places.json.summary: First heard of about 1000. Third in the 1377 poll tax and in the 1520s, and the starting point of English Atlantic voyages from the 1480s.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Start date approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Coventry

phases.label: Priory founded by Leofric and Godgifu
Walled cloth city, fourth or fifth in 1377
Shrinking cloth city, still about fifth by tax in the 1520s

national/places.json.summary: The great boom town of the 14th-century Midlands; it then lost perhaps half its people between about 1440 and 1520 and was 19th in 1662.
national/places.json.uncertainty: VCH Warwickshire: priory founded about 1043, 4,817 poll-tax payers in 1377 (behind only London, Bristol and York on one reckoning), 6,601 people counted in 1520 and 565 houses empty in 1523. The 1601 step down is a judgement; ranks in the 1520s and 1662 follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Plymouth

phases.label: Sutton, a market and fishing harbour
Naval assembly port in the French wars

national/places.json.summary: The base of Drake and Hawkins and the port the fleet sailed from against the Armada in 1588.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Russell's 1377 poll tax figures put Plymouth fourth in England, which is hard to reconcile with other evidence and may reflect soldiers and seamen; the size 4 phase follows that figure with reserve. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: King's Lynn

phases.label: Bishop's Lynn, new town on the Wash

national/places.json.summary: The outlet for the whole Great Ouse basin. Ninth in 1377 and ninth by wealth in the 1520s.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Founded about 1100 by Bishop Losinga (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Boston

phases.label: Leading wool port and international fair
Port in decline as the haven silts

national/places.json.summary: At its 13th-century peak Boston exported more wool than any other English port. Eleventh in 1377.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The 13th-century ranking is from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Great Yarmouth

phases.label: Fishing settlement on a sandbank across the old estuary
Walled herring port with an international autumn fair
Port damaged by plague and a silting harbour

national/places.json.summary: A town built on a sandspit that formed across the Roman-period estuary. Twentieth in 1377, eighth in 1662.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Phase dates approximate. English Heritage confirms a trading quay from at least the 12th century and a 13th-century boom; the phase years are judgement. Ranks follow tables reported on Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Dunwich

phases.label: Possible site of Dommoc, the first East Anglian bishopric
Major North Sea port of about 3,000 people
Remnant village; churches fall into the sea one by one

national/places.json.summary: One of the largest ports of the east coast in the 12th and 13th centuries. Storms in 1286, 1287, 1328, 1347 and 1362 destroyed most of it and shifted its river mouth.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The identification with Dommoc is disputed (Walton Castle is the alternative). The medieval town lies under the sea, so the marker is at the surviving village. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Ravenser Odd

phases.label: Port on a sandbank at the mouth of the Humber; borough 1299
Two thirds of the townsfolk have left

national/places.json.summary: A 13th-century boom port off Spurn Head which sent members to the parliament of 1295 and was drowned in the winter storms of 1356-62.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The site has not been found; the position is approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Winchelsea

phases.label: New Winchelsea, planned hilltop port for the Gascon wine trade
Harbour silted, town shrunk to a village

national/places.json.summary: Edward I's replacement for Old Winchelsea, which the sea destroyed in 1287. Much of its street grid was never filled.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Kingston upon Hull

phases.label: Wyke, wool-shipping quay of Meaux Abbey
Kingston upon Hull, royal port; walled in brick

national/places.json.summary: Bought by Edward I in 1293 as a northern supply port. It was 25th in 1377 and 18th in 1662.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Early dates from memory. VCH East Riding confirms Edward I's acquisition of Wyke from Meaux Abbey in 1293; the 1193 first mention is not checked.

national/places.json.name: Newcastle upon Tyne

phases.label: Pons Aelius, bridge and fort at the east end of the Wall
Walled port shipping wool and coal
Coal port, about fourth richest English town

national/places.json.summary: Named from Robert Curthose's castle of 1080. It was 13th in 1377 and 4th in the 1520s, by then sending coal by sea to London.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The Roman fort is later than the bridge; 122 stands for both. Hadrian's Wall was begun in 122 (English Heritage). Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

national/places.json.name: Berwick-upon-Tweed

phases.label: Scottish royal burgh and Scotland's richest port
Sacked by Edward I; changes hands repeatedly
English garrison town with artillery ramparts (1558-69)

national/places.json.summary: A Scottish town for most of the Middle Ages, finally taken by England in 1482. It is listed under England only for that last phase.
national/places.json.uncertainty: 1296, 1318, 1482 and the ramparts (begun 1558, stopped 1569) are English Heritage's dates. The 1120 start as a royal burgh is from memory.

national/places.json.name: Scarborough

phases.label: Late Roman signal station on the headland

national/places.json.summary: One of a chain of late 4th-century coastal watchtowers, later a major royal castle.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. English Heritage: signal station of the late 4th century; castle begun probably in the 1130s by William le Gros and rebuilt by Henry II from 1159. A chapel stood on the headland by about 1000, so 'deserted' is too strong for the 11th century.

national/places.json.name: Portsmouth

phases.label: Small new town on Portsea Island
Royal dockyard with the first dry dock

national/places.json.summary: A minor port until Henry VII built a dry dock here in 1495; the Mary Rose sank offshore in 1545.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Dartmouth

phases.label: Deep-water haven; crusade fleets assemble here

national/places.json.summary: A Devon port for the Bordeaux wine trade, privateering and later the Newfoundland fishery.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Start date is the first recorded fleet assembly, from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Bodmin

phases.label: Largest town in Cornwall, with a priory and a share in the tin trade

national/places.json.summary: The chief church of Cornwall after its bishops moved east, and a rallying point of the risings of 1497 and 1549.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Reading

phases.label: Danish army camp between Thames and Kennet
Royal abbey, burial place of Henry I
Cloth town, about eleventh richest in England

national/places.json.summary: A small town transformed by Henry I's abbey of 1121, dissolved in 1539 when its abbot was hanged.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Lavenham

phases.label: Cloth-making town, fourteenth richest in England in the 1520s

national/places.json.summary: A Suffolk village that briefly paid more tax than York, on the strength of its blue broadcloth.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Phase dates approximate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Walsingham

phases.label: Augustinian priory at the shrine of Our Lady

national/places.json.summary: The second pilgrim shrine of medieval England after Canterbury.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Battle Abbey

phases.label: Benedictine abbey on the battlefield of 1066
Country house in the abbey buildings

national/places.json.summary: Founded by William about 1071 on the site of his victory, consecrated in 1094 and surrendered in May 1538.

national/places.json.name: Fountains Abbey

phases.label: Cistercian abbey, a great wool producer

national/places.json.summary: The richest Cistercian house in England, dissolved in 1539.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Rievaulx Abbey

phases.label: First Cistercian abbey in the north, about 650 strong in the 1160s
Cistercian abbey with a smaller community

national/places.json.summary: Founded in March 1132. Under Aelred it held 140 monks and about 500 lay brothers. It was shut down on 3 December 1538.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The date of the fall in numbers is nominal.

national/places.json.name: Furness Abbey

phases.label: Savigniac, then Cistercian abbey ruling the Furness peninsula

national/places.json.summary: In 1537 the first of the larger houses to be dissolved by voluntary surrender.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Foundation date from memory. 1127 (after a first settlement at Tulketh in 1124), the Cistercian takeover of 1147 and the surrender of 9 April 1537 are English Heritage's dates.

national/places.json.name: Windsor Castle
national/places.json.summary: One of the ring of castles William built around London, and a main royal residence from the 12th century.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Kenilworth Castle

phases.label: Castle of Geoffrey de Clinton with a great keep
Royal, then Lancastrian fortress ringed by a great mere
Palace of Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester

national/places.json.summary: Begun about 1120. It withstood a six-month siege in 1266, was rebuilt as a palace by John of Gaunt from 1371, and entertained Elizabeth I in 1575.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The 1210 and 1563 phase dates are from memory.

national/places.json.name: Corfe Castle

phases.label: Royal estate where King Edward 'the Martyr' was killed
Royal castle in a gap of the Purbeck Hills

national/places.json.summary: One of the earliest stone castles in England and a favourite stronghold of King John.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Ludlow

phases.label: Seat of the Council of Wales and the Marches

national/places.json.summary: A Lacy and Mortimer castle which became the administrative capital of Wales and the border counties from 1472.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Castle begun about 1086-94 (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Pontefract Castle

phases.label: Castle of the Lacys, later of the house of Lancaster

national/places.json.summary: The strongest castle in Yorkshire.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Richmond Castle

national/places.json.summary: Built after the Harrying of the North to hold the lands of the former English earl; among the oldest stone castles in England.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date from memory. English Heritage: land granted to Alan about 1071 and the castle begun soon afterwards.

national/places.json.name: Alnwick Castle

national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. English Heritage calls it a late 12th-century castle built by Roger Bigod; an earlier castle from about 1100 is not confirmed by the page fetched.

national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates from memory. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Kendal
national/places.json.summary: The main cloth town of the north-west.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Dates nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Dyrham
national/places.json.summary: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says the West Saxons killed three British kings here and took Gloucester, Cirencester and Bath.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Written down three centuries later; many historians doubt the details. Location follows the place-name. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Ellendun
national/places.json.summary: Egbert of Wessex defeated Beornwulf of Mercia; Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex passed to Wessex and Mercian dominance ended.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Usually placed at Wroughton near Swindon; the exact field is unknown. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Edington
national/places.json.summary: In May 878 Alfred defeated Guthrum's army, which then accepted baptism and withdrew to East Anglia.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Probably Edington in Wiltshire; the site has been argued over for centuries. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Brunanburh
national/places.json.summary: Aethelstan defeated the allied kings of Dublin, Scotland and Strathclyde, securing the new kingdom of the English.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The location is unknown: over forty sites have been proposed. The marker is at Bromborough on the Wirral, the most widely supported candidate. Date (late 937) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as unlocated.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Maldon
national/places.json.summary: Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex was killed fighting a Viking fleet on 10 or 11 August 991; payments of tribute followed.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The causeway to Northey Island fits the Old English poem best but is not proven. Date (10 (possibly 11) August 991) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably on the mainland opposite Northey Island, though other sites have been suggested. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Maldon 991' (list entry 1000019).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Brentford
national/places.json.summary: Edmund Ironside crossed the Thames at Brentford two days after relieving London and drove Cnut's army off, at heavy cost to his own men.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Known mainly from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; the exact ground and the month are uncertain. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Assandun
national/places.json.summary: On 18 October 1016 Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside; Edmund died weeks later and Cnut took the whole kingdom.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Either Ashingdon (shown) or Ashdon, both in Essex; the question is open. Date (18 October 1016) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as unlocated.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Fulford
national/places.json.summary: On 20 September 1066 Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar outside York.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The exact field is disputed. Date (20 September 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located around Germany Beck and Fulford Ings.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
national/places.json.summary: On 25 September 1066 Harold Godwinson surprised and killed Harald Hardrada and Tostig.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (25 September 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as different interpretations of where the battle was fought have been suggested. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Stamford Bridge 1066' (list entry 1000035).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Hastings
national/places.json.summary: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold. Battle Abbey was founded on the site about 1071.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (14 October 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably accurately located in the fields south of Battle Abbey. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Hastings 1066' (list entry 1000013).

national/places.json.name: Battle of the Standard
national/places.json.summary: On 22 August 1138 a northern English army raised by Archbishop Thurstan defeated David I of Scotland near Northallerton.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (22 August 1138) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably accurately located north of Northallerton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Northallerton 1138' (list entry 1000027).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Lewes
national/places.json.summary: Simon de Montfort captured Henry III and the Lord Edward on 14 May 1264 and ruled in the king's name for a year.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (14 May 1264) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located on the north side of the town. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Lewes 1264' (list entry 1000018).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Evesham
national/places.json.summary: The Lord Edward trapped and killed Simon de Montfort on 4 August 1265.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (4 August 1265) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located on Greenhill north of Evesham. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Evesham 1265' (list entry 1000010).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Neville's Cross
national/places.json.summary: A northern English army defeated and captured David II of Scotland outside Durham on 17 October 1346.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (17 October 1346) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as accurately located north of Neville's Cross. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Neville's Cross 1346' (list entry 1000024).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Otterburn
national/places.json.summary: A Scottish raiding army defeated the Percys in a moonlit fight in Redesdale.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The exact site is debated. Date (5 August 1388) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located north-west of Otterburn village. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Otterburn 1388' (list entry 1000029). Chroniclers disagree on the day (5 or 19 August).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Shrewsbury
national/places.json.summary: Henry IV defeated the Percy rebellion and Henry 'Hotspur' Percy was killed, on 21 July 1403.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (21 July 1403) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located west of St Mary Magdalene's church at Battlefield. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Shrewsbury 1403' (list entry 1000033).

national/places.json.name: First Battle of St Albans
national/places.json.summary: A street fight on 22 May 1455 in which Richard of York captured Henry VI; usually counted as the opening of the Wars of the Roses.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (22 May 1455) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located among the streets of the city centre.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Towton
national/places.json.summary: Fought in snow on Palm Sunday, 29 March 1461. Edward IV's victory secured him the throne; it is often called the largest and bloodiest battle on English soil.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Army sizes (50,000-65,000 combined) and casualty figures are chroniclers' estimates. Date (29 March 1461) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located between Saxton and Towton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Towton, 1461' (list entry 1000040).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Barnet
national/places.json.summary: On Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471, Edward IV defeated and killed Warwick 'the Kingmaker' in fog north of Barnet.
national/places.json.uncertainty: The battlefield lies somewhere between about 800 and 1,600 m north of Barnet; surveys have not yet fixed it. Date (14 April 1471) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as north of Barnet, but not yet precisely located. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Barnet 1471' (list entry 1000001). The marker (Hadley Highstone) is 0.37 km north of the centroid of the registered battlefield and was left where it is, between the two candidate areas.

national/places.json.name: Battle of Tewkesbury
national/places.json.summary: On 4 May 1471 Edward IV destroyed the last Lancastrian army; Edward, Prince of Wales, was killed.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (4 May 1471) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located south of Tewkesbury. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Tewkesbury 1471' (list entry 1000039).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Bosworth
national/places.json.summary: On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated Richard III, the last English king to die in battle.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Survey finds published in 2009-10 moved the fighting about 3 km south-west of the traditional site on Ambion Hill. The marker now sits at the Battlefields Trust's grid reference in the Fenn Lanes area, inside the enlarged registered battlefield; it is a reference point, not a surveyed centre. Date (22 August 1485) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Bosworth (Field) 1485' (list entry 1000004).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Stoke Field
national/places.json.summary: Henry VII defeated the Yorkist army backing Lambert Simnel on 16 June 1487, the last battle of the Wars of the Roses.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (16 June 1487) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located west of East Stoke. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Stoke (Field) 1487' (list entry 1000036).

national/places.json.name: Battle of Flodden
national/places.json.summary: On 9 September 1513 the Earl of Surrey defeated a Scottish invasion; James IV and much of the Scottish nobility were killed.
national/places.json.uncertainty: Date (9 September 1513) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located in the fields south of Branxton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Flodden 1513' (list entry 1000011).

national/lines.json.name: Watling Street (Richborough–Canterbury–London)

national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 19 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. Itiner-e classes almost all British roads as ‘conjectured’ lines joining known stretches, and its British coordinates are reported to sit about 100 m east of true. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. ‘Watling Street’ is an Anglo-Saxon name. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 8 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. Itiner-e classes almost all British roads as ‘conjectured’ lines joining known stretches, and its British coordinates are reported to sit about 100 m east of true. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. ‘Peddars Way’ is a late medieval name. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.name: Ryknild (Icknield) Street (Bourton-on-the-Water–Alcester–Wall–Derby–Templeborough)
national/lines.json.summary: A road branching from the Fosse Way near Bourton-on-the-Water, running north by Alcester, Metchley (Birmingham) and Wall to Derby (Little Chester) and Templeborough near Rotherham.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 19 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. Itiner-e classes almost all British roads as ‘conjectured’ lines joining known stretches, and its British coordinates are reported to sit about 100 m east of true. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. Built in stages in the 50s to 70s AD. The medieval names Icknield and Ryknild Street are both used for it; it is distinct from the prehistoric Icknield Way. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.name: Chester–Manchester–Castleshaw road (toward York)

national/lines.json.name: Dere Street (York–Corbridge and into Scotland)
national/lines.json.summary: The eastern route north from York by Aldborough, Catterick, Piercebridge, Binchester and Corbridge, then over the Cheviots by High Rochester to Newstead and on toward the Forth.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 35 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. Itiner-e classes almost all British roads as ‘conjectured’ lines joining known stretches, and its British coordinates are reported to sit about 100 m east of true. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. Dated from Agricola’s northern campaigns (AD 79-81). The Scottish part was held only intermittently after about AD 105. ‘Dere Street’ is an Anglo-Saxon name. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.name: Stanegate (Corbridge–Vindolanda–Carlisle)
national/lines.json.summary: The road across the Tyne–Solway isthmus from Corbridge to Carlisle by Vindolanda; with its forts it formed the frontier before Hadrian’s Wall was built just to the north.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 13 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. Itiner-e classes almost all British roads as ‘conjectured’ lines joining known stretches, and its British coordinates are reported to sit about 100 m east of true. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. English Heritage notes that by about AD 100 the northernmost units lay along this isthmus; the road is usually dated to the 80s. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.name: Gloucester–Caerleon–Carmarthen road (‘Via Julia’)
national/lines.json.summary: The south Wales coast road, from Gloucester by Caerwent to the legionary fortress at Caerleon and on by Cardiff, Neath and Loughor to Carmarthen.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 29 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. Itiner-e classes almost all British roads as ‘conjectured’ lines joining known stretches, and its British coordinates are reported to sit about 100 m east of true. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. West of Neath the Itiner-e network has no link, so the line is drawn straight between the forts at Neath, Loughor and Carmarthen. ‘Via Julia’ is an 18th-century antiquarian name with no Roman authority. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.name: Sarn Helen (Caerhun–Tomen y Mur–Pennal–Llanio–Pumsaint–Llandovery)

national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: routed through the Itiner-e road network (2024 version, Britain subset) between the named places and simplified to 35 vertices, so it is good to roughly half a kilometre, not to the metre. The end date marks the end of Roman upkeep about AD 410; much of the line stayed in use as a road or boundary afterwards. Sarn Helen is the traditional Welsh name for several Roman roads, and long stretches of this one are inferred rather than seen; the network path between forts is among the least certain lines in the file. The construction date is an estimate from general knowledge of when the forts and towns on it were founded; no road here is dated directly.

national/lines.json.name: Hadrian’s Wall
national/lines.json.summary: The north-west frontier of the Roman empire for nearly 300 years: a wall 80 Roman miles long from the Tyne to the Solway, built by the army on Hadrian’s orders after his visit in AD 122, with forts, milecastles and turrets. It was given up about AD 142 when the frontier moved north to the Antonine Wall, and reoccupied some twenty years later.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: drawn through the positions of the sixteen forts from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, placed from general knowledge, so the line cuts corners between forts by up to a kilometre. The whole wall lies inside the map. The Antonine Wall (Forth–Clyde, about AD 142-160) lies just outside the map’s northern edge and is not drawn. The break in use about 142-160 is not shown. The end date is nominal: garrisons stayed into the early 5th century and some forts were occupied later.

national/lines.json.name: Military Way (Hadrian’s Wall)
national/lines.json.summary: The road added behind Hadrian’s Wall when it was recommissioned about AD 160, linking the forts and milecastles.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: the fort positions of the Wall shifted about 300 m south so that the road shows as its own line; the real road ran between the Wall and the Vallum, usually within 50-100 m of the Wall. English Heritage says only that a road was added when the Wall was brought back into use; the year is approximate.

national/lines.json.name: Offa’s Dyke
national/lines.json.summary: A bank up to 2.5 m high with a ditch on the Welsh side, the longest earthwork in Britain, marking the western edge of Mercia. Asser, writing about 893, credits it to King Offa (757-796); English Heritage places the work in the 780s.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: a generalised line of the near-continuous central section from Rushock Hill near Kington to Treuddyn in Flintshire, drawn from general knowledge of its route and accurate to perhaps a kilometre. Short gaps, including the stretch along the Severn near Buttington, are drawn through. Dating is debated: radiocarbon samples from under the bank at Chirk (2014) gave dates between about AD 430 and 652, which may mean parts are older than Offa; the Offa’s Dyke Association summarises recent scientific dates as provisionally late 8th to early 9th century. Earlier writers took it on to the sea at Prestatyn; the earthworks north of Treuddyn are now usually treated as separate. The year shown is nominal.

national/lines.json.name: Offa’s Dyke (lower Wye section)
national/lines.json.summary: Lengths of bank on the English side of the Wye gorge, from Sedbury Cliffs on the Severn to near Redbrook and English Bicknor, long treated as the southern end of Offa’s Dyke.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge. Whether these earthworks are part of Offa’s work, or a separate and possibly different-dated boundary, is disputed; between here and Rushock Hill, across Herefordshire, there are only short isolated lengths, which are not drawn.

national/lines.json.name: Wat’s Dyke
national/lines.json.summary: A bank with a ditch on its west side, running about 60 km from Basingwerk on the Dee estuary south past Wrexham and Oswestry to the river Morda at Maesbury, a few kilometres east of Offa’s Dyke.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge of its route through Hope, Wrexham, Ruabon and Old Oswestry. Its date is unsettled: a radiocarbon date from Maes-y-Clawdd near Oswestry gives only ‘after AD 486±75’, which led some to place it in the 5th century, while luminescence dates from Gobowen point to the early 9th century, the reading followed here. It may be earlier or later than Offa’s Dyke.

national/lines.json.name: East Wansdyke
national/lines.json.summary: A massive bank and north-facing ditch running some 20 km along the crest of the Marlborough Downs from Morgan’s Hill to Savernake Forest. The name means ‘Woden’s dyke’.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge. Its date is not established: it is later than the Roman road it cuts and is usually placed in the 5th or 6th century as a British or early West Saxon frontier work, but a later Saxon date has been argued. The year shown is nominal. No source was fetched for this entry (Historic England’s list entries could not be retrieved).

national/lines.json.name: West Wansdyke
national/lines.json.summary: A smaller, broken earthwork south of Bristol and Bath, from the hillfort of Maes Knoll by Stantonbury to Odd Down above Bath.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge. Whether it was built with East Wansdyke is doubted, and the two are not joined: the Roman road between them was once counted as part of the dyke. Date unknown, probably 5th to 7th century; the year shown is nominal. No source was fetched for this entry.

national/lines.json.name: Devil’s Dyke (Cambridgeshire)
national/lines.json.summary: A straight bank and ditch about 12 km long from the fen edge at Reach to the wooded clay at Woodditton, the largest of several dykes barring the chalk corridor of the Icknield Way.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: a straight line between its two ends, placed from general knowledge. It is post-Roman and usually dated to the 5th to 7th centuries, built by the East Angles or their neighbours; the year shown is nominal. No source was fetched for this entry (Historic England’s list entry could not be retrieved).

national/lines.json.name: The Ridgeway
national/lines.json.summary: The chalk ridge route from the Avebury area along the Berkshire Downs to the Thames at Goring, and on along the Chiltern scarp (as the Icknield Way) to Ivinghoe Beacon, passing Barbury, Uffington and Segsbury hillforts. National Trails describe it as in use for at least 5,000 years.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: the modern National Trail, drawn through its main landmarks from general knowledge. That a single long-distance prehistoric road existed here is an old idea that archaeologists now doubt: the monuments along the ridge are real, but a continuous through-route is not evidenced before the early medieval period, when Anglo-Saxon charters name it. The start date is nominal.

national/lines.json.name: Great North Road (London–York–Berwick)
national/lines.json.summary: The main medieval road from London to the north, by Barnet, Hatfield, Baldock, Stamford, Grantham, Newark, Doncaster, Boroughbridge, Durham and Newcastle to Berwick, with York reached by a branch from near Wetherby or Ferrybridge. Kings and armies used it throughout the Scottish wars.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: straight segments between the towns on the route, placed from general knowledge; no source was fetched. The name is post-medieval. In the Middle Ages the route out of London by Ware, Royston and Huntingdon (the Old North Road, on Roman Ermine Street) was at least as important as the Barnet line drawn here, and the two joined near Alconbury. The start date is nominal: the route took shape gradually as the towns on it grew in the 12th and 13th centuries.

national/lines.json.name: England–Wales border
national/lines.json.summary: The boundary between Wales and England as fixed by the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-6 and 1542-3, which assigned each marcher lordship to a Welsh or an English county. It runs from the Dee estuary to the Severn, near but seldom on Offa’s Dyke.
national/lines.json.uncertainty: Course: the modern boundary, extracted from Office for National Statistics county boundaries (2025) as the edge shared by Welsh and English counties, simplified to 64 vertices; the estuary ends and the lowest part of the Wye are added by hand. The modern line differs from that of 1536-43 only in small later adjustments, which are not shown. Monmouthshire is treated as Welsh: the 1542-3 act left its status ambiguous and it was often counted with England until the 20th century.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Silures
national/polities-wales.json.note: The people of south-east Wales, who fought Rome from about AD 48 until their conquest in the mid 70s. Under Roman rule they formed a self-governing community with its centre at Venta Silurum (Caerwent), which lasted to the end of the Roman period. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Demetae
national/polities-wales.json.note: The people of south-west Wales, whose Roman-period centre was Moridunum (Carmarthen). Their name survived in the early medieval kingdom of Dyfed. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Ordovices
national/polities-wales.json.note: The people of central and north-west Wales. Agricola crushed their rising in AD 77 and founded Segontium afterwards. No Roman-period town or self-governing community is known for them. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder: nothing is heard of them after Ptolemy (about AD 150).

national/polities-wales.json.name: Deceangli
national/polities-wales.json.note: The people of north-east Wales, attacked by the Roman governor Ostorius Scapula about AD 48. Lead ingots from Flintshire of the AD 70s are stamped with their name. The name is first recorded by Roman writers in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (Tacitus, Ptolemy); projecting the people back before the conquest is conjecture, and their territory had no known boundary. The end date is a placeholder. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Gwynedd
national/polities-wales.json.note: The kingdom of north-west Wales, with courts at Deganwy and Aberffraw. It became the strongest Welsh power under Rhodri Mawr (844-878), Gruffudd ap Cynan (died 1137), Owain Gwynedd and the two Llywelyns, and ended with Edward I’s conquest in 1282-3. The polygon is indicative for about 1200-1240 under Llywelyn ap Iorwerth: Gwynedd above and below the Conwy with Anglesey, Llŷn, Meirionnydd and Penllyn. The eastern part (the Perfeddwlad, between Conwy and Dee) changed hands repeatedly. The start date is conventional; the dynasty’s origin legend (Cunedda) is not history.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Powys
national/polities-wales.json.note: The kingdom of the central borderland. Its early extent reached further east, into what became Shropshire, before Mercian expansion and the building of Offa’s Dyke. Rhodri Mawr took it over in 855. It was divided for good after the death of Madog ap Maredudd in 1160. The polygon is indicative for about 1100-1160; it is not a surveyed boundary. The start date is conventional.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Powys Fadog
national/polities-wales.json.note: Northern Powys after the division of 1160, ruled from Castell Dinas Brân in the later 13th century; its princes founded Valle Crucis in 1201. It was broken up into marcher lordships (Bromfield and Yale, Chirk) after 1282-3. Only the Valle Crucis foundation is from a fetched source; the rest is general knowledge.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Powys Wenwynwyn
national/polities-wales.json.note: Southern Powys after the division of 1160, centred on Welshpool. Its ruler Gruffudd ap Gwenwynwyn submitted to Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1263, defected in 1274 and fought for Edward I; his heirs kept it as the marcher lordship of Powis.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Dyfed
national/polities-wales.json.note: The kingdom of south-west Wales, heir to the Roman-period Demetae, with a dynasty of partly Irish origin. Hywel Dda acquired it by marriage and joined it to Seisyllwg about 920 to form Deheubarth. The polygon is indicative for about 800. The start date is conventional.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Ceredigion
national/polities-wales.json.note: A small kingdom on Cardigan Bay between the Dyfi and the Teifi, by tradition founded by Ceredig. About 730 its king Seisyll is said to have annexed Ystrad Tywi, creating the larger kingdom later called Seisyllwg. The polygon follows the later county and is indicative. Dates are traditional. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Seisyllwg
national/polities-wales.json.note: Ceredigion together with Ystrad Tywi (the Tywi valley). On the death of its king Gwgon in 872 it came under Rhodri Mawr; his grandson Hywel Dda joined it to Dyfed about 920 to form Deheubarth. The name ‘Seisyllwg’ appears only in later texts and some historians doubt it was used at the time; the start date is traditional.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Deheubarth
national/polities-wales.json.note: The kingdom of the south-west, formed about 920 when Hywel Dda united Dyfed and Seisyllwg. The Normans overran most of it after 1093; Rhys ap Gruffudd (the Lord Rhys) rebuilt it between 1155 and his death in 1197, after which it split among his descendants, who lost their last lands in 1277-87. The polygon is indicative for the Lord Rhys’s rule about 1170-1197: Ceredigion, Ystrad Tywi and parts of Dyfed, excluding the Norman lordships of Pembroke and Gower.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Glywysing (later Morgannwg)
national/polities-wales.json.note: The kingdom between the Tawe and the Usk. In the 10th century, united with Gwent under Morgan Hen (died 974), it came to be called Morgannwg, the origin of ‘Glamorgan’. The Norman Robert fitz Hamon conquered the lowlands about 1091-3. The polygon is indicative for about 950 and excludes Gwent. The start date is conventional. No source was fetched for this entry; it rests on general knowledge of the standard literature.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Gwent
national/polities-wales.json.note: The kingdom between the Usk and the Wye, named after Venta Silurum (Caerwent). It was at times joined with Glywysing. William fitz Osbern began its conquest from Chepstow after 1067. The polygon is indicative for about 1000. The start and end dates are approximate.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Brycheiniog
national/polities-wales.json.note: A small kingdom in the upper Usk valley with a dynasty claiming Irish descent. Its king built the Llangorse crannog about 890; a Mercian army destroyed it in 916. Bernard de Neufmarché conquered the kingdom in 1093 and it became the lordship of Brecon. The polygon is indicative for about 900. The start date is conventional; the conquest date is from general knowledge.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Lands of Rhodri Mawr
national/polities-wales.json.note: Rhodri became king of Gwynedd in 844, took Powys in 855 and Seisyllwg in 872, so that for a few years one king ruled most of Wales outside the south-east and Dyfed. He was killed fighting the English; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives 877, other reckonings 878. His sons divided the lands. No boundary is drawn because none is known.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Lands of Hywel Dda
national/polities-wales.json.note: Hywel held Seisyllwg from 920 and Dyfed by marriage, and on the death of Idwal Foel in 942 took Gwynedd (and with it Powys), ruling all Wales except Morgannwg and Gwent until his death in 950. The Welsh law-books are attributed to him, though no manuscript is earlier than the 13th century. His kingdom broke up at his death.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Kingdom of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn
national/polities-wales.json.note: King of Gwynedd and Powys from 1039, Gruffudd took Deheubarth in 1055 and Morgannwg soon after: the only king ever to rule the whole of Wales, with land east of Offa’s Dyke as well. Harold Godwinson’s campaign of 1063 broke his power and he was killed by his own men (5 August 1063 in the usual reckoning; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography’s revised article argues for 1064). The polygon is modern Wales, used as an indication; his holdings beyond the dyke are not drawn.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Principality of Wales (Llywelyn ap Gruffudd)
national/polities-wales.json.note: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took the homage of the other Welsh lords in 1258 and styled himself Prince of Wales; Henry III recognised the title and the principality in the Treaty of Montgomery (1267). Edward I’s war of 1276-7 cut it back to Gwynedd west of the Conwy; Llywelyn was killed in December 1282 and his brother Dafydd captured in 1283. The polygon is a rough indication of the lands under Llywelyn’s lordship at the treaty in 1267: Gwynedd, both parts of Powys, Builth, Brecon, Gwerthrynion and the Welsh lords of Deheubarth. Its southern and eastern edges were contested and are not well defined.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Anglesey, Caernarfon and Merioneth)
national/polities-wales.json.note: After the conquest the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) annexed Llywelyn’s principality to the English crown and set up counties on the English model, governed from Caernarfon. From 1301 the principality was usually granted to the king’s eldest son. Flintshire, also created in 1284, was attached to Chester and is not drawn. The polygon is indicative: the three north-western shires as they stood from 1284. The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-6 ended the legal distinction between Principality and March.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Principality of Wales (royal counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen)
national/polities-wales.json.note: The southern part of the crown’s principality: the counties of Cardigan and Carmarthen, governed from Carmarthen and built up from royal lands held since the 1240s and the forfeited lands of the princes of Deheubarth (1277-87). The polygon is indicative for about 1300; medieval Carmarthenshire was smaller than the later county and its edges against the marcher lordships of Kidwelly, Llandovery and Emlyn are approximate. The make-up of these counties is from general knowledge.
