national/polities-wales.json.name: March of Wales (marcher lordships)
national/polities-wales.json.note: The belt of some forty or more lordships along the border and across south Wales, conquered piecemeal by Norman lords from 1067 (Chepstow, Montgomery, Brecon, Glamorgan, Pembroke) and enlarged after 1282 with new lordships in the north-east (Denbigh, Ruthin, Bromfield and Yale, Chirk). Each lord held royal powers in his lordship and the king’s writ did not run there. The Laws in Wales Act of 1535-6 abolished these powers and divided the lordships among new and existing shires. No polygon is drawn: the March was not one territory, and its extent changed with every war.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Wales under Owain Glyndŵr
national/polities-wales.json.note: Owain Glyndŵr attacked Ruthin on 16 September 1400 and took the title Prince of Wales. After Bryn Glas (1402) and the capture of Aberystwyth and Harlech (1404) he controlled most of Wales, made a treaty with France and planned a parliament and an independent Welsh church. Defeats from 1405 and the loss of Aberystwyth and Harlech (1408-9) ended his rule; he still raided in 1410 and is not heard of after 1412. The end date is nominal: he never surrendered and probably died about 1415-16. No polygon is drawn because control shifted from year to year.

national/polities-wales.json.name: Wales (shired and united with England)
national/polities-wales.json.note: The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-6 and 1542-3 united Wales with England, abolished the powers of the marcher lords, created the counties of Monmouth, Brecknock, Radnor, Montgomery and Denbigh beside the older ones, gave Wales members of Parliament and made English the language of the courts. The acts also fixed the boundary with England. The polygon is the modern outline of Wales, generalised; it includes Monmouthshire, which the 1542-3 act placed under the Westminster courts and whose status was long ambiguous. The fetched legislation.gov.uk pages confirm the two acts and their dates; the summary of their provisions is from general knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Cantiaci
national/polities.json.note: People of Kent, with a centre at Canterbury. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Trinovantes
national/polities.json.note: People of Essex and south Suffolk; Caesar restored their king Mandubracius in 54 BCE. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Catuvellauni
national/polities.json.note: The dominant power north of the Thames under Tasciovanus and Cunobelin, with centres at Verlamion and, by conquest, Camulodunon. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Iceni
national/polities.json.note: People of Norfolk and north Suffolk, a client kingdom until Boudica's revolt of 60/61. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Atrebates
national/polities.json.note: A kingdom ruled by the heirs of Commius, centred on Calleva (Silchester). Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Regni
national/polities.json.note: People of Sussex; the name's form (Regni or Regini) is uncertain and it may be a Roman creation for Togidubnus's client kingdom. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Belgae
national/polities.json.note: A civitas centred on Winchester; it may be a Roman administrative grouping rather than a pre-conquest people. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Durotriges
national/polities.json.note: People of Dorset and south Somerset, the builders of the last great hillforts. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Dumnonii
national/polities.json.note: People of Devon and Cornwall, later centred on Exeter. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Dobunni
national/polities.json.note: People of the Cotswolds and lower Severn, later centred on Cirencester. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Corieltauvi
national/polities.json.note: People of the east Midlands, later centred on Leicester; formerly read as 'Coritani'. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Cornovii
national/polities.json.note: People of Shropshire and Cheshire, later centred on Wroxeter. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas.

national/polities.json.name: Brigantes
national/polities.json.note: A large confederation across the Pennines, ruled by Cartimandua as a client of Rome until about 69. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Parisi
national/polities.json.note: People of east Yorkshire, known for chariot burials. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Carvetii
national/polities.json.note: People of the Eden valley and Solway plain, attested only by 3rd-century inscriptions; probably a sub-group of the Brigantes before then. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Votadini
national/polities.json.note: People of Northumberland and Lothian, mostly beyond the northern edge of this map. Named in Roman sources (Caesar, Tacitus, Ptolemy) and on coins or inscriptions; the label marks the heartland only, no boundary is known, and the name outlived the conquest as a Roman civitas. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Britannia
national/polities.json.note: The single Roman province, governed by a consular legate. Its limit moved north by stages to Hadrian's Wall (from 122). No polygon: the area held changed decade by decade in the 1st century. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Britannia Superior
national/polities.json.note: The southern province after Severus split Britain; governed from London. The division is placed about 197 by one ancient account and as late as 213 by modern scholars. The line between the two provinces is not recorded. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Britannia Inferior
national/polities.json.note: The northern province, governed from York, which was a colonia by 237. Same dating caveat as Britannia Superior. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Maxima Caesariensis
national/polities.json.note: Usually placed in the south-east with London as capital. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Britannia Prima
national/polities.json.note: Usually placed in the west, with Cirencester as capital on the evidence of one inscription. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Flavia Caesariensis
national/polities.json.note: Usually placed in the east Midlands around Lincoln, though some would exchange it with Britannia Secunda. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Britannia Secunda
national/polities.json.note: Usually placed in the north around York, though some would exchange it with Flavia Caesariensis. One of the four provinces of the Diocese of the Britains, created between 296 and about 312. Their names are certain; their boundaries and, for most, their capitals are not, and the label position is the common modern reconstruction only. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Valentia
national/polities.json.note: A fifth province named by Ammianus as restored by Count Theodosius in 369. Its location is unknown: around Carlisle (shown), around Chester, or between the Walls have all been argued. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of Kent
national/polities.json.note: Traditionally founded about 455; its first securely attested king, Aethelberht, received Augustine in 597. Under Mercian control 764-825, then absorbed by Wessex. The polygon is the kingdom of about 600, roughly the later county. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the South Saxons
national/polities.json.note: Traditional foundation by Aelle in 477; converted by Wilfrid from 681; under Mercia 771-796, subject to Wessex from about 827 and fully absorbed in 860. The polygon is the kingdom of about 700, bounded inland by the Weald forest. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the East Saxons
national/polities.json.note: Founded in the 6th century (527 is a traditional and uncertain date). It ceded itself to Wessex in 825. The polygon is the kingdom of about 650, when it still included Middlesex, London and much of Hertfordshire; Mercia took those by the mid 8th century. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the East Angles
national/polities.json.note: Organised in the first half of the 6th century and ruled by the Wuffingas, of whom Raedwald (died about 624) was the most powerful. King Edmund was killed by the Danes in 869. The polygon is the kingdom of about 700: Norfolk and Suffolk, with the Fens as its western march. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Danish kingdom of East Anglia
national/polities.json.note: East Anglia under Danish kings, including Guthrum (baptised Aethelstan) from 880; it also held Essex. Submitted to Edward the Elder in 917-918. No polygon: its western limit is not known. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the West Saxons
national/polities.json.note: 519 is the legendary date of Cerdic; the historical kingdom grew from the Gewisse of the upper Thames in the 7th century. From 825 it also held Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex, and from about 886 Alfred styled himself king of the Anglo-Saxons. The polygon is the core kingdom of about 800, before those gains, with Devon included and Cornwall still British. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the Mercians
national/polities.json.note: Attested from the late 6th century and dominant south of the Humber under Penda (died 655), Aethelbald and Offa (757-796). The Danes took its eastern half in 877; the western half was ruled by Ealdorman Aethelred and Aethelflaed under West Saxon lordship until Edward the Elder annexed it in 918. The polygon is Mercia proper about 790 under Offa, including Lindsey, the Hwicce, Middlesex and London but not the client kingdoms of Kent, Sussex, Essex and East Anglia. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Bernicia
national/polities.json.note: The northern Anglian kingdom, centred on Bamburgh; 547 is the traditional date of Ida. It may have begun as a British kingdom. United with Deira for good by 654. Extent unknown. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Deira
national/polities.json.note: The southern Anglian kingdom between Humber and Tees, centred on the Yorkshire Wolds and York. Its last king was killed in 651 and it was ruled from Bernicia thereafter. The start date is nominal. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the Northumbrians
national/polities.json.note: Bernicia and Deira united. At its height it ran from the Humber and Mersey to the Firth of Forth; the polygon shows about 700 and is cut off at the northern edge of this map. York fell to the Great Army in 867. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Lindsey
national/polities.json.note: A small kingdom between the Humber and the Witham with its own king-list and bishop. It was fought over by Northumbria and Mercia in the 7th century and was Mercian for good by about 700. Both dates are nominal. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Hwicce
national/polities.json.note: A kingdom of the lower Severn and Cotswolds (roughly the later diocese of Worcester), a Mercian sub-kingdom from about 628; its rulers cease to be called kings about 780. The 577 start is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's and doubtful. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Elmet
national/polities.json.note: A British kingdom around Leeds, annexed by Edwin of Northumbria about 617. Start date nominal; extent unknown. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Dumnonia
national/polities.json.note: The British kingdom of the south-west. Wessex took Devon by the early 8th century; Cornwall kept kings until the 9th century and was brought under English rule between Egbert's victory at Hingston Down (838) and Aethelstan. Label placed in Cornwall; dates nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of York
national/polities.json.note: Scandinavian kingdom between Humber and Tees after the Great Army took York in 866/7. Taken by Aethelstan in 927, lost again, and ended when Eric Bloodaxe was driven out and killed in 954. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Danelaw
national/polities.json.note: Not a state but the part of England under Danish armies and law: East Anglia, the Five Boroughs (Lincoln, Stamford, Leicester, Nottingham, Derby) and York. The polygon shows about 890, with the Alfred-Guthrum treaty boundary (886-890) on the south-west running up the Lea to Bedford and then along Watling Street. Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed retook everything south of the Humber in the 910s; the term itself is first used in the 11th century. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Kingdom of the English (England)
national/polities.json.note: Aethelstan took York in 927 and was the first king to rule all the English. The polygon is the kingdom of about 1000: Cumbria was under Strathclyde until William II took Carlisle in 1092, Lothian had passed to the Scots, the Tweed border was fixed in practice only in the 12th-13th centuries (Berwick 1482), and Wales was annexed in law in 1536-42. Frontiers were zones of shifting lordship, not lines. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of Wessex
national/polities.json.note: Held by Godwin from about 1020 and by his son Harold from 1053 until he became king. One of the great earldoms through which Cnut and Edward the Confessor governed. Label only: earldoms were bundles of shires that were regrouped whenever an earl died or fell. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of Mercia
national/polities.json.note: Held by Eadric Streona, then by Leofric, Aelfgar and Edwin. End date approximate. One of the great earldoms through which Cnut and Edward the Confessor governed. Label only: earldoms were bundles of shires that were regrouped whenever an earl died or fell. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of East Anglia
national/polities.json.note: Held by Thorkell the Tall and later by Harold and Gyrth Godwinson; suppressed after the revolt of 1075. One of the great earldoms through which Cnut and Edward the Confessor governed. Label only: earldoms were bundles of shires that were regrouped whenever an earl died or fell. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of Northumbria
national/polities.json.note: After 954 the north was governed by earls appointed by the English kings, among them Siward and Tostig; the house of Bamburgh kept the land beyond the Tees for much of the time. Label only. The last English earl, Waltheof, fell in 1075-6 (from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of Chester
national/polities.json.note: Marcher earldom created by William I to contain north Wales; a palatinate, annexed to the Crown in 1237 (date from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of Shrewsbury
national/polities.json.note: Marcher earldom of Roger of Montgomery; forfeited by Robert of Belleme in 1102 (dates from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

national/polities.json.name: Earldom of Hereford
national/polities.json.note: Marcher earldom of William fitz Osbern; forfeited by his son after the revolt of 1075 (dates from memory). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Barnet chapel rebuilt
locations/barnet/events.json.note: John Beauchamp, who died in 1453, rebuilt the nave arcades and clerestory of the chapel of St John the Baptist; the tower is early 15th century and the chancel about 1450. The dates are architectural estimates apart from Beauchamp's death.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: First Battle of St Albans
locations/barnet/events.json.note: 22 May 1455, about 15 km to the north-west along the same road: the opening battle of the Wars of the Roses. Off this map.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Towton; Edward IV becomes king
locations/barnet/events.json.note: After the second battle of St Albans (17 February) Edward of York was proclaimed king in London in March and won at Towton in Yorkshire on 29 March 1461. Off this map.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Henry VI restored by Warwick
locations/barnet/events.json.note: The 'readeption': Warwick, now allied with the Lancastrians, restored Henry VI in October 1470 and Edward IV fled abroad. He landed in Yorkshire in March 1471 and entered London on 11 April.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Battle of Barnet, 14 April
locations/barnet/events.json.note: Easter Sunday. Edward IV defeated the Earl of Warwick somewhere between half a mile and a mile north of the town, at dawn in thick mist; Warwick and his brother Montagu were killed. The exact ground has not been found.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Battle of Tewkesbury, 4 May
locations/barnet/events.json.note: Three weeks later Edward defeated Margaret of Anjou's army in Gloucestershire, ending the Lancastrian challenge. Off this map.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Kitts End heath first named
locations/barnet/events.json.note: A close roll entry of 1479 names Kitts (Kicks) End heath, Bentley heath and many hedged closes north of the common: the earliest detailed record of the landscape north of Hadley, eight years after the battle.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Bosworth; Henry VII becomes king
locations/barnet/events.json.note: 22 August 1485, in Leicestershire. Off this map.

locations/barnet/events.json.label: Hadley church rebuilt
locations/barnet/events.json.note: The church of St Mary at Monken Hadley was rebuilt about 1494, the date carved on its west tower, presumably on the site of an older church.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Half a Thames fishery at Brentford granted to Winchester
locations/brentford/events.json.note: King Æthelred granted half of a Thames fishery at Brentford to the church of St Peter and St Paul, Winchester. It is the only record of activity at Brentford found for the half-century before the battle.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Swein's army loses men crossing the Thames
locations/brentford/events.json.note: On its way towards London, the Chronicle says, many of Swein Forkbeard's army drowned in the Thames 'because they kept not to any bridge'. The place is not given and need not be Brentford; it shows what a crossing of the river could cost.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Cnut besieges London
locations/brentford/events.json.note: The Danish ships came to London, dug a ditch on the south side and dragged their ships to the west of the bridge, then shut the city in. Edmund gathered an army, came to London north of the Thames and drove the besiegers to their ships.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Battle of Brentford
locations/brentford/events.json.note: Within two nights of relieving London, Edmund 'went over at Brentford', fought the Danish army and put it to flight. Many of the English drowned 'from their own carelessness', having gone ahead of the army to plunder. Site, numbers and course are unknown; the figures shown are stand-ins.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Edmund fords the Thames at Brentford again
locations/brentford/events.json.note: Later in the year Edmund gathered the English a fourth time, 'forded over the Thames at Brentford' and went into Kent, driving the Danes to Sheppey. He was beaten at Assandun and died on St Andrew's day (30 November); Cnut took the whole kingdom.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Norman Conquest
locations/brentford/events.json.note: Nothing is recorded at Brentford in the sources read. Isleworth, held by Earl Ælfgar in 1066, had passed to Walter of St Valery by 1086.

locations/brentford/events.json.label: Domesday Book: Brentford is not named
locations/brentford/events.json.note: The ground lay in three manors. Isleworth had 118 households, land for 55 ploughs, two mills and woodland for 500 pigs, and was worth £72 (£80 in 1066). Hanwell, held by Westminster Abbey and assessed at 8 hides, had about 17 households and a mill (figures from a secondary summary). The county history thinks Old Brentford was probably counted within the bishop of London's manor of Fulham.

locations/london/events.json.label: Bronze Age farming on the Southwark eyots
locations/london/events.json.note: Plough (ard) marks and timber trackways are known from Southwark and Bermondsey; the cultivation was short-lived and was drowned as water levels rose.

locations/london/events.json.label: Londinium founded
locations/london/events.json.note: The earliest dated feature is a roadside drain of 47 CE (tree-ring date); there is no documented foundation date.

locations/london/events.json.label: Boudican revolt: Londinium burned
locations/london/events.json.note: 60 or 61 CE. Recovery was quick: a fort and a new quay by 63.

locations/london/events.json.label: Hadrianic fire
locations/london/events.json.note: A major fire c. 120–130, most likely the mid 120s.

locations/london/events.json.label: Alfred restores Lundenburh
locations/london/events.json.note: Settlement returns inside the Roman walls; reoccupation may have begun a generation earlier.

locations/london/events.json.label: Great fire of Southwark and the bridge
locations/london/events.json.note: 11 July 1212: Southwark, St Mary Overie and the houses on the new bridge burn.

locations/london/events.json.label: Black Death
locations/london/events.json.note: November 1348 to 1349–50; buildings survive but a large part of the population dies.

locations/london/events.json.label: Dissolution of the London religious houses
St Paul's spire destroyed by lightning
locations/london/events.json.note: 4 June 1561; the roofs were repaired by 1566 but the spire was never rebuilt.

locations/london/events.json.label: Drawbridge tower demolished; Nonsuch House begun
Globe burns; rebuilt 1614
locations/london/events.json.note: Burned 29 June 1613; rebuilt with a tiled roof by 1614.

locations/london/events.json.label: Death of James I — end of timeline

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Coneybury Anomaly feasting pit (date unverified)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: An early Neolithic pit with pottery, bone and flints near the later Coneybury henge. The date of about 3800 BCE comes from the project brief and was not confirmed in any source read; treat as uncertain.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Robin Hood's Ball and first long barrows
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Approximate. Robin Hood's Ball (causewayed enclosure, outside this map) is dated 'centuries around 3500 BC' by English Heritage; Amesbury 42 long barrow gave 3640 to 3370 cal BCE. Most other long barrows are undated.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Greater Cursus built
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: A red deer antler in the west terminal ditch gave 3630 to 3375 BCE; a 2009 paper found another antler about a millennium younger, so the date is debated. Whether the Cursus or the Amesbury 42 barrow is older is unknown.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Stonehenge Stage 1: ditch, bank, Aubrey Holes
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Darvill et al. 2012 Table 3 gives 3000 to 2620 BCE for Stage 1; the ditch itself is modelled at about 2955 to 2830 BCE (68%), and 2990 to 2755 BCE at 95%. The model switches it on in 3001 to 2995 BCE. The Aubrey Holes may predate the ditch.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Cremation burials at Stonehenge (c. 3000 to 2600 BCE)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: More than 150 people were probably buried as cremations in the Aubrey Holes and ditch; the span is a range, not an event. One cremated woman beside Aubrey Hole 7 probably predates the ditch.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Stage 2 begins: trilithons, bluestone double circle
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Start of Darvill et al.'s Stage 2 (2620 to 2480 BCE). Order within the stage is not settled: trilithons first, then sarsen circle, or all in quick succession.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Sarsen circle raised (modelled c. 2560 to 2470 BCE)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: The English Heritage Bayesian model puts the sarsen circle at 2580 to 2475 BCE and the trilithons at 2585 to 2400 BCE (93%). The span shown is a modelling choice inside those ranges.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Durrington Walls village
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Eight houses excavated in 2006 about 5 m square, dated 2600 to 2500 BCE at first; later modelling gives an occupation of only about 10 to 12 years ending c. 2500 to 2460 BCE. The number of houses is unknown (a few dozen is shown, conjecturally).

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Durrington timber ring replaced by the henge bank
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: About 300 posts in a ring 440 to 450 m across were pulled and the sockets packed with chalk; the henge bank and ditch were completed c. 2480 to 2450 BCE. Also the start of Stonehenge Stage 3 (2480 to 2280 BCE).

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Woodhenge ditch dug
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Ditch dated 2470 to 2000 BCE (a wide range). Six oval post rings; the post heights (up to about 7.5 m) are inferred.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: West Amesbury henge (Bluestonehenge): stones removed
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Stone sockets for up to about 27 stones, removed 2469 to 2286 BCE; the ditch and bank are c. 2400 BCE. That the stones were bluestones that went to Stonehenge is suspected, not proven.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Beaker burials: Amesbury Archer and a Stonehenge ditch burial
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: The Amesbury Archer (c. 2340 to 2300 BCE, grave outside this map) and a Beaker burial in the Stonehenge ditch (2340 to 2195 BCE) are of similar date.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: The Avenue is built
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Darvill: 2430 to 2200 BCE; English Heritage: four antler picks date construction to 2345 to 2200 BCE. About 2.5 to 2.8 km long, its first 530 m or so straight on the solstice axis. -2315 is a recommended display date inside the ranges.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Bluestone circle and oval (Stage 4)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Stage 4 is 2280 to 2020 BCE: circle modelled at about 2165, oval about 2060 BCE. Around 80 bluestones were used in all; 43 survive as stones or stumps.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Bush Barrow burial (c. 1950 BCE)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: A rich Early Bronze Age burial on Normanton Down with a gold lozenge plate. The date of about 1950 BCE is from Wikipedia; the other grave goods are not itemised in the research notes.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Z holes dug (date uncertain)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: English Heritage's model gives 2020 to 1745 BCE; its web page says 1800 to 1500 BCE. The holes were filled with windblown sediment. Purpose unknown.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Y holes dug; carvings on the sarsens
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Y holes 1630 to 1525 BCE (modelled). Axe and dagger carvings are dated 1750 to 1500 BCE. The last prehistoric structural change, with the stone settings ending 1630 to 1340 BCE.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Middle Bronze Age fields in the east
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: A 2015 to 2016 survey found early fields and enclosures in the eastern part of the World Heritage Site. The sources say only 'Middle Bronze Age'; the date shown is the brief's.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Vespasian's Camp hillfort (placeholder date)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Iron Age hillfort of about 14 ha above the Avon. No construction date was retrieved; c. 700 to 600 BCE is a placeholder. The name comes from Camden and is not Roman.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Roman coins and pottery at the stones (late 4th century)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Late 4th-century coins and pottery were found at Stonehenge; Darvill thinks some bluestones were broken or removed in Roman times, his view not shared by all. A Roman building lay near the Cuckoo Stone.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Execution burial at Stonehenge (600 to 690 CE)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: A decapitated man aged 28 to 32 was buried inside the stones. One source disputes the range; 'second half of the 7th century' is the safer wording. Low confidence on the exact span.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Amesbury Abbey founded
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: A Benedictine house founded c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth. Its buildings and site within Amesbury are not known from the sources read.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Domesday Book: Amblesberie, 111 households, eight mills
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Amesbury already a crossing of the London to Exeter road.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Henry of Huntingdon names 'Stanenges' (c. 1130)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: One of England's four wonders in his Historia Anglorum, the stones 'raised up like gates'. The date is approximate.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Geoffrey of Monmouth: Merlin and the Giants' Dance (c. 1136)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: In the Historia Regum Britanniae Merlin moves the stones from Mount Killaraus in Ireland. A legend, not evidence of construction.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Amesbury refounded as a Fontevraud priory
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: The abbey was replaced by a priory of the Order of Fontevraud. The medieval buildings are not located in the sources read.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Hardyng: stones 'somwat bowand' (c. 1457)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Hardyng's Chronicle says the stones 'hang' and are somewhat bowed: the only medieval hint of leaning.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Amesbury Priory dissolved (1539 or 1540)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Sources conflict: the project brief says 1539, the Wikipedia Amesbury article says c. 1540. The estate passed to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Lucas de Heere watercolour (1573 to 75)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: The first view drawn on site. The date is a range; the accompanying text was not read.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Camden's Britannia describes Stonehenge (1586)
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: Three circles within a trench, some stones 28 feet high with lintels on top. 1586 is the first edition; later editions followed.

locations/stonehenge/events.json.label: Inigo Jones surveys for James I; Buckingham digs
locations/stonehenge/events.json.note: James I visited Wilton in 1620 and commissioned a survey (per Webb's 1655 publication); the same year the Duke of Buckingham made the first known excavation in the centre. Jones's plan is an idealised restoration, not a record.

national/events.json.label: Farming reaches Britain
national/events.json.note: Around 4000 BCE; the date is a rounded convention.

national/events.json.label: Long barrows and causewayed enclosures
national/events.json.note: West Kennet, Windmill Hill, Hambledon Hill and the first enclosure at Maiden Castle (about 5,500 years ago).

national/events.json.label: Stonehenge: first ditch and bank
national/events.json.note: About 3000 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Avebury henge begun
national/events.json.note: Built and altered from about 2850 to about 2200 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Deep flint mining begins at Grime's Graves
national/events.json.note: About 2600 to 2100 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Sarsens and bluestones raised at Stonehenge
national/events.json.note: About 2500 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Silbury Hill built; first metal and Beaker pottery
national/events.json.note: The mound was raised between about 2470 and 2350 BCE. Copper, gold and Beaker burials appear in Britain at about the same time.

national/events.json.label: Holme timber circle (Seahenge) built
national/events.json.note: Timbers felled in 2049 BCE by tree-ring dating.

national/events.json.label: Fields and farmsteads divide the land
national/events.json.note: From about 1500 BCE; the last digging at Stonehenge dates to 1800-1500 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Flag Fen causeway built
national/events.json.note: In stages between about 1365 and 967 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Iron working begins
national/events.json.note: A conventional date for the start of the Iron Age.

national/events.json.label: First hillfort at Danebury
national/events.json.note: About 550 BCE; hillfort building begins across southern Britain around 600 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Great developed hillforts
national/events.json.note: Maiden Castle is trebled in size about 400 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Cross-Channel trade through Hengistbury Head
national/events.json.note: Italian wine reaches Britain; most amphorae predate 50 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Julius Caesar's first expedition
national/events.json.note: A second and larger expedition followed in 54 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Calleva and Camulodunon founded
national/events.json.note: Coin-issuing kingdoms in the south-east; Calleva was established about 20-10 BCE.

national/events.json.label: Roman invasion under Claudius
national/events.json.note: The army is widely believed to have landed at Richborough.

national/events.json.label: Colonia founded at Colchester
national/events.json.note: The first Roman city in Britain.

national/events.json.label: Boudica's revolt
national/events.json.note: 60 or 61 CE: Colchester, London and Verulamium burned.

national/events.json.label: Britain divided into two provinces
national/events.json.note: Britannia Superior and Inferior; the date lies between about 197 and 213.

national/events.json.label: Emperor Septimius Severus dies at York
Carausius seizes Britain
national/events.json.note: A breakaway 'British empire' until 296; the Saxon Shore forts belong to these decades.

national/events.json.label: The 'barbarian conspiracy'
national/events.json.note: Concerted attacks by Picts, Scots and Saxons; order restored by Count Theodosius.

national/events.json.label: End of Roman rule
national/events.json.note: About 410; no single event is securely recorded.

national/events.json.label: Ship burial at Sutton Hoo
national/events.json.note: About 625, dated by its coins.

national/events.json.label: Death of Bede at Jarrow
national/events.json.note: His Ecclesiastical History, finished about 731, is the main source for the two centuries before.

national/events.json.label: Offa becomes king of Mercia
national/events.json.note: Reigned 757-796.

national/events.json.label: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
national/events.json.note: 8 June 793.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Ellendun
national/events.json.note: Wessex overtakes Mercia; Kent, Sussex and Essex pass to Egbert.

national/events.json.label: The Great Army lands in East Anglia
national/events.json.note: York falls in 866/7, East Anglia in 869, eastern Mercia in 877.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Edington
national/events.json.note: Alfred defeats Guthrum.

national/events.json.label: Alfred and Guthrum's treaty
national/events.json.note: Made between 886 and 890; Alfred also occupied London in 886.

national/events.json.label: Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed retake the southern Danelaw
national/events.json.note: East Anglia submits in 917-918; Mercia is annexed to Wessex in 918.

national/events.json.label: Aethelstan takes York: a kingdom of all the English
Battle of Brunanburh
national/events.json.note: Site unknown.

national/events.json.label: Eric Bloodaxe expelled from York
national/events.json.note: End of Scandinavian kingship in England.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Maldon
national/events.json.note: Renewed Viking attacks and the first payments of tribute.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Brentford; Cnut wins the kingdom
national/events.json.note: Edmund Ironside's victory at Brentford was followed by defeat at Assandun and his death; Cnut became king of all England.

national/events.json.label: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
national/events.json.note: 25 September and 14 October 1066: the Norman Conquest.

national/events.json.label: Harrying of the North
national/events.json.note: Winter of 1069-70.

national/events.json.label: Domesday survey
national/events.json.note: Ordered at Christmas 1085; more than 13,000 places, but not London, Winchester, Durham or Northumberland.

national/events.json.label: William II takes Carlisle
national/events.json.note: Cumbria is brought into the English kingdom.

national/events.json.label: Death of Henry I: the Anarchy
national/events.json.note: Civil war between Stephen and Matilda until 1153.

national/events.json.label: Murder of Thomas Becket at Canterbury
Magna Carta
national/events.json.note: Sealed at Runnymede, 15 June 1215.

national/events.json.label: Salisbury Cathedral founded
national/events.json.note: The see moves down from Old Sarum.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Evesham
national/events.json.note: Simon de Montfort, whose parliament that year included townsmen, is killed.

national/events.json.label: Statute of Rhuddlan
national/events.json.note: Follows Edward I's conquest of Wales in 1282-3.

national/events.json.label: Great Famine
national/events.json.note: Harvest failures of 1315-17.

national/events.json.label: Black Death
national/events.json.note: Arrived at Melcombe (Weymouth) in June 1348 and had crossed the country by the end of 1349; 40-60% mortality is widely accepted.

national/events.json.label: The 'Great Drowning of Men'
national/events.json.note: A January storm surge finishes Ravenser Odd and much of Dunwich; plague had returned in 1361-2.

national/events.json.label: First poll tax
national/events.json.note: The best medieval evidence for the relative size of English towns.

national/events.json.label: First Battle of St Albans
national/events.json.note: Opening of the Wars of the Roses.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Towton
national/events.json.note: 29 March 1461.

national/events.json.label: Battles of Barnet and Tewkesbury
national/events.json.note: 14 April and 4 May 1471: Edward IV recovers the throne.

national/events.json.label: Battle of Bosworth
national/events.json.note: 22 August 1485: Henry VII, the first Tudor king.

national/events.json.label: Dissolution of the monasteries begins; union with Wales
national/events.json.note: Lesser houses suppressed from 1536, the greater by surrender in 1537-40; the Pilgrimage of Grace rises against it. The Laws in Wales Acts (1535-42) end the marcher lordships.

national/events.json.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England

locations/barnet/episodes.json.name: Battle of Barnet
locations/barnet/episodes.json.dateNote: Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471 (Julian calendar; 23 April by the modern calendar). Secure. Edward reached Barnet on the evening of 13 April and deployed in the dark; the Arrivall says the fight began between four and five in the morning and lasted about three hours, Warkworth from four until ten.
locations/barnet/episodes.json.summary: Edward IV, back from exile, marched out of London on 13 April 1471 and in the dark drew up his army close to that of the Earl of Warwick, which was already in position north of Barnet across the road to St Albans. They fought at dawn on Easter Sunday in thick mist, with the lines misaligned so that each overlapped the other at one end. The king's left was broken and fled through the town, but in the confusion Warwick's army collapsed; Warwick and his brother Montagu were killed. Where exactly on this ridge it happened is not known.
attested: Date, commanders and outcome: Edward IV, with his brothers Gloucester and Clarence and Lord Hastings, defeated Warwick, Montagu, Oxford and Exeter. Warwick and Montagu were killed, Exeter was left for dead, Oxford escaped.
Mist: the Arrivall speaks of 'a greate myste' that stopped either side seeing the other; Warkworth independently says neither could see the other perfectly.

Misaligned lines: the Arrivall says the hosts did not meet 'directly frount to frount'. At the west end Warwick's line overreached the king's and drove it back, with many fleeing 'towards Barnet, and so forthe to London'; at the east end the king's line overreached theirs.

The night before: Edward would not let his men stay in the town, lodged them much nearer the enemy than he supposed and kept silence; Warwick's guns fired through the night and 'alway ovarshote the Kyngs hoste'.
Warwick arrived first and chose the ground; the Arrivall has his people drawn up 'undre an hedge-syde' rather more than half a mile from Barnet. Other accounts say a mile, on a 'plain'.
A chapel for the dead was built afterwards on or near the field (Great Chronicle of London, about 1512).

Survey 2015–18: systematic metal-detecting, mainly in Wrotham Park, found no clear battle scatter. A few lead round shot found earlier in the Wrotham Park, Kitts End and Old Fold area are probably from the battle. No mass grave has been found.
tradition: Army sizes. The Arrivall (the king's side) gives 9,000 against 30,000; Warkworth gives Warwick 20,000. Modern figures of about 10,000–12,000 Yorkists against about 15,000 Lancastrians (Battlefields Trust; Barnet Museum gives 10,000–13,000 and 13,000–15,000) are estimates.

The textbook deployment (Lancastrians: Oxford on the right, Montagu in the centre, Exeter on the left, Warwick in reserve; Yorkists: Hastings left, Edward centre, Gloucester right) is a modern reconstruction, not something a contemporary wrote down.
Oxford's badge of a star with streams being mistaken for Edward's sun with streams, and the cry of 'Treason': from Warkworth alone.
Casualties: Warkworth says 4,000; other figures run from about 1,000 to 10,000. None is reliable.

'Dead Man's Bottom': a name for the valley running from Bentley Heath towards Monken Mead, marked in slightly different places on 17th-century and modern maps. The report notes it may have nothing to do with the battle.
The Hadley Highstone (an obelisk of 1740, later moved) marks a traditional spot for Warwick's death; there is no evidence for it.
unknown: Where the battle was fought within a zone about 2 km long from Hadley Green to Kitts End and beyond: the survey report weighs six possible deployments and concludes that the battlefield cannot yet be identified.
The position, length and facing of both lines, and where each commander stood.
The real size of either army.
Which hedge the 'hedge-side' was, and how much of the ground was open common and how much hedged closes in 1471.
Where Warwick and Montagu died, and where the dead were buried.
The number and position of guns on either side.
How dense the mist was, and for how long; the mist shown is a rendering choice.
locations/barnet/episodes.json.locationNote: The point given is the road fork at Hadley Highstone, between the registered area (Hadley Green) and the Kitts End alternative. Treat it as the middle of a zone of possibility, not a site.

locations/brentford/episodes.json.name: Battle of Brentford
locations/brentford/episodes.json.dateNote: 1016; day and month not recorded. In the Chronicle it comes 'within two nights' of Edmund's relief of London, after Cnut's siege had begun in May and after Edmund's fights at Penselwood and Sherston, and before the battle of Assandun and Edmund's death on St Andrew's day (30 November). Summer is likely but is an inference.
locations/brentford/episodes.json.summary: In 1016 Cnut's army besieged London. Edmund Ironside gathered a force, came to the city along the north side of the Thames and drove the besiegers to their ships. Within two nights he crossed the Thames at Brentford, fought the Danish army and put it to flight; many of the English were drowned, which the Chronicle blames on their own carelessness in going ahead of the army for plunder. Edmund then went to Wessex for more men and the Danes returned to London. That is all that is recorded. The scene shows the river, the ford and the banks as best they can be placed, with plain blocks of figures and shaded areas for where the armies may have been. Every one of those is a guess, and the model does not show the fight itself.
attested: The only narrative source is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1016: Edmund 'went over at Brentford; where he fought with the enemy, and put them to flight: but there many of the English were drowned, from their own carelessness; who went before the main army with a design to plunder'.

Just before, in the same entry: Edmund gathered his force a third time, went to London 'all by north of the Thames, and so out through Clayhanger', relieved the citizens and drove the enemy to their ships. Brentford followed 'within two nights'.
Just after: Edmund went into Wessex to gather his army, and the Danes soon returned to London and attacked it by land and water.

Later in the same year Edmund, with a fourth levy, 'forded over the Thames at Brentford' and went into Kent. The Thames could therefore be waded at Brentford by an army, at least at some states of the river.

Brentford was an established, named place: recorded from 705, in connection with a meeting of the kings of Wessex and Essex, and the seat of a council under Offa in 780 and a church synod in 781. Half of a Thames fishery there was granted to Winchester in 996.

The county history judges that the lowest permanent ford on the Thames was probably at Old England, the low ground at the Brent mouth, and (citing Stenton) that the battle was fought on the south bank.
tradition: That the fight was on the Surrey bank after a crossing from north to south: an inference from the order of words in the Chronicle. A poem in praise of Cnut has been read as implying fighting on both banks (reported by Wikipedia; not checked here).
That the English dead fell in the fighting and were not drowned: argued by Frank Stenton and Russell Poole, as reported by Wikipedia (not checked here).

That the crossing was at Old England, and that timber stakes found on the foreshore there defended the ford. The stakes are undated. The older claim that they are the stakes Julius Caesar met when he forced the Thames in 54 BCE is antiquarian tradition; Mortimer Wheeler doubted it in 1929.
That Cnut was 'twice driven back across the Thames at Brentford', as a local history page puts it. The Chronicle records one fight at Brentford and one later crossing by Edmund on his way into Kent.
A Danish strength of 8,000 to 12,000, given in Wikipedia's summary box, has no contemporary basis.
The granite monument at Brentford that commemorates Caesar's crossing and the battle marks tradition, not a located site.
unknown: Where the army crossed, and on which bank or banks the fighting took place.
The day and month.
Numbers on either side, and losses. The figures in the model are stand-ins and are not to scale with any army.
Whether Cnut was there in person, and who led the Danes on the day.
Where, when and how the drowning happened: at the crossing, in pursuit, or somewhere else on the river.
The state of the tide and the river, the weather, and whether the Danes had ships at hand.
What stood at Brentford in 1016. No late Saxon building has been excavated there.
The exact form of the river: its width, the shoals and islands, and the mouths of the Brent.

locations/london/episodes.json.name: Boudica's sack of Londinium
locations/london/episodes.json.dateNote: AD 60 or 61; season unknown. Tacitus puts the revolt under the consuls Caesennius Paetus and Petronius Turpilianus (the consuls of AD 61), but many scholars prefer 60 on the grounds that the events need more than one year. The RCHME volume on Roman London prefers 60; MOLA writes 'AD 60/61'. A Bloomberg writing tablet dated 21 October AD 62 shows London trading again by then, which fits either year. Use 60 with a visible 'or 61'.
locations/london/episodes.json.summary: During the revolt led by Boudica of the Iceni, the governor Suetonius Paulinus reached Londinium ahead of the rebels, judged he had too few troops to hold it, and withdrew, taking those who could march with him. The rebels then destroyed the town and killed those who stayed. Excavation across the City and at the Southwark bridgehead has found a layer of burnt debris of this date. The town was rebuilt within a few years and a fort was built on the eastern hill about AD 63.
attested: Tacitus (Annals 14.33) is the only ancient writer to name Londinium in this context. He calls it a busy centre of merchants and goods, says Suetonius marched there, considered making it his base, decided to sacrifice the one town to save the province, and left; those who stayed behind were killed. Verulamium suffered the same.
Tacitus says Londinium did not have the status of a colonia. It was a trading town about a decade or so old.
There was no defence of the town: the governor abandoned it. No pitched fight at London is described in any source.

A widespread layer of burnt red clay (daub), charred wood and debris, containing pre-60 coins and samian pottery, is recorded on City sites between the Walbrook and the bridgehead. MOLA treats the 'Boudican destruction of the settlement in AD 60' as an event documented by both archaeology and text, and uses it as a dating horizon.

Burning of this date has also been found in buildings beside the Roman road at the south end of the bridge in Southwark (reported from the mid-1990s onward), so the destruction is taken to have crossed the river.
Buildings of the period were timber and clay (wattle-and-daub or mud-brick) and mostly low; burnt daub is the main component of the layer.

Recovery: a stylus tablet from the Bloomberg site records a contract dated 21 October AD 62 to bring twenty loads of provisions from Verulamium to London; a fort of about 3.7 acres with earth-and-timber ramparts and double ditches was built at Plantation Place (Fenchurch Street) in about AD 63.
tradition: Casualties: Tacitus gives 'close upon seventy thousand' Roman citizens and allies killed across the places attacked (Camulodunum, Londinium, Verulamium together, not London alone). Cassius Dio gives 80,000 and 'two cities' sacked, without naming London. Both are rhetorical round numbers; the Loeb editor's note on Tacitus calls the figure probably valueless.

Atrocities: Dio's detailed account of mutilation and impalement of captives is not tied to London and has no archaeological support. Dio survives here only in a later epitome and wrote about 150 years after the event (epitome status not verified here).
Rebel army size: Dio gives 120,000 at the outset and 230,000 at the final battle. Not usable.

Layer thickness: a secondary website gives 'typically 30-60 cm' of bright red burnt daub, with pits filled to 1.5 m; the 1928 RCHME survey records the layer at 10-13 ft below modern ground. No primary excavation figure was verified here, and the figure will vary site to site.
Population of Londinium in AD 60: modern estimates of roughly 9,000-10,000 circulate in popular accounts (seen only in search results, not verified here). There is no ancient figure.
Skulls from the Walbrook as massacre victims: an old suggestion repeated in the press; not established.
unknown: The month and season, time of day, weather, and how long the destruction took.
The direction from which the rebels approached and whether they crossed the bridge or the river to reach Southwark.
How many people remained in the town and how many died there.
Whether Boudica was present in person, and what the rebels looked like in detail.
The exact street plan and building-by-building layout of the pre-revolt town; the form of the bridge or crossing in AD 60.
Whether the whole built area burned or only parts of it; the mapped extent in Southwark.
locations/london/episodes.json.locationNote: Site well known in general, not in detail. The pre-revolt town lay on the eastern hill (Cornhill) between the Walbrook and the area north of the bridgehead, with some occupation west of the Walbrook and a suburb at the south end of the bridge in Southwark. The burnt horizon has been recorded on many City sites (King William Street, Lombard Street, Eastcheap, Miles Lane, Fenchurch Street, the Walbrook west bank) and beside the road at the Southwark bridgehead. The point given is an approximate centre of the early town, not a find spot.

locations/london/episodes.json.name: Battle of London Bridge
locations/london/episodes.json.dateNote: Uncertain. Snorri places it after Swein Forkbeard's death (February 1014) as part of Aethelred's return, hence the usual '1014'; Hagland and Watson accept 1014 following Ian Howard's chronology. Olaf's early career is poorly dated and he is also associated with Thorkell's army, which attacked London unsuccessfully in 1009-10, so some place his London fighting then, and on the Danish side. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1014 says only that Aethelred came home in Lent and was gladly received.
locations/london/episodes.json.summary: Aethelred returned from exile in 1014 after Swein's death and recovered his kingdom; London was central to that. Norse court poetry composed for Olaf Haraldsson credits him with fighting at London and, in one stanza, with breaking 'Lundúna bryggjur'. About two centuries later Snorri Sturluson built these verses into a detailed story of Olaf's ships pulling the bridge down. No English source mentions such an attack. The bridge here is not shown falling.
attested: A fortified timber bridge at London existed at this time: structural timbers are tree-ring dated to c. 987-1032, and the bridge is mentioned in the law code IV Aethelred.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle shows the bridge mattered militarily: in 1013 part of Swein's army drowned in the Thames because they did not use a bridge, and London held out for Aethelred and Thorkell; in 1016 Cnut's ships could not pass it.
Aethelred returned in Lent 1014 and then drove Cnut out of Lindsey (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).

Near-contemporary skaldic verse exists: Ottarr svarti's Hofudlausn, stanza 7, addresses Olaf with 'you broke the bryggjur of London'; Sigvatr Thordarson's Vikingarvisur lists a battle of Olaf's at London and Sudvirki (Southwark). These are praise poems by Olaf's own poets.
Olaf was venerated in London soon afterwards: six medieval churches in London and Southwark were dedicated to him, one at the south end of the bridge (Tooley Street is a corruption of St Olave's).
tradition: The whole narrative of the attack comes from Snorri's Heimskringla (Saga of St Olaf, written c. 1230): Danes holding London and a fortification at Southwark with large ditches and a rampart of timber, stone and turf; a bridge wide enough for two wagons to pass, with towers and breast-high wooden parapets on the downstream side, standing on piles.

The tactics are Snorri's alone: Olaf roofed his ships with platforms made from pulled-down houses (wood bound with hazel or withies, often rendered 'wattle' or 'wickerwork' in modern retellings) on stout posts, rowed up under the bridge under a hail of stones and missiles, fastened cables round the piles, and rowed hard downstream until the piles loosened and the loaded bridge gave way; Southwark was then stormed and London submitted to Aethelred.
That 'bryggjur' means the bridge: the word is plural and can mean wharves or jetties. The editor of Sigvatr's poem argues that his stanza refers to London's wharves, not its bridge.
That Olaf fought for Aethelred: this is Snorri's framing; the Encyclopaedia Romana page notes other sources put Olaf on the Danish side.
The link to the nursery rhyme 'London Bridge is falling down': Samuel Laing's 1844 translation was phrased to echo the rhyme; John Clark's study rejects the folk-memory idea.
unknown: Whether any attack on the bridge happened at all, and if so in which year and on which side Olaf fought.
Whether the bridge was pulled down, damaged, or simply fought over. Hagland and Watson, who think the attack plausible, say the damage may well be exaggerated.
The actual form of the bridge superstructure and of any Southwark defences in 1014; no excavated evidence fixes them for this date.
Numbers of ships and men, the defenders' identity, the season, weather and tide.
Whether 9th-11th-century axes, spearheads and a grappling iron dredged near the bridge relate to fighting at all (they may be carpenters' losses).
locations/london/episodes.json.locationNote: The place is known; the event is not. A timber bridge existed by about 1000 (first phase built of timber felled c. 987-1032) on roughly the line of the later medieval bridge, a little downstream of the present London Bridge, with Southwark at its south end. The point given is approximate mid-river on that line.

locations/london/episodes.json.name: Battle of Brentford
locations/london/episodes.json.dateNote: Summer 1016; day and month not recorded. In the Chronicle's sequence it follows Cnut's siege of London (begun about May), Edmund's fights at Penselwood and Sherston (after midsummer) and his relief of London, with Brentford 'two days' after the relief. It precedes Assandun (18 October 1016).
locations/london/episodes.json.offMap: About 15 km west of the modelled area, up the Thames.
locations/london/episodes.json.summary: In 1016 Cnut's army besieged London, digging a ditch on the south side and dragging its ships to the west of the bridge. Edmund Ironside relieved the city, and two days later crossed the Thames at Brentford and fought the Danish army, putting it to flight. Many of the English were lost by drowning, which the Chronicle blames on their own carelessness in going ahead of the army for plunder. Edmund then went to Wessex to raise more men and the Danes returned to besiege London.
attested: The only narrative source is the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 1016: Edmund 'went over at Brentford', fought the army and put it to flight; many English drowned through their own carelessness, having gone ahead of the main force hoping for booty.

Context in the same entry: the Danish ships came to Greenwich and then London, 'dug a great ditch on the south side and dragged their ships to the west side of the bridge', then enclosed the city with a ditch so that no one could get in or out; the city held.
The bridge was held against Cnut in 1016, which is why the ships had to be taken round it through north Southwark.
After the battle Edmund went to Wessex to gather the army and the Danes resumed the siege of London; later in the year Edmund 'forded over the Thames at Brentford' a second time on his way into Kent.
An anonymous skaldic poem, Lidsmannaflokkr, in the voice of a Danish soldier, celebrates fighting by the Thames and beside the dyke at London in this campaign (it does not describe Brentford).
tradition: That the battle was fought on the south (Surrey) bank after a crossing from north to south: an inference from the Chronicle's wording, repeated by the Victoria County History. Wikipedia reports that Knutsdrapa has been read as implying fighting on both banks (lead only, not verified here).
That the English dead were battle casualties, not drowned: argued by Frank Stenton and Russell Poole according to Wikipedia (lead only, not verified here).
That the crossing was at Old England by the Brent mouth, and that the foreshore stakes there relate to a defended ford: possible, unproven, and the stakes are undated in the source read.
The modern Brentford monument listing the battle marks tradition, not a located site.
A Danish strength of 8,000-12,000 appears in Wikipedia's infobox without contemporary basis.
unknown: The date, the exact crossing point, and which bank the fighting was on.
Whether Cnut was present in person; who commanded the Danes on the day.
Numbers on either side and losses.
Where and how the drowning happened (at the ford on the crossing, or in pursuit).
The course and width of Cnut's ditch through Southwark; no excavated trace was verified here.
The state of the tide, the weather, and the look of the riverbank (the Thames here was wider, shallower and braided with aits).
locations/london/episodes.json.locationNote: Poorly known. The Chronicle says only that Edmund crossed the Thames at Brentford. The Victoria County History notes the place-name is usually taken to mean the ford over the Brent, though a Thames crossing is possible, and that stakes on the foreshore at 'Old England' (near the Brent-Thames confluence, by Syon) may have defended a ford; it places the 1016 fight on the south bank. The point given is the approximate Brent-Thames confluence and is a placeholder, not a located battlefield. No archaeology of the battle is known.

locations/london/episodes.json.name: Battle of Barnet
locations/london/episodes.json.dateNote: Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471 (Julian calendar). Secure. Edward left London about 4 pm on 13 April and deployed in the dark; fighting began around dawn. Warkworth says about 4 am to 10 am; other accounts imply a shorter fight.
locations/london/episodes.json.offMap: About 17 km north-north-west of the modelled area, on the Great North Road.
locations/london/episodes.json.summary: Edward IV, returned from exile, marched out of London on 13 April 1471 and deployed at night close to the army of the Earl of Warwick north of Barnet. The armies fought at dawn on Easter Sunday in thick mist, their lines misaligned so that each overlapped the other at one end. Edward won; Warwick and his brother John Neville, Marquess Montagu, were killed. Their bodies were displayed at St Paul's, and Edward went on to defeat Margaret of Anjou's army at Tewkesbury on 4 May.
attested: Date, commanders and outcome: Edward IV defeated Warwick; Warwick and Montagu were killed; the Duke of Exeter was badly wounded and left for dead; the Earl of Oxford escaped. Henry VI was brought to the field with Edward's army and returned to the Tower.
Mist or fog: reported independently by the Arrivall, Warkworth and Gerhard von Wesel's newsletter of 17 April 1471 (which says the fog was also in London).

Misaligned lines: the Arrivall says the two battles did not meet 'directly frount to frount' because of the mist. At the west end the Lancastrians overreached the king's line and drove it back, with fugitives fleeing through Barnet towards London; at the east end the king's line overreached theirs.
Night before: Edward would not let his men stay in the town, lodged them very close to the enemy and kept silence; Warwick's guns fired through the night and overshot.

Warwick had arrived first and chose the ground; the Arrivall has him 'undre an hedge-syde' somewhat more than half a mile from Barnet; von Wesel and the Great Chronicle of London imply nearer a mile. The battle was fought on foot.

Yorkist order of march and battle (Great Chronicle of London, Hall): Gloucester the vanguard, Edward with Clarence the main battle, Hastings the rearward. Oxford led the Lancastrian vanguard and routed the wing opposite him, which was Hastings's.
A chapel for the dead was established near the field soon after; the hermitage chapel at Kitts End is the usual candidate, but geophysics there found a moat and no graves.
Survey finds 2015-18: of 1,007 recorded objects only 16-17 were certainly medieval; a few lead round shot are known from the Wrotham Park / Kitts End / Old Fold area. No mass grave has been found.
tradition: Army sizes: the sources contradict each other along party lines. Arrivall (Yorkist): 9,000 against 30,000. Warkworth: Edward about 7,000-8,000 against Warwick 20,000. Von Wesel: Edward 15,000-20,000. Polydore Vergil (decades later): Edward 'far superior' in numbers. Modern compromise figures (Hammond: about 12,000 Yorkists, 15,000 Lancastrians; others 10,000 and 15,000) are estimates, and the project report notes historians now tend to reduce such numbers further.

The tidy textbook deployment (Lancastrians: Oxford right, Montagu centre, Exeter left, Warwick in reserve; Yorkists: Hastings left, Edward centre, Gloucester right) is a modern reconstruction. The wing positions are inferred from military convention (vanguard on the right) plus the Arrivall; Hall, the only chronicler to give a Lancastrian order, puts Oxford and Montagu on the left, Warwick and Exeter on the right, and Somerset (who was not there) in the centre.

Oxford's star badge mistaken for Edward's sun and the cry of 'Treason': from Warkworth alone. The History of Parliament notes it 'is perhaps not to be taken too seriously' and that there is no evidence a star with streams was a de Vere badge.
Montagu wearing Edward's livery and being killed by Warwick's own men (Warkworth): regarded as improbable.
Warwick killed fleeing to a wood, or while reaching his horse: details vary by source. The Hadley Highstone obelisk (1740) marks a traditional spot only.

Casualties: Sir John Paston's letter says over 1,000 besides the notables; Warkworth about 4,000; a foreign report 10,000; von Wesel says more than 10,000 broken arrows lay on the field. None is reliable.

Place-names 'Gladmore Heath' and 'Dead Man's Bottom': the project report shows 'Gladmore Heath' grew out of a map label ('Gladmore heath field') on Norden's 1598 map, and treats Dead Man's Bottom as a late, possibly spurious association.
unknown: The exact position, length and orientation of both battle lines (probably roughly east-west across or beside the St Albans road, but six different deployments are considered possible in the project report).
The real size of either army and of each division, and where Warwick, Montagu and Exeter each stood.
Where Warwick and Montagu died.
The number, type and position of guns on either side.
How far the landscape was open heath or hedged enclosure in 1471 (the commons were probably larger than later maps show).
How long the fighting lasted and how dense the mist was through the morning.
locations/london/episodes.json.locationNote: The general area is certain (north of High Barnet along the old St Albans road); the exact battlefield is not. English Heritage registered a battlefield in 1995 centred on Hadley Green / Monken Hadley, following a National Army Museum report. The 2015-18 Barnet Battlefield Project (University of Huddersfield, with the Battlefields Trust and Barnet Museum) concluded 'we cannot accurately identify the battlefield': sources agree it lay between half a mile and a mile north of the town, the terrain of the former Kicks End (Kitts End) Common about 1.9 km north of the Barnet boundary best fits them, and Hadley Green is 'problematic'; but metal-detecting found no conclusive battle scatter. Watson (2022) gives the current best guess as a circle of 1 km radius centred on Kitts End. The point given is near Hadley Highstone, between the registered area and Kitts End; treat it as the middle of a zone roughly 2 km long, not a site.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Midsummer sunrise along the axis, c. 2500 BCE
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: Late June (about 21 June by the solar year) in the sarsen-circle era. The year is a representative one inside 2580 to 2400 BCE; the day is the solstice by astronomy, not a recorded date.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: Looking from inside the circle north-east along the monument's axis, past the Heel Stone and down the first stretch of the Avenue, towards where the sun comes up on the longest day. The scene's one fixed sun is NOT moved: the white line and sun disc are an overlay marking the computed direction (azimuth about 48 to 49 degrees), not real lighting. For 2500 BCE, with the sun's upper edge just visible and standard refraction, the sunrise point is at azimuth 48.2 degrees on a flat horizon or 49.2 degrees if the horizon is raised 0.6 degrees. The Avenue's first straight stretch leaves the stones at about 49.9 degrees (from OpenStreetMap mapping), and the Heel Stone lies at about 51 degrees from the centre, so the sun rose slightly to the left of both. The true horizon height to the north-east was not taken from any source read.
attested: The monument's main axis runs north-east to south-west, shared by the trilithon horseshoe, the bluestone settings, the sarsen circle and the first stretch of the Avenue (Darvill et al. 2012).
Midsummer sunrise is seen over and slightly to the left of the Heel Stone and falls within the Avenue (Sky at Night).

The first straight stretch of the Avenue leaves the stones at azimuth about 49.9 degrees, measured from OpenStreetMap-mapped earthwork outlines (this project's geography research, not a survey azimuth).
William Stukeley recognised the solstice axis in 1720.
tradition: That the builders meant midsummer sunrise: Ruggles favours midwinter as the more important; Hawkins's 1960s claims are generally treated as over-optimistic.
That crowds gathered at the stones on this morning in 2500 BCE; the figures are not shown.
unknown: What, if anything, was done at the stones on midsummer morning, and whether the alignment was meant to be precise to a degree.
The altitude of the true horizon north-east of the stones (woodland, relief): the computed range uses a flat 0 degree and a 0.6 degree horizon as an assumption.
Today the same sunrise is about 1 degree larger in azimuth (49.2 degrees on a flat horizon) because the Earth's axial tilt has fallen from about 24.0 to 23.4 degrees.

Computed with cos A = (sin d - sin phi sin h) / (cos phi cos h), latitude 51.179 degrees, obliquity 23.97 degrees (Laskar series, 2500 BCE), refraction 0.57 degrees, solar semi-diameter 0.27 degrees: my calculation, not a source.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Midwinter sunset through the Great Trilithon, c. 2500 BCE
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: Late December (about 21 December by the solar year) in the sarsen-circle era; a representative year inside 2580 to 2400 BCE, the day fixed by astronomy.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: From the Avenue, 110 m north-east of the centre, looking south-west through the circle at the Great Trilithon on the day of the shortest sun. As in the sunrise episode the scene's single fixed sun is not moved: the line and disc are an overlay marking the computed sunset direction. For 2500 BCE, upper edge just visible with standard refraction, the sun set at azimuth 231.0 degrees on a flat horizon or 230.0 degrees if the horizon is raised 0.6 degrees, within about a degree of the reverse of the Avenue's first stretch (229.9 degrees). Ruggles favours midwinter as the more important of the two solstices, and Parker Pearson cites the midwinter feasting at Durrington Walls; that is interpretation. The horizon height to the south-west was not measured from any source read.
attested: From the far end of the Avenue the midwinter sunset can be seen through the central arches (Sky at Night).
The Avenue's first straight stretch, the trilithon horseshoe and the circles share one axis, open to the north-east and facing the Great Trilithon in the south-west (Darvill et al. 2012).
Durrington Walls pig-tooth evidence points to midwinter slaughter and feasting (cited by Parker Pearson in the Sky at Night account).
tradition: That the monument was built to frame the midwinter sunset (Ruggles's preferred reading; Darvill argues the trilithon layout points to a midwinter focus). Midsummer sunrise as the main intent is the older, popular view.
That people gathered on this evening; none are drawn.
unknown: What ceremonies took place, and whether the alignment was precise to better than a degree.
The altitude of the south-west horizon, so the exact azimuth range: 230.0 to 231.0 degrees assumes a 0 to 0.6 degree horizon, my assumption.
Today the sunset is about 1 degree larger in azimuth (231.0 degrees flat horizon) than in 2500 BCE. Computed as in the sunrise episode; my calculation, not a source.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Raising the sarsens
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: c. 2560 to 2470 BCE in the model; the sarsen circle is dated 2580 to 2475 BCE and the trilithons 2585 to 2400 BCE (93%) by the English Heritage Bayesian model. The day is arbitrary.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: The great sarsen stones go up. The sarsen circle (30 uprights carrying a ring of 30 lintels) and the five trilithons are built over perhaps a century; the model shows the circle part-way through.
