The stones were dragged from the Marlborough Downs, about 25 km north, and shaped on site; the lintels were fitted with mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints borrowed from carpentry. How they were moved and raised is not known: the stones rising smoothly from the ground is the site's way of showing 'under construction', not a method.
attested: A sarsen circle of 30 uprights and 30 lintels, outer diameter about 29.6 m, was designed (Darvill et al. 2012); the uprights are about 4.1 m high, the lintel tops about 4.9 m above ground.
Five trilithons form a horseshoe about 13.7 m across, open to the north-east; the tallest stone (56) stands about 6.7 m above ground with about 2.4 m buried.
Radiocarbon dating of an antler in the socket of stones 53 and 54 gives 2585 to 2400 BCE (93%).
The sarsens come from the Marlborough Downs about 25 km north (English Heritage; Nash et al. 2020, from a search summary only).
tradition: Geoffrey of Monmouth's tale that Merlin brought the stones from Ireland (1136) is legend.
unknown: How the stones were transported and raised, how many people it took and how long it took.

Whether the sarsen circle was ever completed: stones 13, 17, 18, 20 and 24 and 24 lintels are missing today. Ashbee argued it was never finished; Darvill thinks it was robbed; parchmarks from 2013 hint at a complete circle. Unresolved.
The order of the trilithons, circle and bluestone settings within Stage 2.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Midwinter feasting at Durrington Walls, c. 2500 BCE
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: Late December in a representative year of the village's decade or so of use (c. 2515 to 2480 BCE in the model). The village is dated 2600 to 2500 BCE (2007 release) and, by later modelling, to roughly 10 to 12 years ending 2500 to 2460 BCE.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: A village of small square houses with clay floors stands inside the great timber ring at Durrington Walls, about 2.8 km east of Stonehenge on the Avon. Pig teeth from the site point to animals slaughtered in the winter, and the Southern Circle there is oriented to the midwinter sunrise; the usual reading is that people came here for midwinter feasts and, after the village was abandoned, the timber ring was replaced by a henge bank. How many houses there were and how many people came is not known, and none are drawn.
attested: Eight houses about 5 m (16 ft) square, with clay floors, central hearths and box-bed and dresser outlines, were excavated in 2006.
Occupation was brief, about 10 to 12 years, with chalk floors renewed at most nine times (Bayesian modelling).
Pig-tooth evidence points to midwinter slaughter (cited by Parker Pearson in the Sky at Night account); the Southern Circle is oriented to midwinter sunrise (Wikipedia).
Up to about 300 timber posts in a ring 440 to 450 m across stood under the later bank; they were pulled about 2480 BCE.
tradition: That Durrington's occupants were connected with building or using Stonehenge: widely suggested, not proven by the sources read.
That feasting here was tied to a midwinter gathering at Stonehenge, 'up to 4,000 people' being an upper-end speculation.
unknown: The number of houses and people (a few dozen houses are drawn, conjecturally), and exactly where in the henge they stood.
What the timber ring and the circles were for; whether the Avenue to the river was walked at this season.
The height of the posts (5 m per the 2016 excavations, 7 m per Wikipedia: conflict).

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Bush Barrow burial, c. 1900 BCE
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: Wikipedia gives c. 1950 BCE for the burial and the Wilsford G7 group 2000 to 1800 BCE; 1900 BCE is a display year inside the uncertainty.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: Bush Barrow, on the Normanton Down ridge about 1.1 km south-south-west of Stonehenge, is a large round barrow about 49 m across and 3.3 m high, holds a rich Early Bronze Age burial with gold, dated about 1950 BCE. The gold lozenge plate measures about 184 by 156 mm. Round barrows of this period fill the ridges around the stones; here the scene is the barrow standing new on the skyline. Who was buried there is not known from the research notes.
attested: Bush Barrow lies on Normanton Down, 3.3 m high and 49 m overall (or 40 m wide by another count).
It held an Early Bronze Age burial with a gold lozenge about 184 x 156 x 1 mm, dated about 1950 BCE.
Normanton Down has about 40 round barrows (bowl, bell, disc and a saucer), of which at least 35 were surviving in 1957, with burials between about 2600 and 1600 BCE.
tradition: That the burial was a chieftain's or king's: 'chieftain' is a modern label.
That the barrows were meant to be seen from the stones, or the reverse.
unknown: The buried person's name, status or relation to Stonehenge, and the exact date of the burial.
The barrow's original form: its present shape is modern survey, and the model's 'new' mound is generic.
The other grave goods are not itemised in the research notes for this project.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Amesbury Abbey founded, 979
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: c. 979. The foundation date is approximate; the day is arbitrary.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: A Benedictine abbey is founded at Amesbury, in the Avon valley east of Stonehenge, by Queen Aelfthryth. It later becomes a Fontevraud priory (1177) and is dissolved about 1540. What it looked like in 979 and where exactly it stood within Amesbury are not known from the sources read; the precinct on the map is a conjectural rectangle by the church, and the buildings are placeholders.
attested: A Benedictine abbey was founded at Amesbury c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth (Wikipedia).
It was refounded as a Fontevraud priory in 1177 and dissolved c. 1540; the estate went to the Seymours.
The parish church of St Mary and St Melor may be the surviving priory church (Wikipedia; unproven).
unknown: The site, size and form of the 10th-century buildings, and the precinct's boundary.
Whether the Dissolution date is 1539 or 1540: sources conflict.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Inigo Jones surveys Stonehenge for James I, 1620
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: 1620; the fraction 0.6 is an arbitrary display value, no month is known from the sources read. The survey and the Duke of Buckingham's digging are both given as 1620, though English Heritage also says 'the 1620s'.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: King James I, visiting Wilton House in 1620, asks the architect Inigo Jones to survey the stones. Jones's plan (published by his pupil John Webb in 1655) shows an idealised, regular monument which he reads as a Roman temple. The same year the Duke of Buckingham has the centre dug, the first known excavation there. The view shows the stones as they are thought to have stood, with the great trilithon down and the south-west trilithon still standing; which stones stood or lay in 1625 is largely inferred. Jones's plan is a restoration, not a record.
attested: Jones surveyed Stonehenge for James I in the 1620s (English Heritage); Webb's 1655 publication reports the king's commission after his visit to Wilton in 1620.
The Duke of Buckingham's digging in the centre is the first known excavation there (English Heritage).
Stone 55 and the Great Trilithon had fallen before the first 17th-century plans (Darvill); the south-west trilithon (57 and 58 with lintel 158) stood until 1797.
tradition: Jones's claim that Stonehenge was a Roman temple: now rejected.
unknown: Which other stones were fallen, leaning or broken in 1625: no dated record; the model uses inference from later plans.
How accurately Jones measured: his plan is an ideal geometry and cannot be used as a measured survey.

locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.name: Robin Hood's Ball causewayed enclosure, c. 3550 BCE
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.dateNote: 'Centuries around 3500 BC' (English Heritage); Wikipedia: probably built c. 4000 BC, possibly used to c. 3000 BC. Low confidence.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.offMap: Robin Hood's Ball lies about 3.8 km north and 2 km west of the stones, 1 km beyond the north edge of this map, so it cannot be shown here. It is an earlier Neolithic causewayed enclosure with two ditch circuits and low banks, never comprehensively excavated.
locations/stonehenge/episodes.json.summary: One of the first lasting monuments of the Stonehenge landscape, a causewayed enclosure on high ground north of the later Cursus, built when the ditches were fresh white chalk. Its size, internal features and end date are not known.
attested: A causewayed enclosure with two ditch circuits and low banks, with one causeway noted by Wikipedia.
Dated to the centuries around 3500 BCE by English Heritage.
unknown: Its diameter, internal features and the date it went out of use.

locations/barnet/zones.json.label: Chipping Barnet town
locations/barnet/zones.json.note: A small market town strung along the main road on the hilltop, with a Thursday market granted to the abbot of St Albans in 1199 and a chapel where Wood Street branches west. Houses are generic and stand on a lattice, not on real plots. The town's extent in 1471 is not known: there is no early map, and the survey report notes that even its northern end is uncertain (by 1553 shops and cottages had spread north beside Hadley Green). The outline is a guess of about 70 m either side of the street.

locations/barnet/zones.json.label: Hadley village
locations/barnet/zones.json.note: A small, partly green-edge village near the church. Inhabitants of Hadley are named in the 14th century (a William atte Green in 1345) and timber-framed cottages from Hadley Green contained 15th-century work, so some houses stood here in 1471; how many and exactly where is unknown. The later rows along the north and east of the green may be encroachments made after the battle, so they are not shown.

locations/barnet/zones.json.label: Kitts End hamlet
locations/barnet/zones.json.note: A few houses on the west side of the St Albans road. Kitts (Kicks) End is first named in 1479, eight years after the battle; the report accepts that it existed by then but says its extent is unknown and that it may have lain only along the west side of the road. Showing it from 1400 is an assumption. The large coaching hamlet with eight inns belongs to the 17th and 18th centuries and was later swallowed by Wrotham Park.

locations/barnet/zones.json.label: Heath on Kicks End Common
locations/barnet/zones.json.note: Rough heath and furze standing for the open common between the two roads, called Kitts End Heath in 1479 and inclosed in 1781. The common was open in 1471 and was probably larger than later maps show; its vegetation and exact bounds are not recorded.

locations/barnet/zones.json.label: Rough ground on Hadley Green
locations/barnet/zones.json.note: A light scatter of scrub on the old common of Hadley, a grazed green crossed by the main road and never part of Enfield Chase. Its medieval extent probably reached further north-east, opening into the Chase; the outline used is the modern green.

locations/barnet/zones.json.label: Wood-pasture on the edge of Enfield Chase
locations/barnet/zones.json.note: Open pasture with scattered thorn and trees east of the Chase boundary. A map of 1701 shows this western fringe of the Chase almost bare of coppices, and the report suggests that may reflect its late medieval character; nothing records it directly for 1471.

locations/brentford/zones.json.label: Roadside settlement at Old Brentford (conjectural)
locations/brentford/zones.json.note: A handful of timber halls beside the road. Brentford was a named place where kings and councils met in 705, 780 and 781, a fishery existed by 996 and an army could cross here in 1016, so some people probably lived nearby; but excavation has found Saxon occupation at only one site, at Old Brentford, and the county history states that no trace of late Saxon occupation has been found. The cluster is placed at Old Brentford for that one site; its position, size and number of buildings are guesses. Buildings are the engine's generic single-storey timber halls. It is shown as already present when the model begins in 950; when it began is not known.

locations/brentford/zones.json.label: Farmstead by the Brent crossing (conjectural)
locations/brentford/zones.json.note: Two or three buildings east of the Brent crossing, appearing late in the window. New Brentford is first heard of about 1170 as Bordwadestone, 'presumably Bord's tun or farm', within Westminster Abbey's manor of Hanwell. Nothing dates the farm's beginning; the years 1040 to 1090 are an arbitrary way of showing that settlement here was probably later and smaller than at Old Brentford. It is the only change shown between 950 and 1100, and it is a guess.

locations/brentford/zones.json.label: Willow and scrub along the Syon bank (conjectural)
locations/brentford/zones.json.note: Rough growth on the low alluvial strip of the Middlesex bank above the Brent. The bank at Syon is still a natural tidal meadow flooded by the river; what grew there about 1000 is not recorded, and the scrub is a plausible guess. It is shown as already present when the model begins in 950; when it began is not known.

locations/brentford/zones.json.label: Scrub on the low Surrey bank (conjectural)
locations/brentford/zones.json.note: Kew is not recorded before the 14th century and lay within the royal manor later called Richmond; an 18th-century description calls the ground 'dead flat' with barren soil. Nothing is known of this bank about 1000. Thin scrub on low, damp ground is a guess, and no settlement is shown because none is evidenced. It is shown as already present when the model begins in 950; when it began is not known.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Late prehistoric farmsteads
locations/london/zones.json.note: A handful of roundhouses standing for scattered later prehistoric farming. Bronze Age ploughing on the Southwark eyots is excavated but was short-lived (mid 2nd millennium BCE) before rising water buried it; no house shown here is an excavated building, and the mainstream view is that no pre-Roman settlement stood on the site of the City.

locations/london/zones.json.label: First Londinium (c. 48–60)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Timber and clay buildings around Cornhill and the bridgehead, perhaps 10,000 people by 60 CE, destroyed in the Boudican revolt (a burnt layer is found across this area). The earliest dated feature is a roadside drain of 47 CE. Extent approximate; buildings generic.

locations/london/zones.json.label: First Roman Southwark
locations/london/zones.json.note: Roadside settlement on the north island, also burned in 60/61.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Londinium: timber buildings (c. 62–130)
locations/london/zones.json.note: The rebuilt and expanding town up to the Hadrianic fire (c. 120–130, probably mid 120s). The fire was extensive but not total, and rebuilding followed at lower density; showing this whole class of buildings burning is a simplification.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Londinium: larger and stone buildings
locations/london/zones.json.note: Stone-founded town houses and public buildings, which persisted into the 4th century while the town thinned out around them. Institutional estimates put the peak population at 20,000–30,000 by the mid 2nd century.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Londinium after the Hadrianic fire
locations/london/zones.json.note: Reduced rebuilding after the 120s and a long contraction of housing from the later 2nd century, when 'dark earth' began to accumulate over former building plots. No sourced population figure exists for the 3rd–4th centuries; the pace shown is illustrative.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Roman Southwark
locations/london/zones.json.note: A substantial suburb on the two islands south of the bridge, part of Londinium from the start, with some large stone buildings (not individually shown). Its extent in hectares and the pace of late Roman contraction are poorly known.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Scrub and rough ground inside the empty walls
locations/london/zones.json.note: Inside the walls there is an evidence gap from c. 410/450 to the mid–late 9th century. What grew there is not known; scrub among ruins is a plausible guess, and some of the ground may have been cultivated.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Settlement by St Paul's (7th–9th c.)
locations/london/zones.json.note: A cathedral implies some community inside the walls, but there is very little archaeological evidence for it. The cluster is a guess.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Lundenwic (c. 600/670–850s)
locations/london/zones.json.note: The Middle Saxon trading town around today's Covent Garden and Strand: first settled in the early 7th century, dense from the 670s, about 55–60 hectares at its peak c. 730–770. Decline began around 770, before the Viking raids of 842 and 851; a defensive ditch of the 840s is not modelled. Extent from excavation; buildings are generic single-storey timber halls of about 11 × 5.5 m.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Lundenburh: late Saxon city (886–c. 1100)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Alfred's re-establishment of 886 (reoccupation may have begun a generation earlier). Settlement began between Cheapside and the river and spread north of Cheapside only in the early 11th century. Timber buildings, generic.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Medieval city within the walls
locations/london/zones.json.note: Generic timber-framed houses filling the walled area: about 25,000 people c. 1100, 60,000–100,000 c. 1300, 40,000–50,000 c. 1400 after the Black Death (all estimates). Each model stands for several real buildings; streets follow a regular lattice, not the real street plan. The fires of 1087, 1135/36 and 1212 are not animated here.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Tudor and Jacobean city within the walls
locations/london/zones.json.note: Taller, jettied, tile-roofed timber houses replacing the medieval stock: about 50,000 people c. 1500 and about 200,000 by 1600 (estimates, including suburbs). Brick was required by proclamation from 1605 with little effect by 1625. Generic; each model stands for several real buildings.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Parish churches
locations/london/zones.json.note: London had about 126 parish churches, suburbs included, by c. 1180. The number is attested; the positions shown are evenly spread placeholders, not the real churches.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Medieval Southwark
locations/london/zones.json.note: The borough strung along the road south from the bridge. A late Saxon burh here is documented but no defences have ever been found.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Tudor Southwark and Bankside
locations/london/zones.json.note: Southwark grew quickly in the 16th century.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Bankside
locations/london/zones.json.note: The riverside strip of inns, stews, baiting rings and playhouses west of the bridge.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Fleet Street and Holborn (medieval)
locations/london/zones.json.note: The western suburb beyond Ludgate and Newgate, including the lawyers' inns.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Fleet Street, Holborn and the Inns (Tudor)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Continuous building now links the City to the Strand.

locations/london/zones.json.label: The Strand (medieval)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Ribbon development along the road to Westminster.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Strand palaces
locations/london/zones.json.note: The riverside town houses of bishops and, after the Reformation, of courtiers (Durham, York, Arundel, Essex Houses and others). The row is attested; the individual houses shown are generic.

locations/london/zones.json.label: The Strand and Covent Garden fringe (Tudor)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Covent Garden itself was still open ground in 1625; the piazza dates from the 1630s.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Westminster (medieval)
locations/london/zones.json.note: The town that grew up to serve the abbey and palace.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Westminster (Tudor and Jacobean)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Westminster and the court quarter around Whitehall.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Eastern suburbs (medieval)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Aldgate Without, East Smithfield and the St Katharine's precinct.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Eastern suburbs (Tudor and Jacobean)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Fast, poor-quality growth along the river and the Whitechapel road, which Stow deplored in 1598.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Northern suburbs (medieval)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Bishopsgate, Cripplegate and Aldersgate Without and the Smithfield fringe. Moorfields, a marsh until drained in the 16th century, is not separately modelled.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Northern suburbs (Tudor and Jacobean)
locations/london/zones.json.note: Suburban growth north of the wall.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Southwark bridge foot (medieval)
locations/london/zones.json.note: The densely built head of Borough High Street, Tooley Street and the approach to the bridge. Generic houses.

locations/london/zones.json.label: Southwark bridge foot (tudor)
locations/london/zones.json.note: The densely built head of Borough High Street, Tooley Street and the approach to the bridge. Generic houses.

locations/stonehenge/zones.json.label: Durrington Walls houses (Neolithic village)
locations/stonehenge/zones.json.note: Eight houses about 5 m square, with clay or chalk floors, central hearths and box-bed and dresser outlines, were excavated inside the later henge on its east side, towards the Avon (2006); modelling puts the village at only about 10-12 years' occupation ending c. 2500-2460 BCE (the 2007 release gave 2600-2500 BCE). The TOTAL NUMBER of houses is not known: 'up to 1000 houses' (Wikipedia) is an upper speculation, 'hundreds of people' the excavators' phrase. About 60 houses (a count chosen to give 'a few dozen') are drawn on a lattice inside the site polygon 'durrington-settlement' (about 1.1 ha on the east side of the enclosure, an approximation); positions are not surveyed. The village was abandoned about when the henge was dug (the ring of posts and the henge bank follow).

locations/stonehenge/zones.json.label: Amesbury town (medieval)
locations/stonehenge/zones.json.note: Amesbury was a crossing of the London to Exeter road with 111 households and eight mills at Domesday (1086); a Saxon settlement from the 7th century. Houses are generic, on a lattice, inside the site polygon 'amesbury-town' (an approximation round the OSM town point); the town's real extent and layout in any century are not known. The medieval houses are replaced in place by the tudor style from about 1480-1560 (a visual change of style, not a recorded rebuilding).

locations/stonehenge/zones.json.label: Amesbury town (Tudor)
locations/stonehenge/zones.json.note: The same lattice as the medieval town, in the taller Tudor style, standing until 1625. A generic stand-in: no source read describes Amesbury's buildings in the 16th and early 17th centuries.

locations/barnet/eras.json.name: The ridge before the battle
locations/barnet/eras.json.blurb: A small market town on its hilltop, the main road from London to St Albans and the north running across open greens and commons, a moated manor at Old Fold, a small church at Hadley on the edge of Enfield Chase. Barnet's chapel is rebuilt in these decades. How much of the land was hedged closes and how much was open heath is only partly known.

locations/barnet/eras.json.name: The battle and after
locations/barnet/eras.json.blurb: Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471: Edward IV and the Earl of Warwick fight at dawn in thick mist somewhere on this ridge. The two shaded zones and the blocks of figures appear for 1471 only and mark possibilities, not a located battlefield. A chapel for the dead follows, on a site still not proven, and Hadley church is rebuilt about 1494.

locations/brentford/eras.json.name: Late Anglo-Saxon Brentford
locations/brentford/eras.json.blurb: A named crossing place on the road west from London, where the Brent meets the Thames. Kings met here in 705 and church councils in 780 and 781, and half a Thames fishery at Brentford was granted away in 996, but no late Saxon building has been excavated. In 1016 Edmund Ironside crossed the Thames here twice in his war with Cnut.

locations/brentford/eras.json.name: After the Conquest
locations/brentford/eras.json.blurb: Brentford is not named in Domesday Book (1086); its ground lay within the manors of Isleworth, Hanwell and the bishop of London's Fulham. Nothing is recorded as changing here in these years, and the scene is left as it was.

locations/london/eras.json.name: Prehistoric Thames
locations/london/eras.json.blurb: A wide, braided tidal river between gravel terraces and marsh. Woodland is cleared gradually from the Bronze Age. No town stands here; evidence for settlement on the site of the later City is slight.

locations/london/eras.json.name: Roman Londinium
locations/london/eras.json.blurb: A new town founded around 47–50 CE beside a bridge. Burned in 60/61, rebuilt with a forum, amphitheatre, fort and quays, walled around 200, then shrinking through the 3rd and 4th centuries.

locations/london/eras.json.name: Post-Roman & Anglo-Saxon
locations/london/eras.json.blurb: The walled city is largely empty for generations. A trading settlement, Lundenwic, grows to the west along the Strand; from 886 settlement moves back inside the Roman walls.

locations/london/eras.json.name: Norman & Medieval London
locations/london/eras.json.blurb: The Tower, a vast cathedral, a stone bridge lined with houses, over a hundred parish churches and many religious houses. Westminster grows as a separate royal centre.

locations/london/eras.json.name: Tudor London
locations/london/eras.json.blurb: Rapid growth beyond the walls. The monasteries are dissolved and converted, St Paul's loses its spire (1561), the Royal Exchange opens and playhouses rise on Bankside.

locations/london/eras.json.name: Jacobean London
locations/london/eras.json.blurb: The city of James I: a crowded timber metropolis of roughly 200,000 or more, with the first strict classical building, the Banqueting House (1619–22), at Whitehall.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: Earlier Neolithic landscape
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: Before any stone is raised. Woodland is thinning into open chalk grassland. Robin Hood's Ball (just outside this map), long barrows and, by about 3500 BCE, the Greater Cursus mark the first lasting monuments; the Mesolithic pine posts near the later stones are older still and not shown. Dates are approximate and several rest on a single antler.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: First Stonehenge
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: Stage 1 in Darvill et al.'s chronology: a circular ditch and bank about 110 m across with a north-east and a smaller southern entrance, 56 Aubrey Holes (possibly holding the first bluestones, which is argued over) and many cremation burials. Timber structures are inferred from postholes. The model switches the ditch on about 3000 to 2900 BCE; the exact date is a range.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: Sarsens and Durrington
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: Stages 2 and 3. The trilithons, the sarsen circle and the first bluestone settings go up, c. 2620 to 2480 BCE; the Heel Stone, Slaughter Stone and Station Stones belong here too, with uncertain order. At Durrington Walls a village stands for a decade or so and a great timber circle is replaced by the henge bank, then Woodhenge. The Avenue is laid out in this era. Whether the sarsen circle was ever completed is unresolved.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: Beaker and Early Bronze Age
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: Stages 4 and 5. The bluestones are rearranged into an oval and a circle; the Y and Z holes are dug; axe and dagger carvings are made on the sarsens. Beaker burials appear (the Amesbury Archer, c. 2340 to 2300 BCE, lies outside this map). Round barrow cemeteries multiply on the ridges, among them Normanton Down and Bush Barrow.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: Later prehistory
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: Almost nothing is recorded at the stones themselves after the last stone settings (about 1500 BCE). Fields and enclosures spread; the land is largely cleared by 800 to 500 BCE; Vespasian's Camp hillfort is built, with a placeholder date of about 700 to 600 BCE. The model's stone states stay as left.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: Roman to medieval
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: Roman coins and pottery at the stones (late 4th century), a 7th-century execution burial, Amesbury Abbey (founded c. 979, refounded as a priory in 1177) and the first written accounts of the stones (Henry of Huntingdon c. 1130, Geoffrey of Monmouth c. 1136). No dated event changes the stones; which stood or lay by 1625 is inferred from later drawings and plans.

locations/stonehenge/eras.json.name: Tudor and Jacobean rediscovery
locations/stonehenge/eras.json.blurb: The priory is dissolved c. 1540 and the first drawings of the stones appear (de Heere 1573 to 75), then Camden's Britannia (1586) and, in 1620, Inigo Jones's survey for James I and the Duke of Buckingham's dig. These are the earliest views that can anchor the state of the stones.

national/eras.json.name: Neolithic: first farmers and great monuments
national/eras.json.blurb: Farming arrives about 4000 BCE. Communities clear patches of woodland, mine flint and quarry stone axes, and build long barrows, causewayed enclosures and, after 3000 BCE, henges and stone circles. There are no towns and few permanent villages.

national/eras.json.name: Bronze Age
national/eras.json.blurb: Metalworking, round barrows and, from about 1500 BCE, a countryside divided into fields and farmsteads. The great monuments fall out of use; offerings are made in rivers and fens instead.

national/eras.json.name: Iron Age
national/eras.json.blurb: Hillforts dominate much of the south and west until about 100 BCE. In the last century before the conquest, coin-issuing kingdoms and large lowland centres (oppida) appear in the south-east, in contact with Roman Gaul. The peoples named on the map are those recorded by Roman writers.

national/eras.json.name: Roman Britain
national/eras.json.blurb: Conquest from 43 CE brings forts, roads and a network of towns. The north and west stay under the army behind Hadrian's Wall. The province is split in two about 200 and into four about 300; towns shrink in the 4th century and Roman government ends about 410.

national/eras.json.name: Early Anglo-Saxon kingdoms
national/eras.json.blurb: Towns empty. English-speaking kingdoms form in the east and south while British kingdoms hold the west. Christianity returns from Rome (597) and Iona (635); by 700 there are monasteries, bishoprics and a few trading towns (wics), and Mercia is becoming the leading power.

national/eras.json.name: Viking Age and the making of England
national/eras.json.blurb: Raids from 793, then conquest: the Great Army destroys Northumbria, East Anglia and half of Mercia in 866-877. Wessex survives, fortifies its burhs and takes back the Danelaw. From 927 there is a single kingdom of the English, conquered in turn by Cnut in 1016.

national/eras.json.name: Norman and Angevin England
national/eras.json.blurb: The Norman Conquest replaces the ruling class and covers the country with castles, new cathedrals and monasteries. Domesday Book (1086) records it. Towns and population grow fast; Norman lords push into Wales and create the March.

national/eras.json.name: Later medieval England
national/eras.json.blurb: Population peaks about 1300, with new towns, ports and universities. Then famine (1315-17) and the Black Death (1348-9) roughly halve it. Wales is conquered in 1282-3. War with Scotland and France is followed by the Wars of the Roses.

national/eras.json.name: Tudor England and Wales
national/eras.json.blurb: The monasteries are dissolved (1536-40) and Wales is joined to England in law (1536-42). Population recovers; London grows far beyond every other town, cloth towns rise and some old cities decay.

national/eras.json.name: Jacobean England and Wales
national/eras.json.blurb: James VI of Scotland inherits the English crown in 1603. About four to five million people, most of them in villages; London holds perhaps one in twenty of them and Norwich, Bristol, York and Newcastle follow far behind.

_meta.description: Stone-by-stone catalogue of Stonehenge (Petrie numbering). Positions: az = degrees clockwise from TRUE north, r = metres, both measured from the FITTED centre of the sarsen circle (not the provisional site origin). Sizes: w tangential width, t radial thickness, h height above ground (lintels: vertical depth; fallen stones: height when standing). state1625 reasoned backwards from Stukeley (1720s), Wood (1740), Barclay 1895 and dated 19th-20th century events.

centre.note: Fitted from OpenStreetMap stone outlines (sarsen ring, bluestone ring, Station Stones, Heel Stone); move the landmark anchor here or add this offset.

_meta.numbering: Petrie 1880: sarsen uprights 1-30 clockwise from the axis (stone 1 just east of it); lintel k = 100 + number of the higher (western, clockwise) of the two uprights it spans, so 102 is on 1-2 and 101 on 30-1; trilithons 51-60 clockwise from the NE-east end; bluestone circle 31-49; horseshoe 61-72.

Not attested individually in 1625.

locations/barnet/site.json.name: Barnet, 1471
locations/barnet/site.json.subtitle: The ridge north of Chipping Barnet where Edward IV defeated the Earl of Warwick, 1400 – 1500
locations/barnet/site.json.scopeNote: A landscape reconstruction of about 3 × 4 km from Chipping Barnet north through Hadley Green to Kitts End, built to show the ground of the Battle of Barnet (14 April 1471). The battle certainly happened somewhere along this stretch of road, but its exact position is disputed: the registered battlefield centres on Hadley Green, while the 2015–18 survey could not find the battlefield and judged that the ground around Kitts End fits the written sources better. Both areas are shown as shaded zones, not as a located site. The blocks of figures are abstract stand-ins on one modern interpretation: they do not show real numbers, real positions or individual people.

origin.note: The middle of Hadley Green, on the old road north from Chipping Barnet (modern A1000), about 850 m north of Barnet church. Chosen because it lies between the two candidate battlefield areas and is the one open space that survives. Local coordinates are metres east (x) and south (z) of this point.

hills.name: Hadley Common ridge (east of the church)
Ridge crest at the road fork (Hadley Highstone)

valleys.name: Valley south-east of Hadley (towards Pymmes Brook)
Fall to the Dollis Brook valley (south)
Fall to the Mimmshall Brook streams (west)

terrain.note: A flat-topped ridge of pebble gravel over London Clay, about 120–135 m above sea level, runs north from Chipping Barnet through Hadley Green towards Potters Bar; the ground falls west to the Mimmshall Brook streams (about 90–100 m) and east into the Monken Mead and Pymmes Brook valleys (down to about 70 m). Heights here are on a local datum: add 64 m to get an approximate height above sea level, so the lowest ground in the scene is about 5 m and the plateau about 65–72 m. The hills and valleys are smooth analytic shapes fitted to a coarse (250 m) grid of modern elevations, with an average error of about 5 m; they are not a survey, and the modern elevation model includes trees, buildings, the golf course and the 1823 cutting on Barnet Hill. The broad pattern of relief is thought to be much as it was in 1471, but no fine detail (ditches, banks, ponds, marshy patches) is modelled.

woodland.note: Low and steady by assumption. The written record points to little woodland on this side of South Mimms and to open pasture with scattered trees along the western edge of Enfield Chase, but the earliest map evidence is from 1594–1701, not the 15th century. The figure is illustrative, tree positions are generated, and no individual wood is mapped (an 'old wood' on the Old Fold estate is documented but unlocated).

views.name: Both lines and the road fork from the south
From Warwick's presumed side, looking south

locations/brentford/site.json.name: Brentford and the Thames ford
locations/brentford/site.json.subtitle: A river crossing west of London, 950 – 1100 CE, and the fight of 1016
locations/brentford/site.json.scopeNote: About 3 × 2.4 km around the meeting of the River Brent and the Thames, about 15 km west of London Bridge. This is a reconstruction of a landscape, not of a battle. In 1016 the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says only that King Edmund 'went over at Brentford', fought the Danish army and put it to flight, and that many of the English drowned through their own carelessness, having gone ahead of the army for plunder. Where the crossing was, which bank the fighting was on, how many fought and how the day went are not recorded, and no archaeology of the battle is known. No trace of a late Saxon settlement has been excavated at Brentford either. The river, banks and road are placed from the modern map and the county history; the houses, fields, figures and shaded areas are labelled guesses.

origin.note: A point on the low ground called Old England, between the lower Brent and the Thames (the site of the later Brentford Dock), chosen because the county history places the probable Thames ford here. Local coordinates are metres east (x) and south (z) of this point. It is a convenient centre for the model, not a located battlefield.

river.note: The centreline follows the modern Thames (OpenStreetMap) from Richmond to Mortlake; 'left' is the Middlesex bank (Isleworth, Syon, Brentford) and 'right' the Surrey bank (Kew). The course of the river about 1000 is not known in detail and is assumed to be close to the modern one. Half-widths are a modelling assumption: the modern channel is roughly 110 to 150 m wide in the Syon reach and about 240 m from bank to bank across the aits (estimated from the modern map, not surveyed), and it is drawn somewhat wider here to stand for an unembanked river with shelving gravel foreshores. No measured width or depth for the 11th century was found. A writer of 1695 is quoted as saying the Thames at Brentford was 'not above 3ft deep at low water'; that is 700 years later and is the only depth figure found. Whether and how strongly the reach was tidal about 1000 could not be established from the sources read (it is tidal today; Iron Age and Romano-British hut floors on the Brentford foreshore now lie below high-tide level, so the river has risen since). The model shows one water level. No bank is embanked in this period: the two keyframe sets are constant, and the right-bank value of 0.45 is a rendering choice that gives low, damp but mostly firm ground on the Kew side instead of open creeks; it does not represent a flood bank.

eyots.name: Gravel shoal at the later Lot's Ait
Gravel shoal at the later Brentford Ait (upper)
Gravel shoal at the later Brentford Ait (lower)

terrain.note: Relief is the engine's analytic approximation: ground rising gently from the Middlesex bank (the county history describes land 'rising gently from the Thames' to about 23 m some 2 km north), a low flat Surrey bank, and a shallow valley for the Brent with alluvium at its mouth. It is not a survey or borehole model, and the Syon bank west of the Brent is in reality lower and flatter than drawn. The Brent valley follows the modern river and canal line, which was straightened below Brentford Bridge between 1699 and 1760; its medieval meanders and its second mouth (the later dock stood on an island between the Thames and two mouths of the Brent) are not modelled. The three eyots stand at the positions of today's Lot's Ait and Brentford Ait. Those islands are later forms (osiers were grown on aits here by 1397; nothing earlier was found), so low gravel shoals standing just above the water, drawn long and narrow along the stream, are a guess at what was there about 1000; their size and height are not recorded. Brentford Ait lay in Surrey and Lot's Ait in Ealing parish, which hints at which bank each grew from.

woodland.note: Illustrative only. Domesday Book (1086) records woodland for 500 pigs at Isleworth and for 50 at Hanwell, so the manors still held woodland, but it does not say where; it is more likely to have been on the clay to the north than on the gravel by the river (an inference, not a source statement). The slight fall across the window is an assumption, and the percentages are not measurements.

locations/london/site.json.name: London and the Thames
locations/london/site.json.subtitle: One place within the land that became England, 4000 BCE – 1625 CE
locations/london/site.json.scopeNote: This is a single anchor location: about 4.8 × 3 km around the City of London, Southwark and Westminster. It is not a visualisation of England as a whole. Most of the country changed on different timetables.

origin.note: North end of medieval London Bridge (near St Magnus the Martyr). Local coordinates are metres east (x) and south (z) of this point.

river.note: The 1625 bank lines are approximated from the modern river with the Victorian embankments removed. Excavated Roman quays (tree-ring dates 52, 63, c. 70, 102 CE and on to the mid 3rd century) advanced the north bank by roughly 35 m; the Roman riverside wall on the Thames Street line then stayed the landward limit, and the remaining ground was won piecemeal between about 1000 and 1500. No verified figure was found for the medieval advance, so the roughly 110 m total and its timing are modelling assumptions. The prehistoric and Roman south bank is modelled as tidal marsh with channels and gravel eyots (the reach was tidal by the Middle to Late Bronze Age); channel positions are illustrative, not mapped.

terrain.note: Relief is an analytic approximation (two low gravel hills divided by the Walbrook, the Fleet valley to the west, a low marshy south bank) at true vertical scale. It is not derived from a survey or borehole model.

woodland.note: Illustrative trend only: closed woodland in the early Neolithic, progressive clearance from the Bronze Age, a largely open farmed landscape by the late Iron Age, some regeneration after the Roman period. The percentages are not measurements.

district.name: London Bridge bridgehead
district.note: The realism benchmark: the river crossing and both bridgeheads, modelled in more detail than the rest of the scene. Everything outside this rectangle is a schematic overview.

national/site.json.name: England and Wales
national/site.json.subtitle: The land that became England and Wales, 4000 BCE – 1625 CE
national/site.json.scopeNote: This map shows the land that became England and Wales. For most of the period neither existed: 'England' as a single kingdom dates only from the 10th century (Aethelstan, 927), and Wales was a land of separate kingdoms until the conquest of 1282-3. Earlier names, peoples and borders are shown as they stood at each date; borders were zones rather than lines, and the outlines drawn are indicative.

woodland.note: Only two points are anchored. Rackham estimated that half of England had been cleared by about 500 BCE, and that woodland and wood-pasture covered about 15% of the land recorded in Domesday Book (1086); Domesday omits the far north, and the average hides big regional differences. For 1350 secondary accounts of Rackham give between about 6% and 10%; 8% is used. Everything else is interpolation: the early Neolithic 'wildwood' was not a closed canopy everywhere and 75% is a convention; Roman-period and post-Roman values (including a modest regrowth after 400) are guesses; the 1625 figure assumes little net change after the Black Death. The trend is for England; Wales was more wooded at most dates.

locations/stonehenge/site.json.name: Stonehenge and its landscape
locations/stonehenge/site.json.subtitle: From the first earthworks to the Jacobean antiquaries, 4000 BCE to 1625 CE
locations/stonehenge/site.json.scopeNote: A 6.4 by 5 km piece of the Stonehenge World Heritage landscape, from 4000 BCE to 1625 CE, with the sarsen circle at the origin. Two levels of detail: the whole landscape is a schematic overview (barrows, cursus, henges, hillfort and town are placed from mapped outlines and published dates, but their form is generic), while the 'district' round the stones (about 800 by 650 m) has stone-by-stone megaliths from a catalogue, the ditch and bank, the Aubrey Holes, the first stretch of the Avenue and the Heel Stone. No feature is shown before its date, and where a date is a range or a model the landmark says so. The state of the stones before the first drawings (de Heere, 1570s) is mostly undated: which stones stood, leant or lay in 1625 is inferred, not recorded. Height comes from a modern LIDAR surface with modern works removed, with the ditch and Avenue ditches cut back in on their dates. Ground cover, trees and house positions are reconstruction. The solstice episodes mark the sunrise and sunset directions with overlay lines and discs; the scene's one fixed sun is not moved to the solstice. Amesbury's outline and the Durrington settlement area are schematic envelopes, not surveyed boundaries.

origin.note: FINAL. Centre of the sarsen circle to within ~3 m (geography research: circle fitted to OSM-mapped uprights 51.178859, -1.826208; EH 2010 survey NGR SU 12244219; the stone catalogue's fitted centre 51.178868, -1.8261962). Megalith landmarks are anchored at the catalogue's fitted centre. Local x = metres east, z = metres south.

hills.name: King Barrow Ridge (central: New King Barrows; the Avenue climbs it)
Normanton Down ridge (Bush Barrow and the Normanton Down barrows)
North-west upland (beyond the west end of the Greater Cursus / Lesser Cursus)
Larkhill rise (high ground north of Larkhill)
High ground north-west of Durrington Walls
Vespasian's Camp spur (hill-fort promontory above the Avon)
Stonehenge Down knoll (flattens the ground under the stones)

valleys.name: River Avon valley (broad flood-plain and valley flanks)
River Avon channel and steep valley sides (Vespasian's Camp, Amesbury)
Stonehenge Bottom (dry valley east of the stones; the Avenue crosses it)
Wilsford dry valley (south-west of Normanton Down)
Dry valley between King Barrow Ridge and Durrington

terrain.note: Heights are metres above a local datum of Ordnance Datum minus 62 m (stones about 39.5, the Avon floor about 0 to 2: the engine clamps land at 2 m). Analytic fallback: a least-squares fit of the engine's own terrain formula (base + tilt + 12 gaussian hills - 6 valleys) to 1,302 EU-DEM 25 m samples, with the 2 m of datum difference removed from the base (hills and valleys are relative). Error against the DEM: RMS 4.5 m over the whole area (3.1 m, max 6.9 m, within 500 m of the stones); the two DEMs themselves disagree by RMS 2.6 m. It is a broad-shape model, not a survey. Where terrain-lidar.json is present the Environment Agency 1 m bare-earth LIDAR (datum offset 62) replaces this relief and only the dated ditches below are cut into it. The Stonehenge ditch is a closed 72-point ring of radius 53 m (a ditch centreline taken from the monument's c. 110 m overall diameter; the ditch width and profile are not recorded in the sources read), 1.5 m deep, dug about 3000 to 2900 BCE (the model switches it on in 3001 to 2995 BCE). Its silting (0.35 filled by 2400 BCE, 0.6 by 1500 BCE, 0.8 by 1625 CE) is MODELLED, not measured: the real ditch was also re-cut (Stage 3) and its later fill is not dated here. The two Avenue ditches (23 m apart, from the OpenStreetMap-mapped centreline) are dug 2400 to 2380 BCE in the model and 70% silted by 1625: the Avenue's date is 2430 to 2200 BCE (Darvill 2012) or 2345 to 2200 BCE (English Heritage antler dates), and the ditches were later ploughed nearly flat, so the depth shown is a gentle stand-in for ditches about 2 m deep when new.

woodland.note: ESTIMATE, not measured. The values are my estimate of the fraction of the ground within about 3 km under woodland or scrub (the engine uses it as the share of possible tree sites that stand), from qualitative statements only: partly open woodland with clearings around 4000 BCE (Blick Mead pollen and DNA), open chalk grassland by 3500 BCE (snail evidence at the Cursus), stable grassland on thin soils about 3000 BCE, patches of woodland near Durrington Walls and alder-hazel carr on the Avon floodplain in the 3rd millennium, and clearance by about 800 to 500 BCE. The rise to 0.06 around 500 CE (post-Roman scrub) is speculative and unsourced; 1000 and 1625 are estimates. Where the trees stand is generated, not mapped. There are no hedgerow trees: the downland was open until enclosure.

district.name: The stones
district.note: Detailed round the monument: stone-by-stone megaliths from the stone catalogue (sarsen circle and lintels, trilithons, bluestone settings, Altar Stone, Station Stones, Slaughter Stone, Heel Stone), the ditch and bank, the Aubrey Holes and the first straight stretch of the Avenue. Positions and sizes come from surveyed plans and the catalogue; the form of timber structures, the original height of the bank and the state of each stone in 1625 are inferred. Everything outside this box, including the barrows, the Cursus, Durrington Walls and Amesbury, is schematic.

notes: GRID: present-day elevation, land and sea floor. Land is the Copernicus DEM GLO-90 (a surface model: it includes buildings and tree canopy, so towns and woods read a few metres high) area-averaged to this grid; sea floor is the GEBCO_2025 Grid (15 arc-seconds). Cells are about 300 m east-west by 480 m north-south, so sharp summits read low (Snowdon's cell is about 900-970 m against a true 1085 m). Vertical datums differ slightly (EGM2008 geoid for land, mean sea level for sea floor); treat anything within about 2 m of zero as uncertain. Depths are clamped at -300 m (only Beaufort's Dyke comes close).

DECODING: elevation = (R*256 + G)*0.1 - 300. Read the PNG as raw bytes with no colour-space conversion and decode to a float array before any interpolation; filtering the R and G bytes separately gives garbage where G wraps (every 25.6 m).

SEA-LEVEL CURVE: one relative sea-level curve (mean sea level, 0 = present) for the Thames / Fenland / Hampshire-Sussex-Kent region, drawn through the medians of the validated sea-level index points in the Shennan, Bradley & Edwards (2018) database for those regions: about -6 m at 4000 BCE, rising at a slowing rate to about -1.6 m in the Roman period. Confidence: medium. The scatter of individual index points is +/-1.5 to 2 m before 1000 BCE and about +/-1 m after, partly because buried peat compacts (which makes old shorelines look too low; the Thames and Kent points for the last 2500 years sit 1.5-3 m below this curve mainly for that reason). After 1000 CE there are very few index points; the last three keyframes are an interpolation to zero, not measurements.

HOW WRONG THE CURVE IS ELSEWHERE: relative sea level differs by region because the land is still adjusting to the loss of the last ice sheet (south sinking, north rising). Index-point medians for about 4000 BCE: Devon and Cornwall about -8 m (curve too high by 2 m); Bristol Channel / Somerset about -6 m (close); Lincolnshire Marshes and Norfolk -6 to -7 m (close); Humber -4 to -5 m; Tees about -3 m; mid Wales about -3.5 m; Mersey and Lancashire about -2 m; Morecambe Bay and Cumbria -0.5 m to 0; Northumberland about +1.5 m and the Solway +2 to +4 m (sea level there was HIGHER than today and has fallen since). So north of a line roughly from the Mersey to the Tees this curve drowns too little or shows the wrong sign; apply it at full strength only south of about 53.5 N.

TIDES: the values are mean sea level. The line people saw as the coast was high water, 2-3.5 m above mean level on most of these coasts (more in the Bristol Channel), and tidal range itself has changed: in the Thames at London the tidal limit and high-water level rose markedly between the Roman period and today as the river was embanked.

A PRESENT-DAY GRID CANNOT SHOW PEAT GROWTH, SILTING OR EROSION. Lowering the sea on today's surface reproduces drowned valleys and offshore shallows, but not land that has since been built up (alluvium, peat, shingle, dunes), cut away (soft cliffs) or lowered (drained, shrunken peat). The cases below matter at national scale and need masks or hand corrections.

FENS (about 3,900 sq km around the Wash): until drained they were peat fen, meres and tidal salt-marsh with islands (Ely, March, Whittlesey), settled only on the silt 'Townlands' and the islands. Large-scale drainage began in the 1630s and continued in the 1650s, i.e. after this timeline ends, so for the whole period 4000 BCE-1625 CE the Fens should be drawn as wetland, grading from forested lowland being inundated in the 4th-3rd millennia BCE to its greatest marine extent in the Iron Age. The grid will mislead: drained peat has shrunk and wasted by several metres, so much of the southern Fens now lies below 0 m (Holme Fen about -2.75 m, the lowest land in Britain) and a simple 'below sea level = water' rule floods it as open sea even at present sea level, while the pre-drainage surface was actually a few metres higher and was marsh, not sea.

SOMERSET LEVELS (about 650 sq km): marsh with winter freshwater floods and occasional sea floods; the Sweet Track (3800s BCE) and the Iron Age Glastonbury lake village were built in it. Medieval abbeys (Glastonbury, Athelney, Muchelney) embanked and drained parts in the 13th century, but by 1500 only about 20,000 of 70,000 floodable acres were reclaimed and about 30,500 acres were still undrained in 1638; the 1607 Bristol Channel flood covered about 500 sq km. Today's surface is 3-6 m above datum and lies below high spring tides behind sea walls, so the grid shows it as dry at every keyframe; draw it as wetland throughout.

HUMBERHEAD LEVELS, HULL VALLEY AND HOLDERNESS MERES, LANCASHIRE MOSSES, ROMNEY AND PEVENSEY LEVELS: the same applies on a smaller scale. All were fen, mere or salt-marsh for most or all of the period and were drained mainly in the 17th-19th centuries.

ROMNEY MARSH: in prehistory a shallow bay and lagoon behind a shingle barrier; reclaimed piecemeal ('innings') from the early Middle Ages, much of Walland and Denge marshes by the 14th century. The 13th-century storms (especially 1287) destroyed Old Winchelsea, blocked New Romney's harbour and turned the River Rother west to Rye. Dungeness is a shingle foreland that has grown throughout the period and is still growing; its present shape is wrong for every earlier date.

WANTSUM CHANNEL: Thanet was an island, separated from Kent by a tidal strait reported as up to about 3 km wide, with the Roman forts of Reculver and Richborough at its two mouths. It silted heavily in the 12th-13th centuries and was dry apart from a central drain by the 16th century. The channel floor is now 1-5 m above datum (alluvium), so the grid never reopens it; it needs a mask for dates before about 1500.

THE WASH AND OTHER ESTUARIES: the Wash extended much further inland (see Fens); medieval and later sea banks have moved its shore seaward by several km. The Dee, Ribble, Humber and Thames estuaries and Poole/Chichester harbours have likewise been narrowed by silting and embanking; Chester, Sandwich, Rye, Winchelsea and others were working sea ports that are now inland.

ERODING COASTS: soft cliffs have retreated, so past coasts lay SEAWARD of today's, which lowering the sea on this grid only approximates. Holderness (boulder clay) retreats about 1.5-1.8 m a year, about 5 km since Roman times, with at least 23 lost towns and villages; Ravenser Odd, a borough on a sandbank at the Humber mouth (chartered 1299, over 100 houses), was abandoned after the floods of 1356-57 and destroyed by the storm of January 1362. On the Suffolk coast Dunwich, a major port with about 3,000 people in 1086, was wrecked in stages from the surges of 1286-87 through 1328, 1347 and 1362, its decline driven as much by the river mouth shifting north as by cliff loss. At about 300 m per pixel these losses are 1-15 pixels wide.

DOGGERLAND: already drowned. Britain was cut off from the continent around 6500 BCE; Dogger Bank survived as an island until at least about 5000 BCE. At 4000 BCE (-6 m) the bank's crest (about -15 to -20 m today) was 10 m or more under water, so no North Sea land should be drawn; the grid agrees. Only nearshore shoals and a fringe of coastal lowland (the outer Wash, the Thames estuary flats, Bridgwater and Morecambe bays) emerge at -6 m: about 2.6% of the grid's cells lie between -6 and 0 m.
RIVERS AND LAKES: tidal rivers that Copernicus flattens to 0 m (Thames tideway, Severn, Humber) are encoded as shallow water (at most -0.5 m); inland lakes carry their surface level, not their bed.
